---
title: "6. Relocating Greatness"
---

Everything the tradition most wants to say about God is active: God knows, acts, creates, sustains, answers, and loves. Everything it wants God to *be* is withdrawn from the conditions those acts require — outside time, outside space, made of nothing.

This chapter holds those two claims against each other, one attribute at a time. Can a subject placed beyond Time, Space, and Substance still bear what the tradition needs it to bear? The chapter tests that question attribute by attribute, distinguishing a contradiction from a relocation, an explanatory cost, and a residual metaphysical burden. What becomes of the greatness the tradition reached for is the question the title names.

The classical theist tradition credited God with certain structures: identity, necessity, eternity, presence, awareness, knowledge, power, agency, sovereignty, relation, description, love. Each was named at its perfect form (omniscience, omnipotence, immutable knowledge, *creatio ex nihilo*, simplicity, perfect love, ineffable revelation) and held to be the elevated form of what creatures merely participate in.

This chapter reverses the placement. The reversal is structural, attribute by attribute. Awareness is real, but it requires an inside, and the conditions for an inside live in Nature, not in ∅. Agency is real, but it requires transition, and transition requires Time. Knowledge is real, but it requires a position from which to hold a cognitive state. Necessity, eternity, presence, power, identity, sovereignty, relation, description: the same in each case. The structures the tradition tried to give God *are* the structures Nature necessarily instantiates.

The chapter focuses on the Christian-Scholastic synthesis because that is where the doctrinal bundle (simplicity, atemporality, aseity, *creatio ex nihilo*, meticulous providence) is most fully assembled and most demanding to defend. The pressures collected here are not, however, in-house Christian difficulties. The same structural difficulty arises wherever the same conceptual moves are made: Maimonides's negative theology in the *Guide for the Perplexed* [@maimonides1190; @seeskin2000; @stern2013], Avicenna's distinction between necessary and possible existence in the *Kitab al-Shifa* [@avicenna1020; @mcginnis2010; @adamson2013], Al-Ghazali's occasionalist account of causation in the *Incoherence of the Philosophers* [@alGhazali1095; @frank1992; @griffel2009], and the parallel Vedantic identification of Brahman as the unconditioned ground of conditioning [@shankara800; @deutsch1969]. The Christian tradition is the one this chapter engages in detail. The inversion's reach is the family of doctrines that places the structural conditions of T, S, and Φ inside a being defined as standing outside them.

The chapter engages three families of theistic position.

*The classical position.* God is atemporal, aspatial, immaterial, simple, *actus purus*, immutable, impassible, and the necessary ground of created reality. Aseity is preserved as a feature of the divine being. Substantive modal predication applies to God: God necessarily exists, necessarily knows, necessarily loves. The position is best represented in the Christian-Scholastic synthesis (Aquinas, Anselm, Boethius) and its contemporary defenders (Dolezal, Feser, Stump, Leftow on selected points).

The classical position is the chapter's primary target. Two further commitments depart from it, each defined by a different response to the no-way-possible argument ([§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10)):

*Commitment A.* God grounds modal structure rather than fitting within it. The substantive predication *is possible* does not apply to God, since God is proposed as the source of possibility rather than one of its instances. Theistic activism [@morrisMenzel1986; @pruss2011; @leftow2012] is the most developed version; presuppositionalism [@vanTil1955; @bahnsen1998] and Cartesian voluntarism [@descartes1630; @frankfurt1977] are variants. The position trades the no-way-possible argument ([§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10)) for the task of supplying a determinate grounding relation and explaining what remains of *necessarily exists* once substantive modal predication has been refused. Sections [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10), [§5.1.8](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-8), and [§5.1.10](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-10) show that no candidate already specified within the modal domain can ground that domain from outside; an essence-prior or transcendent ground remains a further metaphysical posit whose credentials this chapter tests through its active predicates.

*Commitment B (modest theism).* God can do all possible things but does not source possibility itself; possibility is external. Simplicity, *actus purus*, and immutability are dropped or weakened, so that God is a possibility-respecting agent rather than the ground of modal structure. Process theology [@hartshorne1948; @cobbGriffin1976; @suchocki1988; @oord2015], open theism [@pinnock1994; @hasker1989], and the temporal-theism wing [@wolterstorff1975; @padgett1992; @mullins2016; @craig2001 on selected points] sit in this region. Process theology's dipolar panentheism is the structurally most ambitious member of this group, and it is not merely classical theism with attributes subtracted: Hartshorne's God pairs an abstract pole that is necessary and immutable with a concrete pole that actualizes contingently. That reframing is engaged on its own terms rather than only as a member of Commitment B: the abstract/concrete pole-relation is pressed at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) (Q5, Q8) and closed at [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3), where the directed crossing between the poles is shown to run within T, S, and Φ. The position survives the no-way-possible argument by surrendering the doctrinal claim that God has no alternative way to be. Its consequence is that any restriction on divine nature carves a proper subset out of the space of possibilities (divine power is constrained at the level of *which* possibilities God can do), and this consequence runs as the moral-domain instance at [§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1).

Each subsequent transfer specifies which position it targets. Some run against all three; some against Commitment A only; some against Commitment B only. The chapter does not assume one and ignore the others. All three are positions on a personal God. The non-personal alternative (a Neoplatonic One from which the modal structure emanates, neither a ground that stands over it nor an instance that stands within it) is engaged separately, at [§5.3.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-2) and again at [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2).

Each transfer tests a bilateral pressure. The chapter asks whether a predicate can apply to a wholly structureless subject and whether a structural relation can reach a subject defined outside every relation. Where a doctrine removes every differentiating feature and every determinate relation, the structural account diagnoses an ∅-like failure of specification. Where it retains active predicates or real relations, it reinstates at least the relevant structural roles. The bilateral form clarifies the pressure; it does not substitute for a separate argument about every possible essence-prior or apophatic ground.

The attribute-by-attribute form can be misread as a cumulative case in which twenty-three independent arguments each add an increment. It is not that: the transfers are applications of two master results. The first is the simplicity/differentiation dilemma developed at [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1): strict simplicity must explain how one undifferentiated reality grounds differentiated identity and predication. Every *static* attribute (simple, necessary, eternal, holy, perfect) therefore carries a determinate-content burden; it does not follow merely from predicative plurality that God has spatial parts. This is why [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) is both the first transfer and the hinge of the rest: once simplicity no longer holds the attributes together as a single act, they come apart and can be taken one at a time. The dilemma is itself an application of the Way–Possibility Convertibility ([§3.2](convergence.html#sec-3-2)), pressed to its theological edge at [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1): to be anything at all is to be some way rather than another, and a way decomposes without remainder into direction (T), difference (S), and link (Φ). The second master result is the directed-relation analysis ([§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3)): to ground, donate, sustain, or know requires determinate relata, asymmetric order, and a bearer of the relation. These are thin role-level requirements. Whether they entail metric Space, temporal succession, or physical Substance must be argued in each active-attribute case rather than assumed by the metaphor of crossing. Read from the agent's side, the directed-crossing result takes a plainer form. Every active predicate names a capacity (to begin, sustain, or interact) and its exercise requires determinate relational content. Thomistic pure actuality forecloses passive potency, not active power as such. The chapter must therefore press the relation between an unchanged fully actual cause and contingent effects, rather than infer that pure act has no causal capacity. Several attributes fall to both. The convergence is real but not additive: the chapter exhibits two results across twenty-three predicates, not twenty-three proofs of twenty-three things. The concentration is stated explicitly at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10), which shows that the chapter's theorem of record (the Trilemma Closure) is independent of it and stands whatever becomes of the individual reductions.

That concentration locates the one place an opponent can press. Both master results share a central pressure point. The escape from the first is that *way*-talk of God is merely analogical or apophatic, or that perfections are present only by eminent containment; the escape from the second is that the divine relation is real on the creature's side but merely conceptual on God's. The chapter argues that a terminus bearing no feature that discriminates it from ∅ faces an ∅-like specification problem ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7); [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)). Against an opponent who grants real divine predicates and relations, the structural burden bites directly. Against an apophatic, analogical, or mixed-relation exit, the residual issue is whether the proposed semantics or metaphysics can make those predicates and relations determinate without reintroducing the role-level structure. The honest claim is not that every exit has already been contradicted, but that the discernibility and grounding burden remains active at the chapter's single hinge.

The twenty-three transfers sort by which master result carries them. On the static side, where the simplicity/differentiation dilemma does the work, four groups: *constitution* (simplicity, unity, infinity, perfection), *aseity and modal standing* (necessity, eternity, immutability, impassibility), *cognition* (awareness, knowledge), and *intrinsic value* (holiness, beatitude). On the active side, where the directed-crossing analysis closes them, three groups: *agency* (power, causality, interaction, sovereignty), *reach and contact* (presence, relatability, describability, revelation), and *moral act* (benevolence, righteousness). Life stands between the two, billed as a constitutive perfection but inverting as the self-activity of Substance in time, so that it lands among the active attributes by its own argument. One static-type predicate crosses the same seam: impassibility is static in type yet does its work on the active arm, the lone predicate whose inversion runs in the 'nature cannot act on God' direction rather than the 'God cannot have the structure' direction. These two crossings, life and impassibility, are distinct from the [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) hinge: simplicity hinges the chapter by releasing the attributes to be taken one at a time, whereas life and impassibility mark where the two master results meet.

What governs the transfers is Modal Pressure ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)), the necessity-propagation rule introduced earlier in the argument. The necessity-propagation form has Anselmian antecedents: Hartshorne [@hartshorne1965] recovers the modal-ontological structure; Plantinga [@plantinga1974b] formalizes it in S5. Once necessity is admitted anywhere in a classical attribute (necessary existence, necessary creation, necessary knowledge, necessary goodness), Modal Pressure requires every real entailment of that attribute to be treated with the same modal seriousness. The interlocutor who posits a necessary creator cannot stop the inference at necessary creation but contingent extension, or at necessary extension but contingent laws, or at any intermediate position the tradition has reached for. Modal Pressure marks that stopping point as ad hoc unless the entailment itself is denied. It follows the attribute's actual commitments, and what those commitments require, as Chapter 2 established, is T, S, and Φ. The same engine presses the book to mark its own stopping point rather than help itself to one: the structural frame T∧S∧Φ is necessary, while the particular modes that fill it (this cosmos, these constants) remain contingent, the type necessary and the token not. That restricted-PSR stopping point, and the asymmetry it rests on, are taken up directly at [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7). The transfers that follow do not refute the attributes from outside. They trace each attribute to the structural conditions it requires. *The modal-ontological argument is handled directly at [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7), where Modal Pressure's necessity-propagation structure meets Plantinga's.*

Each transfer mirrors a section of Chapter 8. What Chapter 6 takes off the wrong subject, Chapter 8 finds inside the right one. The book reads the same structure twice: Chapter 6 in the predicates the tradition assigns to God, Chapter 8 in the self-modeling life that actually bears them.

The chapter arrives at a disciplined coordinate. A God defined within possibility is subject to the structural and grounding conditions the chapter identifies. A God placed beyond possibility must supply a metaphysics of how its predicates and relations are determinately contentful without belonging to the modal domain. The chapter argues that strict classical formulations face an ∅-like specification problem when every differentiating feature and active relation is withdrawn; it does not simply identify every doctrine of *actus purus* with ∅ by stipulation. The active and predicative work the doctrine retains is where the structural burden lands.

## 6.1 Greatness {#sec-6-1}

Start where the theist starts, and grant the whole construction before pressing it. Perfect-being theology builds God by taking each property that makes a thing great (knowledge, power, goodness, presence, life) and pressing it to its ceiling: not much knowledge but *all* of it, not great power but power over everything, not merely good but without defect. God, on this measure, is that than which no greater can be conceived (Anselm, *Proslogion* [@anselm1078, II]), every great-making property held to the maximal degree at once, the maxima taken to compose into a single being who has them all together and has them of necessity. That is the measure the tradition sets, in its own terms, and this chapter takes it exactly as given and runs it.

The decisive move, made before any single attribute is named, is to treat these maxima as a *starting ground*: possessed complete and from the outset, as pure actuality, with nothing in the being left unrealized. A maximum with no unrealized passive potency is the classical doctrine of pure actuality, not nothing by definition. Knowledge, power, and goodness are properties or capacities whose exercises have determinate content. The pressure is whether one immutable act can ground contingent, differentiated knowing and action — not whether the grammar of the predicates already refutes the doctrine.

This is the inversion the book is named for, taken at its root. The tradition seeks greatness by *subtracting* the conditions of being (atemporal, aspatial, immaterial) and arrives at ∅ ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)); the same maximization run the other way, toward the fullest instantiation of those conditions rather than their negation, is what the political argument later develops and crystallizes as the Maximal Greatness result (§9). What the tradition placed in the evacuation of structure, this book relocates in its plenitude. Greatness so relocated changes category: it is not a completed actuality (possessed whole at the start or reached as a final state) but a self-maintaining standing, held open only in its own exercise, and so achievable, losable, and deepenable rather than finished; what a subsistence does at its fullest reach, not a perfection it is awarded.

::: {.definition}
**Greatness** · *Definition*

The gradable dimension along which any subsistence stands: the great-making properties (knowledge, power, goodness, presence, life) held to a degree, admitting of more and less, so that one subsistence may stand higher on a given property than another. Stated neutrally, the maxima are *maximum possible* degrees, the most of a property that could actually be held, whether by a single individual or by a subsistent collective (there is a most knowledge that humankind could come to hold), not stipulated absolutes. Its ceiling, where every property stands at the maximal degree compatible with the rest, is what the tradition calls *maximal greatness*, developed in Plantinga's modal form at [§5.1.7](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-7) (maximal excellence in every possible world).


:::

The classical God is defined by three denials: outside time, outside space, not made of anything. The structural difficulty arises when such a God is also said to act, be present, affect the world, know, create, or sustain. Those predicates require determinate relations and therefore at least the role-level floor of directed order, relational non-identity, and real bearing. The chapter does not infer creaturely clock-time, metric extension, or material composition merely from these roles; it asks how a classical account makes its active predicates intelligible while withdrawing the roles they appear to require.

To act at one moment rather than another is to be in Time. To be present here rather than there is to be in Space. To affect the physical world is to exercise Substance. The theist who describes God as responding to prayer, directing influence, knowing what is currently the case, or creating at a moment has already committed to a God that instantiates the structural roles, not because the argument forces this conclusion from outside but because the theist's own descriptions of divine activity presuppose it from within.

The classical God is defined by the negation of creaturely temporal succession, spatial extension, and material composition. Atemporality negates Time, and with it Asymmetry, Transitivity, and Directionality; strip one and the others collapse with it. Aspatial existence negates Space, and with it Extension, Exclusivity, and Traversability. Immateriality negates Substance, and with it Distinctness, Substantiality, and Persistence. Classical theologians treat these as denials of creaturely modes, not necessarily as denials of every thin ordering, differentiation, or bearing role. The argument shows where positive divine predicates reintroduce such roles rather than defining that conclusion into the negative attributes. By the convergence / co-instantiation result ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)), lacking any one entails lacking all three; by the Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)), the instantiation of T, S, and Φ is analytically equivalent to the possibility of Change. A being instantiating none of the roles is equivalent to ∅ ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)): not a state in which nothing happens but not a coherent state at all.

::: {.theorem}
**Supernatural Preclusion** · **T8** · *Theorem 8 — preview; stated and proved at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10)*

The classical theist's atemporal, aspatial, immaterial God — the being defined by the joint absence of T, S, and Φ — faces a specification burden. If the doctrine removes every differentiating feature and every determinate relation while retaining active divine predicates, the result is ∅-like: the predicates no longer state what they need to state. If it retains determinate grounding, cognition, or action relations, it reinstates the role-level structure it sought to deny. This section fixes the scope of the Trilemma Closure at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10): the theorem tests classical theism as a package of aseity, active predicates, and structural withdrawal across fundamental ontologies; it does not treat an unarticulated essence-prior posit as refuted merely by naming it. ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5), [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), [§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6); statement and proof [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10))


:::

The structural diagnosis that drives the result attaches not at the level of *way* simpliciter but at the level of *possible*. The classical commitments are simplicity, *actus purus* (pure actuality: a being with no unrealized potential, nothing in it waiting to be made actual), and immutability. They converge on a single doctrinal claim: God has no alternative way to be; and a being with no alternative way to be is not a possible modal subject. The formal demonstration is carried at the chapter's close, where two lines reach ¬◇(classical theism intact): the no-way-possible argument takes the quickest road, on the assumption that God is a modal subject, and the Trilemma Closure at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) (No Exit) reaches the same verdict without that assumption, by exhausting the theist's three responses. The present section states the result and fixes the framework-invariance and embedded-deity scope that closure draws on.

This is the chapter's foundational move at the level of the conjunction. What runs next, one attribute at a time, is the inversion at the level of the predicate. Take any classical attribute (creation, will, goodness, providence, revelation) and unpack what the predicate requires. A temporal creative episode requires succession; a directed reaching relation requires distinct terms; knowing requires a knower and determinate content. Classical accounts may construe creation and knowledge as one timeless act, leaving a relation and contingency burden rather than conceding succession in God. Each unpacking points back at Nature. The predicates are not waiting for the classical definition to land on them. They already contain the structure the classical definition denies. The inversion is internal to each attribute: the word the tradition reached for to say something contentful about God is already the word Nature permits.

The inversion runs farthest at the predicate that does not merely operate within the structure but purports to install it. *Create* requires a succession across which creation occurs and, before that, requires that whatever does the creating already instance the structure the creating is supposed to install. Whatever brings about possibility must already be possible, and what is already possible is already inside the structure that makes possibility a fact. It is not possible to create possibility. The constraint binds at two layers: at the level of the act, the act would have to perform what it claims to produce; at the level of the target, possibility is necessary ([§3.2.5](convergence.html#sec-3-2-5); *Intermediate Necessity*, [§2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-3)), and what is necessary cannot have been contingent on a maker. Neither line can be repaired without sacrificing the other (see [§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3), where the constraint is registered against any candidate ground for the roles).

The theist who maintains the classical attributes alongside divine action faces a serious coherence burden: the account must explain how an immutable, non-spatial, immaterial subject bears determinate causal relations without importing creaturely modes. That is not yet a contradiction until the proposed analogical or timeless account is assessed. The apologetic that most relies on divine action (miracles, revelation, answered prayer, creation) is the apologetic that puts the classical attributes it invokes under the most direct strain. Every miracle is an event in Time, Space, and Substance. The classical attributes and the active God of religious practice stand in a well-known tension that requires a worked account of timeless action, relation, and responsive practice [@mullins2016].

*Framework invariance.* The preclusion holds across every fundamental ontology on offer, not naturalism alone.

Under physicalism, the structural roles are instantiated by physical fields and spacetime geometry; a being defined by the negation of physical structure is defined by the negation of what it was supposed to create.

Under idealism, the fundamental medium is mental, and the roles survive the relocation intact: any experience that unfolds requires succession (T), any experience that differentiates requires extension (S), and any experience that persists requires a substrate of continuity (Φ). Berkeley's God must perceive, and perception is a T/S/Φ event; the idealist renames Nature without eliminating the roles.

Under the Kantian transcendental framework, Time and Space are forms of intuition any cognitive act presupposes, and Strawson's reconstruction (*The Bounds of Sense* [@strawson1966]; engaged in the Cartesian / transcendental change-witness treatment at [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)) establishes that succession, coexistence, and persistence are conditions of self-conscious experience. The modal argument extends the Kant–Strawson line from the conditions of any possible experience to the conditions of any possible ground of experience.

Under panpsychism, the roles are instantiated twice (once in the physical exterior, once in the experiential interior) since proto-experiential combination requires a relational manifold, a succession, and a persistence medium all over again. The preclusion is not relaxed under the richer ontology. It is doubled.

Under ontic structural realism [@ladymanRoss2007], structure is fundamental and what physicalism treats as bearers are nodes in the structural relations; the relocation does not remove the roles, since any structure must be individuable from another (S), must persist as the relation it is (Φ), and admits succession wherever it is dynamic (T); and where the structure is purely static, the static structure just is Nature under another name. This is where the henological worry presses hardest: if the roles are three, what makes them one ground rather than three coordinate relations — and must their unity not derive from a prior unity, the One beyond being from which structure emanates? The triad needs no such source, because it is not an aggregate. By the Triconditional Identity ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)) Time, Space, and Substance are one Nature read three ways, not three ingredients awaiting an external unifier, so the unity a henological One is summoned to supply is already internal to the structural ground; and that One, placed beyond being and so beyond T, S, and Φ, is by the Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)) equivalent to ∅ ([§2.7.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-7-1)) and grounds nothing. The unity-priority reading is engaged on its own terms as a rival ultimate at [§5.3.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-2).

Under Russellian monism, the intrinsic categorical base of physical structure is phenomenal; the dual aspect specifies the first-person perspective on T, S, and Φ rather than escaping them.

Under analytic idealism (Kastrup, *The Idea of the World* [@kastrup2019]), the cosmic mental field whose dissociated alters constitute individual minds is itself structured: dissociation requires distinguishable contents (S), persistence of the field across the dissociations (Φ), and temporal differentiation between the alters' arising and dissolution (T). The relocation does not eliminate the roles; it specifies them at the cosmic-mental level rather than the physical level.

Each framework locates T, S, and Φ in its own register. None of these frameworks removes the structural difficulty for the classical God.

*The embedded-deity concession.* The argument does not rule out every conceivable theology. Process theism, open theism, and some forms of panentheism posit a temporally embedded deity with genuine causal power operating within the structure; such a being instantiates T, S, and Φ and therefore does not collapse into ∅. Hartshorne's dipolar theism warrants naming as a distinct sub-position within this family: God's abstract pole (the necessary, eternal, essential nature) is held to be atemporal and immutable, while the concrete pole (God's actual, contingent states of experience and response) is held to be temporal, cumulative, and genuinely affected by creaturely events (*The Divine Relativity* [@hartshorne1948]; *Man's Vision of God* [@hartshorne1941]). The abstract/concrete bifurcation is designed precisely to retain classical honors at the level of essence while accepting temporal embedding at the level of actuality. Whether a single subject can coherently sustain both poles under the structural constraints the chapter develops (and in particular whether the abstract pole, if genuinely atemporal and immutable, can stand in the act-relations the concrete pole requires) is the live question the relevant attribute sections (§[§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), 6.3.2, 6.3.3, 6.3.4, 6.7.2, 6.7.4, 6.9.1) carry. What the argument does establish is that any such being incurs an aseity burden: its existing *from itself*, dependent on nothing outside itself for its being (Latin *a se*, 'from itself'); in classical theism the root divine attribute, the source of God's independence and necessity.

::: {.corollary}
**Aseity Forfeiture** · **R15** · *Result of T5*

Any being that instantiates temporal, relational, and active roles escapes the ∅-like specification problem but incurs an aseity burden. A being embedded in structural conditions cannot straightforwardly be their independent ground; it must either be a configuration within Nature or articulate a revised account of aseity and dependence. The chapter records that cost rather than treating every revised theology as contradictory. An embedded deity cannot simply retain the classical project's claim to ground T, S, and Φ while depending on the roles required for its own action. Follows from the Triconditional Identity ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)) and the structural analysis developed across this chapter.


:::

Structure is ontologically prior to any being embedded within it, not temporally prior in the sense of preceding it in a sequence, but constitutively prior in the sense that it is the precondition of the embedded being's existence rather than the reverse.

If God is real, God is part of Reality; if God is part of Reality, God is inside structure, and a God redefined to instantiate the structural conditions is not the classical target but a configuration within Nature, subject to the same structural constraints as any other. The Spinozist or panentheist relabeling (the necessary structure is God rather than Nature) does not alter the result. It establishes, at most, that what is ultimate is necessary, all-encompassing, and explanatorily basic. The God of theism is supposed to be personal, agential, provident, and in some sense capable of care; the structure, as the argument establishes, is the necessary condition of all possible occupancy and exchange, not thereby a person, not thereby a center of concern, not thereby an object of worship. Re-labeling structure as God changes the word while conceding the substance. What survives is not classical theism repaired but theology thinned into a metaphysical honorific for Nature.

*The eternalist reply.* The answer aimed most directly at the temporal horn does not deny God's timelessness but reconciles it with real relations to time. Stump and Kretzmann ([@stumpKretzmann1981]; developed in Stump's *Aquinas* [@stump2003]) posit *ET-simultaneity*, an eternal-temporal simultaneity on which God's single unextended eternal act is simultaneous, in the mode proper to eternity, with every temporal moment at once, so that God acts, knows, and answers without succession by standing in a simultaneity relation to each time from the standing present of eternity; Leftow (*Time and Eternity* [@leftow1991]) develops a kindred account on which temporal events are present within an eternal reference frame. The reply grants that acting requires a relation to time and claims to secure the relation without placing God in time. It relocates the difficulty rather than escaping it. A simultaneity relation is still a relation: it requires relata distinct from one another (S), it persists as the relation it is (Φ), and where a single act is simultaneous with a succession of moments the ordering of those moments is exactly what the act must answer to (T). An eternal present that genuinely stands in the ET-relation bears determinate relational roles and must explain their compatibility with simplicity and aseity. An eternal present that stands in no relation to temporal events cannot perform the explanatory work for which ET-simultaneity was introduced. And the deeper line does not wait on the temporal question at all: grant a coherent atemporal standing-present, and the eternal act is still one act with no alternative, actus purus with nothing unrealized, so its subject has no alternative way to be and is not a possible modal subject to begin with. ET-simultaneity, even if it worked, would show only how a timeless God might relate to time; it supplies none of the modal room the being lacks, answering the temporal horn while leaving the no-way-possible horn untouched.

*The subsistent-being reply.* The most resourceful classical answer refuses the framing the result rests on. On the Thomist account God is not a being among beings, one more item that either has or lacks the structural roles, but *ipsum esse subsistens*: the subsistent act of being itself, that by which everything else is, of which created time, space, and substance are analogical participations rather than constituents (Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* [@aquinas1947, I.4.2]; the analogy of being at I.13.5; pressed in the contemporary literature by Stump). On this reading the argument equivocates: to show that *a being* defined by the negation of T, S, and Φ collapses into ∅ is not yet to touch *Being Itself*, which is not defined by negating the roles but is said to stand beneath them as their ground, and to which "lacks succession," "lacks distinction," and "lacks a bearer" apply only in the deficient, creaturely sense the analogy was built to displace. This is the deepest version of the reply, and it cannot be dismissed as mere relabeling. Analogical predication is not free; it requires a *ratio* the analogates share, and the chapter has already fixed what that *ratio* would have to be: a *way to be* ([§3.2.5](convergence.html#sec-3-2-5)). Either the subsistent act of being grounds T, S, and Φ by standing in some real relation to them: sustaining, knowing, or causing. On that horn, it exercises succession, distinction, and bearing, and thereby instantiates Time, Space, and Substance in type rather than merely at the level of the bare roles (the role-to-type upgrade is earned at [§3.5.3](convergence.html#sec-3-5-3), on the realizer biconditionals whose anti-Finean necessity is discharged at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10)). It escapes ∅ only by forfeiting the aseity the doctrine exists to secure (Aseity Forfeiture, above). Or it stands in no such relation, exercises no act, and is the subsistent act of being with no way to be. That is not the plenitude of being opposed to nothing; it is the exact content the Co-instantiation Result ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)) and the Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)) identify with ∅, precluded by Exclusivity of Nature ([§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6)). The analogy cannot span the gap, because there is no way-to-be on the far side for it to reach; "Being Itself" purged of T, S, and Φ does not name a higher mode of the roles but the very absence the no-way-possible argument already closes (the analogical-predication escape is met at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1)). *Ipsum esse subsistens* is therefore not an exception to the preclusion but its sharpest instance: the one candidate that most explicitly tries to be wholly real while standing outside every condition of being a possible subject at all.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** The sharpest reply: God isn't a being that *lacks* time, space, and substance—God is *Being Itself*, the ground beneath them, so saying he 'lacks succession' misfires like asking what a color weighs. The answer turns on one demand: words about God earn real content only if they track something on God's side. So ask whether Being Itself stands in any real relation to the world—sustaining, knowing, causing. If it does, it exercises succession, distinction, and persistence, and so instantiates the very structure it was meant to stand above. If it doesn't, it connects to nothing and is indistinguishable from nothing at all. There's no third place to stand.

:::


The preclusion is not a contingent fact about how the argument defines its terms; it is a necessary consequence, established at the level of the conditions of Change (Chapter 2), of what any possible medium must be. The framework survey above is eliminative confirmation, not the ground of the result, and the ground is exhaustive in a way no survey could be. The Chapter 2 derivation does not enumerate the fundamental ontologies on offer and eliminate them one by one; it derives T, S, and Φ from the conditions of Change as such, from what it is for anything to be possible rather than ∅ ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5), [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), [§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6)). A genuinely novel fourth ontology is therefore not an unsurveyed gap in a list but an already-decided case: whatever it nominated as fundamental would still have to make room for the possibility of Change, and to make room for the possibility of Change is to instantiate the three roles. The survey illustrates the result for the live contenders; the derivation secures it for any contender there could be.

Perfect-being theology functions as the methodological engine producing the attributes the chapter examines [@morris1991; @murphy2017]; the chapter examines the produced attributes rather than the engine. Whether the maxima compose coherently into a single being is taken up at [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) (Is God Perfect?) and the cumulative case closes at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) (Does God Exist?). Swinburne's theistic personalism (God as everlasting rather than timeless, simple in a methodological rather than ontological sense, personal in the agent-causal sense) is the leading analytic alternative to classical theism and does not map cleanly onto either the classical or the embedded-deity options as characterized above: it rejects strict atemporality and strong Thomistic simplicity while retaining aseity, necessity, and omnipotence (*The Coherence of Theism* [@swinburne1977]; *The Existence of God* [@swinburne1979; @swinburne2004]). Its everlasting God is temporally embedded enough to instantiate T and, by Co-instantiation ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)), the rest, so the Aseity Forfeiture result reaches it as well: the aseity it claims to keep is exactly what the result places in question. The chapter tests theistic personalism alongside classical theism at each attribute and includes it in the three-horn disjunction at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10).

## 6.2 Constitution {#sec-6-2}

The first cluster gathers the attributes that specify what God is made of — the constitution the tradition assigns to the divine essence itself: simplicity ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)), unity ([§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2)), infinity ([§6.2.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-3)), and perfection ([§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4)). Each is a claim about internal makeup: that God is without parts, without division, without limit, and without defect.

Together they fix the static apex the chapter's first master result turns on — the simplicity/differentiation dilemma of [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1), which the remaining three inherit. Pressed, each is shown to require the very structure it was defined by denying: a being with no internal differentiation cannot be distinguished, sustained, or characterized at all, and the line to that result runs through T, S, and Φ rather than around them.

### 6.2.1 Simplicity {#sec-6-2-1}

Simplicity is the claim that God has no parts: no inner distinctions of any kind, so that each divine attribute, the divine essence, and the bare fact that God exists are one and the same undivided reality. The strain is that telling anything apart as the being it is (even telling its wisdom from its goodness) takes exactly the internal differentiation the doctrine removes. A being with nothing in it to distinguish is not the most unified being but the one whose identity has lost the structure identity tracks. What *subsistent being itself* reaches for, fully stated, is not the absence of structure but its ground, and that ground is Nature.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** Divine simplicity says God has no parts and no inner distinctions whatsoever—God's power just *is* God's knowledge just *is* God's very existence, with nothing to tell apart. It's meant to be the deepest unity there could be. The strain: telling anything apart as the thing it is—even telling its wisdom from its goodness—takes exactly the inner difference the doctrine erases. A being with nothing inside to distinguish isn't the most unified being; it's one whose identity has lost the structure that identity is tracked by. What 'being itself' reaches for, spelled out fully, isn't the absence of structure but its ground.

:::


*What the tradition holds.* Divine simplicity holds that God has no parts and no inner distinctions at all: God's power just *is* God's knowledge just *is* God's existence, with nothing to tell apart. The classical tradition makes this identity definitive of God in a register the structure cannot host: no real composition, no distinction between essence and accidents, no distinction between essence and existence, no distinction among the divine attributes themselves: a stripping of internal differentiation from the divine being (Augustine, *De Trinitate* [-@augustine416, VI]; Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.3]). *Ipsum esse subsistens* (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.3.4]) identifies essence with existence, so that God *is* being rather than *has* it: a being whose what-it-is is its that-it-is, and so a being whose identity is not contingent on anything beyond itself.

The doctrine of the Trinity (Athanasian Creed; Augustine, *De Trinitate* [-@augustine416]; Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.27–43]) holds three persons in one substance, distinguished only by relations of origin (paternity, filiation, procession), preserving distinction without composition. Necessary being [Anselm, *Proslogion* -@anselm1078, II–III; @plantinga1974b] extends self-sameness modally across every possible world, so that divine identity is preserved not just within a world but across the space of worlds.

Each formulation tries to keep divine identity from being one more identity among identities, and each is defended in contemporary form [@stump2003; @stump2016; @dolezal2011; @dolezal2017; @prussRasmussen2018; @leftow2004; @leftow2012; @browerRea2005] as expressing not a property but the condition under which a being can be without dependence. Taken at the tradition's own fullest formulation, the doctrine names the deepest unity philosophical theology has reached for: a being whose identity rests on nothing prior, because there is no internal structure to rest on and no external structure to depend on. Classical simplicity is not the only target in the neighborhood: the temporalist repair (drop simplicity and keep a temporal, personal God) is engaged at [§6.7.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-3), and the embedded-deity concession at [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1), so the pressures below are not aimed as if strong simplicity were the sole option. The doctrine's full treatment, run end-to-end against the nine forms of its defense, is at [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1); the present section presses simplicity specifically as a great-making attribute and draws on that treatment rather than re-litigating it.

*What cannot be answered.* Six questions press simplicity where the doctrine owes its most demanding answers.

**Q1.** *If God has no parts, then how are his wisdom and goodness distinct?* Plantinga's [-@plantinga1980] pressure on strong simplicity has not been answered in the form it was put. If God's wisdom is identical with God's power, and God's power with God's goodness, transitivity gives wisdom-is-goodness, and these are clearly distinct properties on any predicative reading. The contemporary defenses [@stump2003; @dolezal2011; @dolezal2017; @prussRasmussen2018] recast simplicity as non-composition rather than strict property-identity, and the most developed form of the recast invokes the analogy of being (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.13]): *wisdom*, *power*, and *goodness* pick out distinct content at the level of signification (grounded in diverse creaturely perfections eminently contained in the one undivided essence) without internal differentiation in God and so without composition. That move slips between the two crude horns, so it has to be met on its own terrain. Analogical predication earns its distinct content only if each predicate tracks something real about the divine subject: a real proportion between the creaturely perfection and a divine correlate that holds it. Ask what that correlate is. If *wisdom* and *goodness* track the same undifferentiated correlate, they track one thing under two names: the senses do no metaphysical work, and the attribute-tradition collapses into synonymy: a being of which only one thing can truly be said. If they track distinct correlates (distinct aspects of the essence in virtue of which the one predicate applies rather than the other), then those aspects are real features the predicates discriminate among, and discrimination among real features within one being is relational non-identity wearing the name *aspect*. Eminent containment does not dissolve the dilemma; it relocates it inward, and the relocation is worth making explicit, since eminence is the one horn the dilemma cannot be charged with begging. Grant the Thomist exactly what is asked: a superabundant actuality determinate enough that *wisdom* applies to it truly and *goodness* applies to it truly. Then press the discriminating question the predicates themselves force: in virtue of what does *wisdom* apply rather than merely *goodness*? Either something on the divine side answers to the difference between the two true predications, in which case that something is content the predicates discriminate among, and discrimination-among is differentiation whatever its dignity; or nothing answers to it, in which case the two predications are made true by the same feature-less actuality, one truthmaker under many names, which is the synonymy horn in superabundant dress. Eminence does not name a third region between the determinate-and-differentiated and the undifferentiated-and-empty; it names the demand that there be one, and the discriminating question is the test that demand has to pass. The one apparent counterexample, abstracta (determinate, it seems, yet not spatiotemporally differentiated), is not one: [§3.4.3](convergence.html#sec-3-4-3) finds the familiar candidates for a determinate-but-structureless residue, abstracta among them, each presupposing T, S, and Φ rather than exhibiting determinacy without them. The content-requires-differentiation step is substantive: one truthmaker can in principle ground several truths. The pressure is therefore not an automatic truthmaker rule but whether the single divine reality explains why these predicates have different inferential and modal profiles without treating their difference as merely creature-side. The most refined Thomist names the relation precisely here: the perfections are *virtually* distinct: a *distinctio rationis ratiocinatae* in the Cajetanian idiom, distinct neither really nor by any relation in God, but by a distinction of reason carrying a foundation in the thing, *wisdom* and *goodness* picking out one eminent perfection under aspects the intellect cannot fuse. The virtual distinction does not escape the dilemma; it restates it. Ask what the *foundation in the thing* is. If it has a *fundamentum in re* (some feature of the divine essence in virtue of which *wisdom* applies rather than *goodness*, the foundation the qualifier *ratiocinatae* is coined to claim), then that foundation is a real feature the predicates track, and the differentiation the doctrine denies has been readmitted at the level of the foundation; the distinction is virtual only in that we read off in two concepts a duality already seated in the essence. If it has no foundation in the thing (a *distinctio rationis ratiocinantis*, purely in our minds with nothing in God answering to it), then *wisdom* and *goodness* track one undifferentiated point under two names, and the attribute-tradition collapses into the synonymy the analogy of being was invoked to avoid. The Cajetanian middle demands that the distinction be founded in the thing *without* being a real or relational feature of it; but a foundation that grounds the discriminating application of one predicate rather than another simply is a feature the predicates discriminate among, and discrimination among features within one being is relational non-identity whether it is christened *real*, *formal*, or *virtual*. The 'aspect = relational non-identity' step is therefore not assumed against the sophisticated Thomist; it is what remains once the virtual distinction is held to the foundation its own name promises. Either the perfections collapse to a single nameless point, or the essence carries the differentiated content the doctrine was built to deny: composition readmitted under a more careful label. A last Thomist resort relocates the diversity from the foundation to the manner of signifying. On Aquinas's distinction between the *res significata* and the *modus significandi* (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.13.3]), *wisdom* and *goodness* signify one undivided *res*, the simple essence, under diverse *modi significandi* grounded in diverse creaturely effects, so that the senses do their metaphysical work in the mode of signifying rather than in distinct correlates in God: the synonymy horn is supposed to fail without composition being readmitted. The reply is given in full at [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3), the chapter's meta-home for religious language; in brief, the defense does not clear the fork, because the differentiated modes must themselves be grounded in something the predicates discriminate among (the diverse creaturely effects taken back to the essence as variously imitable) and a ground in virtue of which *wise* applies rather than *good* is once more a real feature the predicates discriminate among, relational non-identity under the name *mode*. The structural cost reappears at the level of grounding, exactly as it did for the virtual distinction [@mullins2013]. The same dilemma is pressed against omniscience in [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2): a being that knows a differentiated manifold needs differentiated content to do the knowing, and a simple essence cannot carry that content without reinstating the internal differentiation the doctrine rules out. Identity in creatures is a function of the structural relation between a being and the differentiated content the being carries. A being whose essence has no differentiated content is not a being whose identity has been preserved more strictly than ours; it is a being whose identity has lost the structure identity tracks.

**Q2.** *If there's nothing in God to tell apart, what tells the Father from the Son?* Trinitarian distinction has to be real distinction or there is no Trinity, and real distinction requires determinate non-identity between the persons. It does not by itself require a spatial interval. The patristic and Thomistic reply locates the distinction in relations of origin (paternity, filiation, procession; Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.27–43]) rather than in real composition. But relations of origin are themselves structured: paternity and filiation are not interchangeable, procession is a directed relation of source and term, and origin-order is asymmetric even when it is explicitly denied to be ordinary temporal before-and-after. That is the book's Temporality role in non-clock form: directed order, not a sequence of divine moments. Latin trinitarianism [@leftow2004; @leftow2012; @browerRea2005] keeps distinction-without-extension by treating the persons as distinct only by relation within a single divine consciousness; social trinitarianism [@swinburne1994; @hasker2013] keeps distinction-with-extension by treating the persons as distinct centers held in perichoresis (their mutual indwelling in one another). The first preserves unity by attenuating distinction toward modalism (collapsing the persons into mere aspects of one God); the second preserves distinction by attenuating unity toward tritheism (three separate gods). The middle the tradition has wanted for sixteen centuries is the middle T, S, and Φ pick out (three relata distinguished by asymmetric origin-order and held in a persisting substance), and the doctrine has placed every term of that middle outside divine being.

**Q3.** *When we call God necessary, are we saying something about God, or just about every possible world?* Kant's [-@kant1781] objection (existence is not a real predicate) is sharper than Plantinga's modal reframing acknowledges. Plantinga [-@plantinga1974b] reads necessary existence as instantiation in every possible world and so escapes the Kantian objection at the level of the predicate. Instantiation in every possible world can be expressed either as a de re modal property of a thing or as a fact represented by the modal structure. Plantinga's reframing therefore can say something about God. The remaining issue is whether the relevant individual and cross-world identity conditions are coherent and whether the possibility premise is warranted. The locus of necessity has shifted from the being to the modal structure. What modal-structure necessity comes to is taken up at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1); the present concern is more local. The predicate the doctrine wants (necessarily existing as a way of being self-same across modal space) has been preserved by relocating its referent from a being to a feature of how worlds are structured. What is necessarily instantiated across every possible world is T, S, and Φ; what is not necessarily instantiated is a being defined by not instantiating any of them.

**Q4.** *If all we can say is that God is, have we said what God is?* *Ipsum esse subsistens* (subsistent being itself) closes the gap that, in creatures, makes existence contingent on something other than essence. The closing preserves aseity; what it does not preserve is identity in a sense the predicate could pick out. Every creaturely being is a particular kind of being, and being-this-kind is what makes the being identifiable as the being it is. A being whose essence is its existence is not the most identifiable being but the one whose identity has thinned to the bare fact that it is, a fact with no kind-content for identity-talk to track. Stump [-@stump2016] and Dolezal [-@dolezal2017] defend the position as expressing divine non-contingency rather than as a determinate metaphysical claim, and the move is genuinely available. The doctrine survives, on that reading, by narrowing the work the predicate is asked to do: *ipsum esse subsistens* names God's non-dependence rather than supplying a determinate kind-description. That is not a mere retreat; it is the most defensible Feser-style way to keep the doctrine from becoming one entity inside a wider genus. The structural cost remains that the believer who calls God *the Holy One of Israel* is not invoking the bare fact that something is; they are invoking a determinate being with a determinate kind. *Ipsum esse subsistens* preserves the term while leaving the being without determinate content.

**Q5.** *If God isn't a being among beings, what makes God anyone at all?* The post-Heideggerian critique [@heidegger1927; @heidegger1957; @marion1991; @marion2002] puts the dilemma sharply. If God is a being among beings, divine transcendence collapses into supremacy within a category; if God is being itself, divine identity loses the structural conditions any identity requires. The Thomistic reply [@burrell1979; @westphal2001] reads *ipsum esse subsistens* as precisely the move past being-among-beings. Plotinus gives the older and more radical version of the same pressure: the One is prior to being and to number, the source of intelligibility rather than an intelligible item within it (*Enneads* [-@plotinus270, V.5, VI.9]; [§5.3.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-2)). The reply trades one structural concern for its mirror image: a being among beings has identity but loses transcendence; being itself, or the One beyond being, has transcendence but loses identity. The analysis here does not pick a horn. What *being itself* names, when fully stated, is the conditions under which any being can be individuated, distinguished, and sustained across the time within which it persists. T, S, and Φ are not a being among beings, and they do the work *being itself* was meant to do without leaving the structural side of identity unprovided.

**Q6.** *If God is the greatest in every way at once, what makes God this being and not another?* Perfect-being theology [@anselm1078; @morris1991; @murphy2017] generates the divine attributes by maximizing each great-making property. The methodological assumption is that maxima compose: that maximally wise, maximally powerful, maximally good, maximally simple, maximally eternal can be jointly predicated of one being without internal contradiction. Swinburne's use of simplicity is different: it is a theoretical virtue in a cumulative explanatory case, not the strong ontological identity of attribute and essence the Thomistic doctrine asserts (Swinburne [-@swinburne1979; -@swinburne2004]; [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4)). Each Chapter 6 section presses the ontological attribute against its structural conditions and finds the predicate unable to land on a being defined by the negation of those conditions. The cumulative case is developed from the joint side at [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4); this section presses the same point from the individuating side. Sobel [-@sobel2003], Martin [-@martin1990], and Everitt [-@everitt2004] press incompossibility (the impossibility of the maximized attributes being jointly instantiated in one being) from a different angle. What individuates an identity is the structured content the maxima have been defined to exclude. There is no determinate identity for a being whose individuation has been removed at the level of every great-making property at once.

*What is required.* What the six pressures together surface is the structural inventory identity actually depends on. Identity depends on six conditions. (i) Internal differentiation: distinct predicates of a being have to pick out distinct content, or the predicates collapse into verbal identity without the work the predicate was supposed to perform. (ii) Asymmetric relational ordering: distinct relata require an interval (S) and a directionality (T) between them, without which "distinct" is a verbal claim with no structural correlate. (iii) A structure-grounded locus of necessity: what is necessary across modal space is necessary because the modal structure is configured a particular way, and that configuration is where the necessity lives. (iv) Determinate kind-content: a being is the being it is by virtue of being *a kind of being*, and identity-talk tracks the kind, not the bare fact that something is. (v) Structural individuation: what makes a being identifiable is not the withdrawal of all dependence but the structural conditions under which the being can be individuated, distinguished, and sustained. (vi) Structured content sufficient to support each great-making property: the maxima cannot compose into a coherent identity unless the structured content the maxima predicate is preserved rather than negated. These six conditions are not extrinsic to identity; they are what the predicate *identity* names when its referent is examined. T, S, and Φ (succession, distinction, and the substance-substrate through which both run) are not optional supports for identity that some beings can do without. They are the conditions under which any being is the being it is across the moments through which it persists.

*What is inverted.* For persisting concrete beings, identity includes persistence through time; identity more generally also covers instantaneous and abstract candidates. The inversion therefore needs a determinate individuation and continuity floor without defining every identity as temporal substance. *Ipsum esse subsistens* (Latin *esse*, "to be," present-participial *subsistens*, "standing-under, standing-firm") names exactly the substrate that stands under and the standing-through that holds it together: Substance (Φ) that stands under, Time (T) that runs through, Space (S) that holds it distinct. The Latin tradition's deepest formulation reaches for the conditions under which a being can be the being it is, and names Nature without recognizing what is being named. Nature has no kind because it is the condition for kind. It has no internal composition in the sense of being assembled from prior parts, because composition among parts is what it makes possible. Nor is Nature's changeability the unrealized potency the objection presses (that a mutable, composite Nature is act/potency-laden and so cannot occupy the unactualized terminus reserved for Pure Act, Feser's frontal move): the mutability is the *necessary possibility* of change internal to a Nature whose co-instantiation is itself necessary ([§2.8.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-6)), not a potency awaiting actualization from without; and since potency cannot reduce itself to act save through the substance-ontology the scheme itself presupposes ([§3.1.2](convergence.html#sec-3-1-2)), the regress terminates not in an *actus purus* stripped of structure but in the changeless ground the act/potency scheme runs within ([§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1)).

Nor is a structureless Pure Act available as the other horn: *pure act* is itself a structural predicate. It is marked off from impure act by a distinction, and a distinction is relational non-identity (S) by the step Q1 already presses; and it is *act* only as the actualizing of what it affects, a directed relation of actualizer to actualized (T) across the interval between them (S), exercised by what persists as the agent of the actualizing (Φ). An actuality that causes an effect must stand in a determinate causal relation to it. Thomistic pure act forecloses passive potency in God, not active causal power; the seam at [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) is whether an unchanged necessary act can explain contingent effects without modal collapse. What structures whatever it touches cannot itself be structureless, and proportionate causality, the doctrine's own principle, says as much from the effect's side: a cause produces only what it contains, so a structured world needs a cause proportioned to structure, and the retreat to eminent containment carries the very differentiated content the production discriminates among, structure readmitted in the cause (Q1). The terminus is therefore neither horn the objection offers, neither a composite item within the order nor a bare actuality above it, but the conditions any actuality meets in being one; strip even the structure by which *pure act* differs from empty actuality and what remains is not a supreme simple but ∅ ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)). *Actus purus*, when used to support differentiated causal and cognitive predicates, incurs the thin role-floor of determinate order, difference, and bearing. The upgrade from those roles to T, S, and Φ remains a further argumentative step. And the triad the doctrine would press as a many is no aggregate: by the Triconditional Identity ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)), Time, Space, and Substance are one Nature read three ways, co-instantiated so completely that to lack any one is to lack all three ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)). The unity a henological One is summoned to supply is therefore not added to the triad from above but is what the triad is; closing the regress needs neither a fourth relation binding the three nor a One beyond structure standing over them. It is necessarily what it is because there is no second vantage from which it could be otherwise.

*Subsistent being itself* is what T, S, and Φ are, read in the structure that supports the phrasing. The property-list classical theism specifies for *ipsum esse subsistens* (atemporal, aspatial, prior to composition) is the property-list [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) specifies for the Null State; where the doctrine refuses Nature, what it names is ∅.

The one premise this verdict turns on is the one the doctrine cannot surrender: that *God is* (*God is not nothing*) is made true by something on the divine side rather than by nothing at all. That is aseity, read as a truthmaker demand; a being whose existence answered to nothing in it would exist from nothing, the one thing aseity forbids. The discernibility principle the inversion uses is not imported against the doctrine: it is the doctrine's own first commitment, turned on the bare predicate *is*.

The doctrine of divine simplicity, pressed through these questions, either supplies a determinate account of differentiated predication and relation or leaves the structural burden unresolved; it is not thereby identical to Nature by definition.

### 6.2.2 Unity {#sec-6-2-2}

Monotheism's core is that God is one, not merely one being among others, but uniquely and indivisibly one. Counting something as one, or telling it apart as *this* being rather than another, takes the very distinctness that space and structure provide. Applied to a being placed beyond all structure, "one" has nothing to fix it as one. The oneness the argument can actually secure is the oneness of Nature itself.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** Monotheism says God is *one*—not merely one being that happens to be alone, but necessarily and indivisibly one. But consider what fixes a count. Calling something one, or telling it apart from a second, takes distinctness: a location, a boundary, some structure that marks *this* off from *that*. Put the being beyond all time, space, and structure and the word 'one' has nothing left to pin it down—it can't even rule out a second copy, since there's no feature by which two would differ. The oneness the argument can actually secure isn't the headcount of a structureless being; it's the oneness of Nature, the single frame anything real must sit inside.

:::


*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine unity holds that there is exactly one God, not as a contingent count but as a necessary feature of what divinity is. Distinct from simplicity, which concerns God's internal lack of parts ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)), and from necessity, which concerns God's modal status ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)), unity is the cardinality claim monotheism rests on [@aquinas1947, I.11; Anselm, *Monologion* III; @swinburne1994, ch. 8]. The classical argument runs from the great-making properties to the count: a being than which no greater can be conceived must be unique, since two such beings would either be indistinguishable (and hence one, by the identity of indiscernibles) or distinguishable (and hence each lacking some perfection the other has, contradicting maximal greatness). Aquinas's parallel line argues from simplicity: a being identical with its essence cannot be one among others sharing that essence, since *one among others* requires a principle of individuation outside the shared essence, and a simple being has no such principle [@aquinas1947, I.11.3; @stump2003; @dolezal2017]. The Christian tradition complicates the picture at the Trinitarian level: one divine being in three persons, with the unity preserved at the level of *substance* and the threeness located at the level of *persona* or *hypostasis* [@augustine416, V; @aquinas1947, I.29–43; @rea2009]. The unity claim survives the Trinitarian complication in the sense that the divine substance remains one; the multiplicity is *internal* to the one God, not a multiplicity *of* gods. The position the doctrine, fully stated, holds is that the count *one* is fixed at the level of the divine essence and that no metaphysically possible world contains two distinct divine beings.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions put to the doctrine what it cannot answer once the count has to be fixed and nothing structural is left to fix it. What lies underneath them is structural, what fixes the count: if the conditions that could pick out a divine being are satisfiable at all, what prevents their being satisfied more than once?

**Q1.** *What makes God one rather than two, if God has no place, time, or matter to be told apart by?* Two beings of the same kind are distinguished by some principle of individuation: spatial location, temporal trajectory, material constitution, qualitative difference, or haecceity. A divine being on the classical bundle has none of the first three: God is non-spatial, atemporal, immaterial. Qualitative difference between maximally great beings collapses to indiscernibility (Anselm's argument above). Haecceity (primitive thisness without further principle [@adams1979; @plantinga1974b]) is what remains. The classical reply is that the divine being's uniqueness rests on the impossibility of two beings each maximally exemplifying the great-making properties: two such beings would collapse into one (Anselm) or would each lack a perfection [@swinburne1994]. The concern here is that the collapse-or-lack argument runs through *distinguishability*, and distinguishability is what the structural conditions provide. Where the structural conditions are absent, the question *are these two beings or one?* has no resource on which to settle either way. The argument's force, on the classical bundle, depends on the very structural distinctness the bundle denies the divine being. Plotinus offers the most radical dissolution of Q1's individuation problem. In *Enneads* V.5 (*That the Intelligibles Are Not External to the Intellect*) and VI.9 (*On the Good, or the One*) [@plotinus270], the One does not require a principle of individuation because it is beyond being, and hence beyond the entire domain in which individuation questions arise. The individuation question (*what makes this being one rather than two?*) presupposes enough structure for the question to get purchase; the Plotinian One is prior to all structure, all relation, all multiplicity, and hence prior to the individuation question itself. The One is not *one* in the numerical sense (the source of all number is itself beyond number) and the Anselmian collapse-or-lack argument, which quantifies over indistinguishable or distinguishable divine beings, does not reach the One's level. The concern for the Plotinian dissolution is that *beyond being* terminates the individuation question by terminating the domain of predication entirely: [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3), Q5 traces the convergence between the Plotinian ascent and the chapter's structural analysis at that same terminal point. Spinoza's *Ethics* [@spinoza1677, I.5] offers a complementary argument within the framework of attribute-individuation: there cannot be two or more substances sharing the same attribute, since substances are individuated by their attributes; if God is the substance possessing all attributes, there can be only one such substance. The argument is simpler than the Anselmian line and settles Q1 from within substance-metaphysics without requiring the *via negativa*. The concern here is Spinoza's own conclusion: once the one-substance result is reached, the particular modes (individual temporal events, spatial configurations, creaturely substances) are modes of the one substance: the *deus sive natura* identification follows, and the classical God/world distinction has already been collapsed.

**Q2.** *How is God exactly one, if a being without parts gives nothing to count?* Aquinas's individuation argument holds that a simple being is identical with its essence, and so cannot be one among others sharing that essence [@aquinas1947, I.11.3]. The concern here is that *one among others* is a cardinality claim, and cardinality presupposes the very structural distinctness simplicity refuses. A being identical with its essence is not less enumerable than a non-simple being for any structural reason; it is unenumerable in the sense that *enumeration* presupposes distinguishable members, and a simple being has no distinguishable features by which to be a member. The argument secures *exactly one* by removing the resource on which *exactly two* could be coherent, which secures uniqueness at the cost of removing the cardinal predicate itself. The reply that *one* applies to the simple being as a transcendental rather than as a number [@aquinas1947, I.11.1; @wippel2000] preserves the count by treating it as analogical; the concern here is that the analogical *one* is consistent with *no others of the kind* and with *no further determinable count of the kind*, and the doctrine of monotheism needs the determinate count, not the indeterminate transcendental.

**Q3.** *What tells the three persons apart, if nothing in God divides one from another?* The Christian tradition holds one God in three persons: a unity at the level of *ousia* / *substantia*, a threeness at the level of *hypostasis* / *persona*. The classical reply distinguishes the levels and locates the multiplicity at the personal level while preserving the unity at the substantial level [@augustine416, V–VII; @aquinas1947, I.29–43; @swinburne1994, ch. 8]. The contemporary literature is divided: social trinitarians [@plantinga1986; @swinburne1994] emphasize the threeness; Latin trinitarians [@leftow2004; @rea2009] emphasize the oneness; constitution accounts [@browerRea2005] provide a metaphysical apparatus for both. The concern here is that *three persons in one substance* requires a principle of individuation at the personal level that does not run at the substantial level. The traditional reply is that the persons are individuated by their relations of origin: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten of the Father, the Spirit proceeding from the Father (and the Son, in the Western tradition). The concern here is that *relations of origin* are directional relations (*begotten of* and *proceeding from* are asymmetric) and asymmetry is the structural feature of T ([§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4)). The reply that these are eternal relations of origin preserves the asymmetry by relocating it into a register that the doctrine of divine atemporality forecloses ([§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2)). The Trinitarian complication does not merely sit alongside the classical bundle; it reaches into the structural features the bundle was preserving God from.

**Q4.** *What makes two ultimate frameworks two, if telling them apart takes a wider frame over both?* The structural reasoning the chapter has run treats Nature as the necessary condition of any possible world (§[§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), 2.6.10). The question presses whether *more than one* such Nature is coherent. Two distinct modal structures would each have their own T, S, and Φ, with no cross-structure relations. The concern here is that *two distinct frames* requires a meta-structural condition that hosts the distinctness, and that meta-structural condition would be the more comprehensive frame the two were supposed to be alternatives to. The argument is parallel to the cosmological-isolation case [@kraay2010; @almeida2008] at the level of worlds, but runs at the level of modal-structure conditions rather than world-content: two structures each with their own T, S, Φ would either share a meta-condition (collapsing into one) or be related by no condition at all (in which case they are not two of anything, since *two* requires a structural relation in which the cardinality holds). The concrete-world form of this reductio — run against Lewis's modal-realist plurality, where isolation leaves no crossable interval to make two totalities two — is deployed at [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1), its honest ceiling owned in-text (it shifts the burden onto the determined primitivist rather than deductively refuting one). On the structural reading, the count of modal structures is not a contingent feature of the actual structure but a feature of what a modal structure can be — and the pressure just run pushes that count toward one without yet foreclosing primitive plurality.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** If Nature is just the structural frame, why think there's only one? Why not two sealed-off frames, each with its own time, space, and substance? Try to make them *two*. Counting them as two already needs some relation holding them apart—a wider frame both sit inside—but then that wider frame is the real single structure, and the two were only regions of it. Cut every relation between them instead, and nothing is left to make them two of anything rather than simply all there is. Either way you land back at one.
