Nature is unique not by lucky headcount but because 'two structures' can't be coherently stated in the first place.

:::


**Q5.** *What makes many gods divine, if no one of them is the ground of the rest?* The contemporary literature on theological pluralism [@hick1989; @heim1995; @knitter2002] and the historical literature on polytheism [@versnel2011; @pakkanen1996] have pressed alternatives. The concern here is that each alternative either treats the multiple divinities as multiple conditioned beings within a single structural frame (in which case the frame is the genuine ground and the divinities are particulars within it) or treats them as ungrounded multiples (in which case the question of what holds them together is unanswered). The pluralist reading registers, rather than resolves, the structural concern: the *something common* across the multiple divine names is what the structural reading identifies as Nature itself, and the *plurality* across the names is what the structural reading identifies as the multiplicity of particulars within Nature. The pluralist tradition has been reaching toward the destination from the opposite direction: where monotheism collapses the multiplicity into one being, pluralism preserves the multiplicity by treating no one of them as the ground; the structural reading is that there is one ground and the names track the particulars within it.

*What is required.* Followed to the end, the five pressures pin down what the predicate *one* actually depends on. Cardinality presupposes distinguishability, and distinguishability is what the structural conditions provide; an *exactly one* claim about a being lacking all structural distinctness depends on the structural distinctness for its content. Simplicity secures uniqueness by removing the resource on which *exactly two* could be coherent, but the move converts the *one* into a transcendental that is consistent with no determinate count of the kind. Trinitarian threeness-with-substantial-oneness requires asymmetric relations of origin, and asymmetry is the structural feature of T; the eternal-relations reply preserves the asymmetry by relocating it into a register the classical bundle forecloses. Two distinct modal structures raise a meta-level individuation problem: if they share a common framework, that framework may be more comprehensive; if they do not, their plurality may be primitive. This shifts a burden onto the pluralist but does not deductively establish that modal structure is necessarily one. Theological pluralism registers the multiplicity at the level of names while leaving the *what holds the names together* unaddressed. What the predicate *one* survives as, after the five pressures have run, is at least the integrated unity of the modal frame — not the cardinality of a being lacking the structural conditions of cardinality, but the unity-of-structure that *frame* names.

*What is inverted.* Unity can be predicated of Nature as the integration of its structural conditions. The stronger claim that exactly one modal structure is metaphysically possible requires an argument against primitive plurality; the meta-structure pressure alone does not settle it. Any candidate framework satisfying the same T, S, and Φ roles may count as structurally equivalent to Nature. Numerical uniqueness beyond that equivalence remains subject to the primitive-plurality objection. Returned to the structure that hosts it, *one* names the modal-structure necessity of having exactly one structure of conditions. The tradition has been performing the universal of cardinality-without-distinguishability onto a being defined as lacking the structural conditions of cardinality. Taken at the level of structure, *one Nature* names the unity of the framework within which actual occupancy and exchange occur. Identifying that unity with the personal monotheistic God would require further claims about agency, cognition, and value. The identification has a name: Spinoza's *deus sive natura*, God or Nature (*Ethics* [@spinoza1677, I, Props. 14–15, 29]; *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus* ch. 4). Spinoza identifies God with Nature, but the structural analysis need not treat the personal monotheistic God and Nature as interchangeable descriptions. It recovers an ultimate unity while leaving agency, cognition, and value as further claims. This is the divergence [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) reaches and carries forward: where *Divine Necessity* arrives at the point at which the naturalist and monotheist readings of the modally invariant finally part (the monotheist reading the unity of the necessary as a personal ground binding a plurality, the present account reading it as the triconditionality of one structure), it is here, at unity, that the divergence is carried and receives the reading just given. The chapter does not endorse every element of Spinoza's substance-metaphysics, but the one-substance result at the level of necessary ground is structurally reproduced. The PSR-symmetry pressure that runs against Spinoza's system runs against the chapter's inversion at the same point: if Nature is one and necessary, what grounds the contingency of the particular modes (specific temporal sequences, specific spatial configurations within the necessary T, S, Φ frame)? Spinoza's unrestricted PSR eliminates contingency at every level; the chapter preserves contingency at the level of the particular. The resolution of this tension (how a necessary structural frame hosts genuinely contingent particulars) is what [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) carries.

### 6.2.3 Infinity {#sec-6-2-3}

The tradition calls God *infinite*: unlimited, unbounded, without measure. Quantitative infinity is always infinity along a magnitude, number, degree, or intensity. Classical divine infinity is offered instead as non-quantitative absence of ontological limitation, so the section must assess that analogical sense rather than assume the quantitative one exhausts the term. In its familiar uses, infinity is a fact about a magnitude with no greatest, a series that does not terminate, a scale that runs on without end. The classical God, though, has no magnitude (it is immaterial), no number (it is one and simple), no parts to be many, no degrees of more-and-less (simplicity admits no composition of intensities). Strip away every dimension along which a thing could be unbounded, and the question presses: infinite in *what*?

*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology makes infinity a divine perfection: God is *infinitus*, without limit, and the tradition is careful about the sense. God is not infinite in magnitude or quantity: Aquinas follows Aristotle in holding an actual infinite magnitude impossible, so divine infinity is neither spatial nor numerical bulk (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.7.1–4]; cf. Aristotle, *Physics* [-@aristotle1984, III]). Divine infinity is infinity *of being*: God's act of existing (*esse*) is unlimited because it is not received in, and so not contracted by, any matter or essence that would bound it, a form unlimited by reception. Where a finite being's existing is limited by the essence that receives it, God's existing is its essence and is subject to no such limit; God holds the whole perfection of being without restriction. Infinity, so understood, is the negative face of the divine fullness: *in-finite*, not-bounded, because there is nothing outside God to bound God. The doctrine keeps the believer's intuition that God exceeds every creature without measure, and binds it to the unlimited perfection of being rather than to any quantity.

*What cannot be answered.* Four questions leave the doctrine without an answer once *infinite* has to specify what it is the infinity of. What presses beneath them is that unboundedness has content only relative to a dimension, and the classical God is defined to have none.

**Q1.** *If God has no magnitude, no number, and no degree, what is God infinite in?* To be infinite is to be unbounded along a dimension: a magnitude with no greatest, a count with no last, a scale with no ceiling. The classical God has no magnitude (immaterial), no number (simple, one), no parts and so no quantity, no degrees of intensity (simplicity excludes more-and-less). With every dimension of unboundedness removed, *infinite* has no variable to range over. If no positive account of unlimited *esse* is supplied, the predicate risks becoming merely negative. That is a determinacy burden, not yet a category mistake, because the Thomist explicitly denies that divine infinity is a magnitude.

**Q2.** *If God's infinity is unlimited being rather than unlimited size, what is the more-and-less of being along which God is the maximum?* The tradition's best move relocates infinity from quantity to *esse*, and refuses to concede that this names a scale at all. Infinity of being, on the Thomist account, is a *negative* determination: God's *esse* is unlimited not because it tops some dimension of intensity but because it is unreceived, not contracted by an essence that would bound it (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.7.1]). Unboundedness here is the *absence* of a limiting receiver, not a maximal rung on a ladder of more-and-less, so the demand "unbounded along what?" is said to misfire. It is the strongest reply the doctrine has, and [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) has already run it to its end. *Esse* unreceived by any essence is *ipsum esse subsistens*, and [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) fixes what that construal delivers: an act of existing with no receiving essence has no determinate kind-content, no what-it-is, nothing but the bare that-it-is. Press the infinity-claim through that result. Either the unreceived *esse* has determinate content (it is *this* plenitude and not another, full in *these* respects rather than those) and that content is contrastive, a being thus-and-not-otherwise, which reinstates the very differentiation a scale records and seats divine infinity back inside the order of more-and-less; or it has no determinate content, and then its property-list is the property-list [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) assigns the Null State, so "infinite being" names not the maximum of being but ∅. The negative determination does not slip the fork; it inherits it. What is genuinely unbounded (limited by nothing outside because there is no outside) is not an unreceived *esse* standing beyond the order but the structural conditions within which bound and measure are defined at all.

**Q3.** *If no completed actual infinite is possible, how is God an actual infinite, and if God's is merely potential or qualitative, in what does it exceed the finite?* The theistic tradition that presses the impossibility of a completed actual infinite to argue for a beginning of the world [@craig1979] cannot then help itself to a completed actual infinite in the divine being without strain. The charge must be stated precisely or it equivocates: what that tradition forbids is an actual infinite *magnitude or multitude* (an infinite of quantity) and [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) defends the actual infinite on exactly that quantitative terrain against the Kalām. Divine infinity, the Thomist rightly answers, was never quantitative (the first question), so the prohibition does not reach it directly. The remaining question is whether "unlimited being" has intelligible non-scalar content; failure to provide it would make the predicate obscure, but it would not revive the mathematics of completed multitudes. If it is merely potential, it is a never-completed limit, the infinity of a process rather than of a perfect being. And if it is "qualitative," the second question returns unanswered: qualitative along what?

**Q4.** *If God's infinity just is God's simple essence, what tells it apart from finitude?* On simplicity ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)), infinity is not a feature added to the essence but the essence itself. Yet the marks by which the infinite is told from the finite (the finite can be exceeded, added to, bounded; the infinite cannot) are all marks along a dimension, and a partless essence standing on no dimension of more-and-less bears none of them. Where there is no scale at all, *infinite* and *finite* lose their contrast together, exactly as [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) finds a simple essence admitting no internal differentiation losing the contrasts identity needs. An infinity that differs from finitude in no specifiable respect is *infinite* in name only.

*What is required.* Taken in order, the four pressures settle what *infinite* depends on. Infinity is unboundedness along a dimension; remove every dimension and the predicate has nothing to range over. Relocating infinity from magnitude to being does not escape this: *more-and-less of esse* is itself a scale, and the negative-determination reply forks, by [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1), into scale or ∅. The tradition's own anti-infinitism forbids a completed actual divine infinite of quantity, and the retreats to potential or qualitative infinity either reintroduce process or reopen the demand for a dimension. And an infinity identical with a partless, scaleless essence loses its contrast with finitude altogether. What *infinite* survives as, once the pressures have run, is not a perfection a simple being could hold but unboundedness along the dimensions there are, which are the structural ones.

*What is inverted.* Infinity is the limitlessness of the structural conditions themselves. *Infinite*, in the sense that comes through intact, names what has no outer bound, and what has no outer bound is not a being among beings but the structure within which bound and measure are defined. The structural roles do not by themselves establish that physical space is spatially unbounded or that time has no first or last moment. Cosmological boundary questions remain distinct from the claim that any boundary is represented within a broader structural description; the structural conditions admit no *outside* by which they could be bounded, because *outside* is itself a structural notion. □(T∧S∧Φ), if established, is unrestricted in modal scope. Calling that "infinite" in Aquinas's sense is an analogy that requires care, not a direct consequence of the absence of a spatial or temporal exterior. The tradition reaches for *infinite* to say that God is limited by nothing outside; traced honestly, what is limited by nothing outside is Nature, since only the condition of all limits can fail to stand under one. The infinite God is Nature's own limitlessness, named as though it belonged to something beyond Nature, when *beyond Nature* is the one place that cannot be.

### 6.2.4 Perfection {#sec-6-2-4}

Perfection is the attribute behind all the others: God as the greatest conceivable being, each good quality maxed out. Two problems surface. If God is the *standard* of perfection, nothing else can be perfect in the same sense; but a *perfect maker* should produce perfect work, and creation is not perfect. And the maxed-out qualities resist composition — each proposed fix must show it can reconcile two of them without weakening a third. If none can, the ontological argument's "a perfect being is possible" premise is blocked at the point of entry.

*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology assigns God the meta-attribute of perfection: that-than-which-no-greater-can-be-conceived, with each great-making property held to apply to maximum degree [@anselm1078, II; @morris1991; @murphy2017]. Perfect-being theology functions as the methodological engine producing the attributes the chapter has examined ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)). The doctrine binds *perfectus* to *completus*: that which lacks nothing it could have, that which has every property the having of which would constitute a greater being [@aquinas1947, I.4; @anselm1078, V]. On the most developed contemporary refinement, perfection is the meta-attribute by which the great-making properties are selected and assembled: each property is included if having it constitutes greatness; the maximal assembly is the divine essence [@morris1991; @hoffmannRosenkrantz2002; @speaks2018]. Perfection is also, on the tradition, the *standard* of perfection in lower beings: a creature is perfect insofar as it participates in the divine perfection, which it does in the analogical sense Aquinas's *analogia entis* develops [@aquinas1947, I.4.3; Cajetan; @teVelde1995; @long2011]. The doctrine preserves the believer's intuition that God is what greatness names by binding the standard and the bearer in one being: God is perfect by being what perfection is.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions draw the doctrine up short of what it can answer, once *perfect* is held to the form structural reasoning works in. What sits underneath them is structural, the bind between standard and bearer: if God is the standard of perfection, then perfection is by-reference-to-God; if God is also the perfect creator, then the creator's perfection should propagate into creation.

**Q1.** *If God is a perfect maker, why is creation not perfect?* If God is the *standard* of perfection (that against which all perfection is measured) then perfection is by-reference-to-God, and nothing outside God can be perfect *in the same sense*. A perfect creator need not produce a creation perfect in every respect: the aim may be a finite order, valuable freedom, or goods requiring vulnerability and development. The sharper question is whether this particular creation is proportionate to the creator's stated aims and whether its evils are compatible with perfect goodness and competence. No simple propagation principle settles that issue. The classical analogical move (creation is perfect "in its way," not God's way) either collapses into homonymy (the two senses share only a name) or smuggles in a univocal core (in which case the exclusivity horn revives). The *analogia entis* machinery [Cajetan; @aquinas1947, I.13; @teVelde1995] runs into exactly this dilemma; it does not escape it. Hartshorne's dual-transcendence doctrine [@hartshorne1941] dissolves the standard/bearer dilemma at the level of the framing: God transcends all creatures in the abstract pole's invariant excellence, and surpasses God's own prior states in the concrete pole's growing actualization. Neither horn of Q1 applies straightforwardly, because the abstract pole is not a bearer that propagates perfection into creation, and the concrete pole is not a static standard but a growing excellence that always exceeds its prior state. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: the two forms of transcendence (invariant excellence over creatures; growing excellence over prior states) are attributable to one subject only through the relation between the poles, and [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows that relation requires the structural conditions either pole was framed to escape. The single perfection-predicate is borne, if at all, by a subject whose pole-relation instantiates those conditions rather than escaping them. Swinburne's theistic personalism offers a different handle on Q1 [@swinburne1979; @swinburne2004]: divine perfection is not the metaphysical attribute of a being at the apex of the *analogia entis* but the feature that makes theism the simplest explanatory hypothesis. An infinitely powerful, omniscient, free person is the simplest causal explanation for the universe's existence because a person without physical complexity, spatial location, or temporal constraints on the will is the least arbitrary explanatory posit. On Swinburne's account, *perfect* is as much a methodological as an ontological term: it names the simplicity-of-nature that makes the theistic hypothesis maximally parsimonious. The concern for the Swinburnian recasting is whether simplicity-of-nature for an explanatory agent escapes the chapter's analysis of what any possible explanatory ground requires.

**Q2.** *How do God's maxed-out qualities fit together, if reconciling any two weakens a third?* Perfect-being theology assembles God's attributes by selecting each great-making property and holding that God has each to maximum degree. Whether the maxima compose coherently into a single being has been the central battleground of the literature: Mackie [@mackie1955], Sobel [@sobel2003], and Oppy [@oppy1995; @oppy2006] press the incompossibility cases. These include: omnipotence vs. omniscience (the freedom-and-foreknowledge problem); omnibenevolence vs. omnipotence (the problem of evil); immutability vs. responsiveness (the prayer problem); aseity vs. relatedness; and the stones-too-heavy-to-lift classics. The classical replies attempt either to refine the great-making properties so that the alleged incompatibilities dissolve [@plantinga1974b on free will and foreknowledge; @stump2010 on suffering and love] or to argue that the apparent incompatibilities reflect inadequate understandings of the properties [@adams1999; @murphy2017]. Some refinements relax a traditional property; others clarify its content or deny a contested entailment. The dialectical task is to test each repair rather than assume that every reconciliation is a weakening: the maximally-knowing being on the open-theist refinement does not know what creatures will freely do until they do it; the maximally-loving being on Stump's refinement is constrained by what creaturely natures can receive; the maximally-good being on the free-will-defense refinement permits suffering its omnipotence could prevent. The composition problem is what perfect-being theology has been engaging at every chapter of this book: the repairs surveyed here each purchase composition by relaxation, each relaxation moves the bearer further from what the engine was designed to produce, and no repair has yet composed the maxima without such loss. Hartshorne's dipolar account addresses the composition problem directly: the great-making properties do compose for the dipolar God, because the abstract pole handles the invariant, necessary great-making dimensions (formal omniscience of necessary truths, necessary existence, eternal simplicity) while the concrete pole handles the relational and growth-admitting dimensions: responsive knowing of contingents, cumulative benevolence, aesthetic agency. On the dipolar account, the apparent incompatibilities that drive the classical composition problem dissolve, because each horn of each incompatibility (immutability vs. responsiveness; aseity vs. relatedness; impassibility vs. love) is assigned to a different pole. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses, and it is the convergence point of the pattern traced from §[§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)–6.7.4: the relation between the poles is the directed crossing [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) analyzes, requiring an ordering between abstract and concrete aspects (T), a substantial carrier of both (Φ), and the relational structure in which they are aspects of one being (S). The composition problem the dipolar God was meant to solve reappears at the level of the composite. Swinburne's cumulative-case framework [@swinburne1979; @swinburne2004] reframes the composition question: the relevant test for the composition of great-making properties is not metaphysical co-instantiation in a single infinite being but whether the composite makes theism simpler and more explanatorily powerful than the naturalistic alternative. Swinburne argues that a perfectly free, omniscient, omnipotent person is a simpler hypothesis than the initial state of a purely physical universe, because simplicity for a person is the absence of constraints on the will, and a person unconstrained by physical complexity, spatial location, or temporal structure is as simple as any explanatory posit can be. The concern here is whether the absence of physical constraints constitutes the kind of simplicity relevant to the chapter's analysis: a person unconstrained by physical structure still requires the structural conditions that make personhood (agency, knowledge, will) coherent predicates.

**Q3.** *What is the most loving or most beautiful, if there is no greatest such thing to reach?* Some great-making properties admit a clear notion of maximum (e.g., omnipotence as the property of being able to do every possible thing). Others do not: maximal beauty, maximal love, maximal wisdom. What is the maximum of these? Morris [@morris1991], Murphy [@murphy2017], and Plantinga [@plantinga1974b, ch. 10] defend the notion of *intuitive maxima*: the maximum is whatever the great-making property's content requires; if the content does not admit a maximum, the property is not strictly great-making. The concern here is that this defense secures the maxima by stipulating that any property without a clear maximum is excluded from the great-making list, which converts the engine from *select the great-making properties and maximize them* into *select the maximizable properties and call those the great-making ones*. The exclusion is the structural concern: a perfect being on the resulting account is perfect in the maximizable dimensions only, which leaves open whether the bearer is perfect *simpliciter* or perfect *in those respects in which perfection admits a maximum*.

**Q4.** *How can the greatest possible being hold every perfection, if each one needs conditions God is said to lack?* Each preceding section of this chapter has examined one classical attribute and located its structural conditions outside the divine being on the classical bundle. The engine that produces the attribute list is the perfect-being engine. The concern here at the level of the engine is that the very procedure for selecting the divine attributes produces, when run consistently, an attribute set the bearer cannot bear: the great-making property *necessary existence* requires structural necessity, the great-making property *omnipresence* requires position, the great-making property *omniscience* requires tensed knowledge, the great-making property *creative power* requires directed transition. The engine is faithful to what greatness names; the bearer is defined as lacking the structural conditions of every great-making property the engine produces. Running the engine to completion is what produced the chapter's inversions. Hartshorne agrees that running the classical perfect-being engine to completion produces contradictions, and proposes an alternative dipolar engine: start not with the negation of all structural conditions but with a bifurcated attribution (invariant formal excellence to the abstract pole, maximal responsive creativity to the concrete pole) and let each pole's great-making properties be selected relative to its pole's structural register. The dipolar engine is designed to produce a being that does not generate the chapter's inversions; it selects its great-making properties with the composition problem in view. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) settles: a being with two poles standing in irreducible relation is, on structural analysis, a dyad (two relata in a directed crossing) and [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows that crossing obtains only within T, S, and Φ. The dipolar engine produces an entity that instantiates the structural conditions rather than one beyond them.

**Q5.** *By what standard is God perfect — God's own, or one beyond God?* The tradition has resisted this move on the ground that any standard external to God would be a constraint on God, which is incompatible with aseity. The contemporary literature has pressed alternatives. Murphy [@murphy2017] and Speaks [@speaks2018] defend a methodological perfect-being theology that takes the great-making properties as what the religious life requires of a worship-worthy being, rather than as what the bearer is the standard of. The *Euthyphro*-style move locates the standard in something other than God's will: Adams [@adams1999], Murphy [@murphy2002], and Wielenberg [@wielenberg2014] explore the options for moral perfection. The concern here is that each move that locates the standard outside God admits the structural feature the classical doctrine refused: a standard outside God is a feature of Reality not identical with God, which is what aseity denies. The methodological refinements register, rather than resolve, the structural concern: the standard against which the great-making properties are great is a structural feature of what greatness *is*, and *what greatness is* is a fact about the structure of value within Reality rather than a property of any one bearer.

*What is required.* Worked through, the five pressures spell out what the predicate *perfect* actually depends on. Perfection is either by-reference-to-the-bearer (in which case nothing else can be perfect in the same sense, and the perfect maker's perfection cannot propagate into creation) or by-reference-to-a-standard (in which case the standard is structural and the bearer is at most an instance of it). The analogical reply collapses into homonymy or smuggles in a univocal core. The surveyed reconciliations compose the great-making properties only by relaxation, and each relaxation moves the bearer further from what the engine was designed to produce. Maximal degrees are specifiable for some great-making properties and not others, and the resulting engine selects the maximizable properties rather than the great-making ones. Running the engine to completion produces an attribute set the bearer cannot bear, since the structural conditions of each great-making property are what the bearer is defined as lacking. Locating the standard outside the bearer admits the structural feature aseity refused. After the five pressures, perfection remains a value-laden completeness notion whose compossibility and standard require defense. It cannot be reduced without argument to the modal property of being necessary.

*What is inverted.* The inversion can relocate one aspect of perfection — unconditioned structural completeness — to Nature. But perfection also concerns value, excellence, and fitting activity; necessity alone does not entail any of these. Nature is *perfectus* in the etymological sense of *thoroughly made*, *completed*, but the completion is not the maker's act on a making; it is the modal-structure fact that the conditions of any possible world are the conditions of any possible world. The engine that produced the chapter's inversions produced them faithfully: each great-making property the engine selected pointed at a structural feature the engine then attributed to a bearer defined as lacking it. The inversions returned each property to its structural home. Placed back in the structure that hosts it, *perfect* names the necessity of Nature: the only feature of Reality that cannot have been otherwise, because it is the condition of *otherwise* obtaining at all. Perfection's facet of that necessity is completeness: not the structure's reach across worlds, nor its constancy across time, nor its answering to no higher law, but its lacking nothing it could have, since there is no further condition outside T, S, and Φ for the structure to be missing. The standard of perfection and the bearer of perfection are identical on the structural reading: Nature is what cannot fail to be what it is, and what cannot fail to be what it is is the standard against which lesser perfections are measured. The aporia the engine produces at the level of God dissolves at the level of Nature: there is no separation of standard and bearer to begin with, and the *analogia entis* is a vertical reach within a single structure rather than a relation between two beings of different kinds.

The analysis carries a direct implication for the modal ontological argument. Plantinga's [@plantinga1974b] S5 argument moves from the possibility of maximal greatness to its necessary instantiation in every world: if it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated, and maximal greatness includes necessary existence, then by S5 maximal greatness is instantiated in every possible world. The chapter's pressures challenge the compossibility of a broad classical-theist bundle. Plantinga's modal ontological argument itself defines maximal excellence through omnipotence, omniscience, and moral perfection, with maximal greatness adding necessary existence; atemporality, impassibility, and immutability are additional doctrines. Objections to the broader bundle therefore do not by themselves establish that Plantinga's narrower definition is impossible. If the bundle is not possibly co-instantiated, Plantinga's first premise is blocked at the point of entry, and the S5 inference does not run. The result is carried forward at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10).

## 6.3 Aseity and Modal Standing {#sec-6-3}

This cluster gathers the attributes that fix God's self-existence and modal-temporal standing: necessity ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)), eternity ([§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2)), immutability ([§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3)), and impassibility ([§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4)). Each says how the divine being stands to time, change, and dependence: that God exists of itself, outside succession, beyond alteration, and unaffected from without.

Pressed, each requires the structural conditions it was meant to escape — necessary existence, timeless standing, changelessness, and unaffectedness cannot be specified without reintroducing the succession, persistence, and exchange that T, S, and Φ name. Impassibility ([§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4)) is a boundary-crossing: classified here by attribute-type, its inversion runs on the reach-arm, the demonstration that Nature cannot act on God.

### 6.3.1 Necessity {#sec-6-3-1}

God, the tradition says, does not merely happen to exist. God exists necessarily: in every possible world, unable to be otherwise. The reply is that necessity of that kind is a feature of the modal structure any world must have, not something that can be pinned to a being defined as standing apart from that structure. What exists necessarily, on the argument, is Nature itself.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** The tradition says God doesn't just happen to exist—God exists necessarily, in every possible world, unable to be otherwise. Necessity is the highest compliment the argument can pay. The hitch is what necessity actually describes. To call something necessary is to say it holds in every way things could have gone, which is a fact about the space of possibilities itself, the frame every world shares. A being defined as standing outside that frame can't inherit the frame's built-in status—you can't pin the weather to one house. What genuinely can't fail to be is whatever the frame is made of: time, space, and persistence. Necessity names their standing, not a tenant's.

:::


*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine necessity assembles several reinforcing claims. God exists in every possible world [@anselm1078, II–III; @plantinga1974b; @hartshorne1962]. God exists *a se*: not depending on anything else for divine being [Anselm, *Monologion* 6; @aquinas1947, I.3.4; @pruss2011]. God is the *ens necessarium*, the being whose non-existence is incoherent [@leibniz1714, §§38–45; @leibniz1710]. The same modal status is developed in the Islamic *falsafa* tradition by Avicenna's distinction between *wajib al-wujud* (necessary existence) and *mumkin al-wujud* (possible existence) in the *Kitab al-Shifa* [@mcginnis2010; @adamson2013], with the *wajib*'s necessity made the ground of the *mumkin*'s possibility. On the most developed contemporary refinement, God grounds the modal structure itself: there are no possibilities prior to God for God to range over (Leftow, *God and Necessity* [@leftow2012]; cf. @morrisMenzel1986 on theistic activism). Each move tries to keep necessity from being a feature borrowed from elsewhere by a being whose excellence might otherwise have been contingent. At its most ambitious, the doctrine reaches for a being whose non-existence is held to be incoherent precisely because the being's existence is held to be what makes coherence possible to detect at all.

*What cannot be answered.* Eight questions fall to divine necessity that the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning addresses, cannot answer. What runs underneath all eight is structural, modal invariance (§[§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)–2.1.5): modal status does not vary across worlds. What is necessary is necessarily necessary; what is possible is necessarily possible; what is impossible is necessarily impossible. A modal structure is not the kind of thing whose status another agent or being could fix. The S5 framework on which the necessity operator runs here is defended for metaphysical-modal scope at [§1.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-1) and [§2.1.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-3). The possible worlds the operator ranges over are read here in actualist terms: ways the one actual Nature could be configured, the alternatives grounded in the structural conditions T, S, and Φ rather than in concrete Lewisian worlds standing alongside it, in merely abstract ersatz constructions, or in primitive potentiality; the alternatives are alternatives of Nature, not parallel universes beside it. The eight pressures run three at the level of the predicate, five at the level of the conditions necessity-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *In which possible worlds does the ground of all possible worlds exist?* Modal predicates can apply non-trivially to an invariant subject: necessary beings, propositions, and mathematical objects are standard candidates. The sharper issue is whether God is represented within the modal domain or proposed as its ground, and how those two roles relate. A modal subject is a coordinate of modal space: existing in some worlds and not others (contingent), in every world (necessary), or in no world (impossible). The classical doctrine wants God to be a modal subject in the strongest sense (necessary in every world) while defining God as outside the modal structure, as the being whose existence makes that structure possible at all [@leftow2012; @pruss2011]. Wanting both at once is the structural difficulty itself. If God is constitutive of the modal structure, then God's existence is not a coordinate over which the operator ranges; it is a part of the apparatus that makes ranging possible. The verdict the operator returns is then degenerate: trivially-true (every world is God-grounded) or trivially-false (no world contains God as an element of its furniture), with neither tracking the informative modal claim the believer's intuition reaches for. The believer who says *God could have existed* (or its negation, *God could not have failed to exist*) is making a modal claim about a being whose existence is alleged to be the precondition of any *could*. The claim cannot be both a substantive modal predication and a claim about the precondition of modal predication without trading on the very ambiguity the predicate was supposed to settle. The mathematical analogue is instructive: *possibly 2+2=4* collapses harmlessly into the truth claim itself because mathematical truth is itself the abstract overlay of what quantitative event-modality supports, and the operator's trivialization preserves the content. For God's existence the trivialization is the cost: the believer wants the operator to do substantive work, and the doctrine has removed what the operator could substantively track. The line of treating divine necessity as ontological independence [@prussRasmussen2018] preserves the verbal *necessary* by relocating it to aseity (Q4); the line of grounding modality in God [@leftow2012; @morrisMenzel1986] applies the predicate at the level whose conditions it presupposes (Q6). The present pressure runs prior to both: before asking whether necessity-as-aseity or necessity-as-frame-grounding can do the work, the question is whether the modal predicates apply to God at all. The seven pressures that follow proceed under the assumption (granted for the sake of the argument) that the predicates do apply, and find that each of their applications has been preserved by removing what the predicate tracks.

**Q2.** *If all the proof shows is that something exists in every world, what makes it a being rather than the structure?* Anselm's *id quo maius cogitari nequit* (*Proslogion* II) reasons that the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality, since existence-in-reality exceeds existence-in-the-understanding alone. Gaunilo's island and Kant's predicate-objection are well-known; Plantinga's [@plantinga1974b] modal recasting, anticipated by a decade in Hartshorne's revival of the modal ontological argument (*Anselm's Discovery* [@hartshorne1965]), the structural ancestor of the modern form, answers them at the level of the predicate by treating necessary existence as instantiation in every possible world rather than as a real property added to a thing. The recasting is genuinely available, and the formal validity of S5 ontological arguments is not in question. What is in question is the being the argument's conclusion picks out. Plantinga's premise (it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated) entails, in S5, that maximal greatness is instantiated in every world. Maximal greatness does not name whatever is instantiated in every world; it includes maximal excellence—omniscience, omnipotence, and moral perfection—across every world. Showing that T, S, and Φ are invariant would not show that they satisfy those personal predicates. The argument has shown that something modally invariant must obtain. It has not yet shown that the modally invariant something is a being defined by the negation of the structural conditions invariance requires. The conclusion fits Nature more cleanly than it fits the being the doctrine names.

**Q3.** *If 'exists in every world' is a fact about the worlds, what has it told you about God?* Kant's [@kant1781] objection has been treated as resolved by the modal recasting. The resolution is only partial. Existence in every possible world can be treated as a de re modal property of a subject as well as represented by a fact about the modal landscape. The live question is whether the subject is coherently specified and whether its necessity is explained rather than whether the grammar permits de re predication. Pruss and Rasmussen [@prussRasmussen2018] and Leftow [@leftow2012] argue that necessary existence is properly construed as ontological independence rather than as cross-world ubiquity, and so escapes the Kantian concern at a different level. The reply rephrases necessity as aseity (treated at Q4) and so shifts the locus rather than answering the original question. Even granting the de re reading, the informative content of the predicate lies not in an additional way the being is but in the relation between the being and the modal structure. The distinction is *de re* / *de dicto*: the modal-structure necessity affirmed here is *de dicto* of Nature (necessarily, Nature obtains) and *de re* of its conditions (each of T, S, and Φ is such that it necessarily obtains) while no *de re* necessity attaches to a being specified apart from the modal structure. The same point is pressed from the side of identity at [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1), Q3; here it returns from the side of necessity itself.

**Q4.** *If aseity just means depending on nothing, what can it ground?* The classical reading of divine aseity (being-from-itself, *a se*) holds that God depends on nothing for divine being [@aquinas1947, I.3.4]. The doctrine is sometimes pressed into service as the ground of divine necessity: God exists necessarily because God exists *a se*. The concern here is that aseity, fully stated, is the negation of every dependence, not a positive ground from which existence flows. To exist *a se* is to fail to depend, and a failure to depend is not yet a positive explanatory base. What grounds the necessity, on the doctrine, is asked for and not delivered: aseity tells us what God is not (dependent), without telling us what makes God's existence not-otherwise. The analysis here points, in answer, to Nature: T, S, and Φ do not depend on anything else, because there is no anything-else for them to depend on: Nature is the condition for there being something rather than nothing for any subsequent dependence to obtain within. Aseity, on this reading, is the negative shadow of Nature's positive role.

**Q5.** *What makes creation contingent, if God's act is God's necessary nature?* If God's nature is necessarily what it is, and God's act is identical with God's nature (the strongest version of divine simplicity), then God's act is necessarily what it is, and what God's act produces is necessarily what God's act produces [@mullins2013; @mullins2016; @tomaszewski2019]. Creation collapses into necessity. The classical reply distinguishes God's act-in-itself from the act's *terminus ad extra*, holding the act necessary while leaving the terminus contingent [@aquinas1947, I.19; @stump2003; @dolezal2017]. The reply preserves the contingency of creation by introducing a structured relation between act and effect that the doctrine of strong simplicity is supposed to disallow. The concern here is that the more strictly simplicity is held, the more sharply the modal collapse follows; the more relaxedly simplicity is held, the more the doctrine has surrendered the ground from which divine necessity was supposed to flow. The doctrine wants both (strict enough simplicity to ground necessity, loose enough simplicity to let creation be contingent) and these are two incompatible commitments joined only by the shared term. Hartshorne's dipolar account addresses the modal-collapse pressure directly: God's abstract pole is necessarily and immutably what it is; the concrete pole actualizes contingently, responsive to the open alternatives creaturely co-creation supplies, and so provides the modal contrast creation requires without implicating the abstract pole in contingency. On the dipolar reading, the modal-collapse concern targets the abstract pole alone, and the concrete pole's contingency is the structural resource the doctrine needed. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses against dipolar theism generally: the abstract pole sustains the concrete pole's act-relations only across the directed crossing between them, and that crossing obtains within T, S, and Φ. The modal-collapse question does not dissolve; it migrates from the necessity predicate to the abstract/concrete relation, where [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) records it as a standing account rather than a solution.

**Q6.** *How do you ground possibility by an act, when acting already needs it?* Leftow's [@leftow2012] theistic activism is the most ambitious contemporary defense. What is possible is grounded in divine activity; there are no possibilities prior to God for God's selection to range over. The doctrine preserves divine sovereignty over the deepest layer the doctrine could reach. The structural concern is the one [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q7 raises at the level of agency: to ground a modal structure is to stand in an asymmetric explanatory relation to it. The relation requires determinate ground, grounded content, and direction; it need not be a temporal transition from ungrounded to grounded. To remove those conditions while preserving ground is to keep the verb and lose the structure that gave it its content. Pruss [@pruss2011], Mullins [@mullins2016], and others have raised structural concerns from inside the literature. The point this section adds is that the deepest version of the doctrine, when its predicates are read in the structure that supports them, names Nature and not a being beyond it. Modal invariance is a structural fact about how possibility works, not a contingent product of any agent's exercise. Pruss's positive argument presses from the other side: that only an agent freely selecting among possibilities explains why one contingent cosmos is realized rather than another. Granted in full, the selecting it posits must distinguish alternatives and explain the contingent realization. A timeless-selection model avoids a temporal transition in God but still owes an account of differentiated alternatives and contingent effects. The contingent realization it seeks to explain is Nature's own: the actual configuration among those the structure permits, which calls for no selector standing outside the conditions any selecting would presuppose.

**Q7.** *By what logic does God author logic?* Descartes (Letters to Mesland [@descartes1644]) extends divine sovereignty to the eternal truths themselves: God could have made 2+2=5, and God's not having done so is a free divine choice. The Thomistic mainstream rejects the move [@aquinas1947, I.25.3] by indexing omnipotence to logical possibility — God can do whatever does not involve contradiction, and *square circle* names no candidate for divine action because it names no candidate for anything. The contemporary literature [@swinburne1977; @wierenga1989; @plantinga1980] sides decisively with the Thomistic restriction. The cost is that logical necessity is treated as a condition on divine action rather than a product of it, and the locus of the deepest necessity has moved beyond the being. The options include external constraint, grounding in divine nature, identity between divine rationality and logical truth, and voluntarist authorship. The latter faces the presupposition problem; the nature and identity accounts instead face explanatory circularity and content burdens.

**Q8.** *What makes one being necessary, if necessity belongs to the frame it sits in?* The phrase *necessary being* presupposes a contrast with contingent being and a category broad enough to contain both. Beings, on the contrast, range from those that might not have been to those that could not fail to be, with the necessary case at one limit. The concern here is that the limit is not a maximally exalted being. It is a structural condition. What cannot fail to be, when the modal verb is taken seriously, is what would have to be in place for any *could-have-been-otherwise* to be a coherent thought. Possibility presupposes a frame within which alternatives can be set against each other. The frame requires a manifold across which alternatives can be located (S), an ordering across which they can be considered as alternatives at all (T), and a substantial reality whose features the alternatives are alternatives of (Φ). Treating one being within the frame as the being of necessity in its highest form tries to import the modal status of the frame into one of its inhabitants. The status does not transfer. Hartshorne's dual-transcendence doctrine (*Man's Vision of God* [@hartshorne1941]) attempts to escape the transfer problem by bifurcating the necessity: the abstract pole carries modal invariance; the concrete pole carries contingent, responsive actuality; the same subject bears both by being the single reality whose abstract dimension is invariant and whose concrete dimension is what creaturely events contingently make it. The structural concern is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: a single subject bears two irreducible modal statuses only by way of the relation between its poles, and that relation is the directed crossing [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows obtains within S, T, and Φ, the very frame whose status the transfer problem found could not pass to an inhabitant. The bifurcation relocates the transfer problem into the pole-relation rather than escaping it.

*What is required.* Eight pressures surface what the predicate *necessary* actually runs on. Before it substantively applies at all, its subject has to be a coordinate of the alternation the operator ranges over: a being defined as a constituent of the modal structure rather than as a value within it is not a candidate for the modal verb. Invariance can characterize both a modal framework and entities represented as existing throughout it. The structural account must argue comparatively for Nature as the best ground of necessity rather than infer that no invariant entity can be necessary. The frame requires differentiation among alternatives, modal relations, and a domain or bearer of modal content. Calling these roles Space, Time, and Substance is a substantive identification that depends on the earlier machinery; possible worlds need not themselves be temporally ordered. Necessity is the modal status of these three in their joint operation. Two further conditions follow negatively. The not-otherwise of the necessary is what is in place, not what fails to obtain, so aseity construed as the bare negation of dependence does not do the grounding work the doctrine asks of it. And whatever could author the modal structure appears to presuppose structural conditions only the frame itself can supply, which leaves agent-authored modality facing a presupposition problem at the level the deepest version of the doctrine reaches. The structural form of this reasoning replaces the Principle of Sufficient Reason rather than running through it: where strong PSR demands a sufficient reason for every contingent fact and weak PSR a possible one, the present account reads necessity from the conditions any *otherwise* presupposes. These are not optional supports the predicate could trade among. They are what the verb *necessarily* picks out when its referent is examined.

One rival reading of this result must be met, since it grants that something is modally invariant and presses only on its number. Aggregation arguments [@rasmussen2009; @prussRasmussen2018] hold that multiple necessary foundations collapse into one, and so ask why T, S, and Φ are not three necessary beings whose constant co-occurrence requires a single ground to bind them (the structural form of monotheism) rather than one Nature. The reply runs on two levels, and either suffices. First, there is no seam to bind: T, S, and Φ are not three separable necessities that happen to co-occur but are mutually constitutive (succession with nothing persistent to undergo it is not time, a persistent something with no interval to stand in is not substance, an interval with no succession across it is not a manifold), so their co-instantiation is internal and analytic, one structure under three descriptions rather than an arrangement an external ground maintains ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)). To ask what binds them is to ask what binds a figure's three-sidedness to its three-angledness: nothing does, because they are one fact differently stated. Second, even were the seam granted, binding could not be the work of a being beyond Nature. A proposed binder may ground without acting temporally, so the issue is not exhausted by an act/no-act disjunction. If it acts, it operates in T, S, and Φ, a denizen of the conditions rather than a ground above them, and by the transfer result (Q8) cannot itself carry the necessity such a ground would require. If it does not act, it is nothing more than the standing co-obtaining of the conditions, which is Nature already, relabeled. And the necessary needs no binding in the first place: holding-together is a function only where the parties could come apart, and there is no world in which T, S, and Φ decohere, so a binder of the necessary prevents an impossible collapse and does no work. The grounding refinement (that such a being does not hold the conditions against collapse but confers their necessity) returns to the results of Q4 and Q6: a ground that confers necessity is either itself the prior necessary base, in which case it is Nature under another name and the transfer is conceded, or it is contingent, in which case it cannot confer necessity at all. This is the stage at which the naturalist and monotheist readings of the modally invariant finally diverge, and where the divergence is located and carried ([§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2)): the monotheist reads the unity of the necessary as a personal ground binding a plurality, while the present account reads it as the triconditionality of one structure — requiring no binder because admitting no seam.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** Grant that something must hold in every possible world. Why is that one Nature rather than three necessary items—time, space, and persistence—that happen to travel together and need a single ground to bind them? That's monotheism's opening. Two replies, either one fatal. First, there's no seam to bind: succession with nothing to persist through it isn't time, persistence with no interval isn't substance—the three are one structure under three names, and asking what binds them is like asking what binds a triangle's three sides to its three angles. Second, any binder either acts, and so runs on the very conditions it was meant to ground, or it doesn't act, and is just those conditions standing together—Nature already, relabeled.

:::


A second rival reading presses not on the number of the necessary but on the contingent. Pruss's cosmological argument from the Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact (the conjunction of all contingent truths, the actual cosmos with just these features and no others) holds that this conjunction is itself contingent and, on the Principle of Sufficient Reason, demands an explanation that cannot lie within it, terminating in a necessary being whose act explains why this conjunction obtains rather than another [@prussRasmussen2018]. The argument is distinct from the aggregation just met: it asks not why the necessary foundations are one rather than three, but why the contingent whole is this one rather than another. The reply is the restricted Principle of Sufficient Reason this section has already named. What the argument needs is the strong PSR (every contingent fact has a sufficient reason) and that is the principle the present account replaces rather than honors. The necessary frame T, S, and Φ is no member of the contingent conjunction and so is not among what the argument asks after: it is the type, it is necessary, and against the necessary the explanatory demand runs out of contrast, exactly as Q4 and [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3) found. The particular configuration the conjunction records (this cosmos, these constants) is the token, and the token is contingent; its explanation is the cosmic-historical one [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) develops, not a selecting act by a being outside the frame, since any such selecting (Q6) runs on the very conditions the frame supplies. Pruss's charge that a brute contingent whole is intolerable has force only against the strong PSR that generates it; under the restricted PSR the contingent token is not a necessity-demanding brute fact but a configuration the necessary frame permits and cosmic history fills in, and the regress of contingent explanation terminates not in a necessary being but in the necessary frame whose modes the token varies. The stopping point is marked, not helped to: the type is necessary, the token is not ([§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7)).

*What is inverted.* Necessity is what cannot fail to be, and what cannot fail to be is what would have to be in place for any *otherwise* to be a coherent thought. The English *necessarily* renders the Latin *ne + cedere*: not to yield, not to withdraw. The word that names what cannot be otherwise is built from the impossibility of retreating, and retreating is a structured act: succession of positions (T), distance to retreat across (S), persistent something that does the retreating (Φ). The etymology of necessity illustrates non-yielding but does not analyze the modal operator: □ expresses truth in every accessible world, not the impossibility of a literal act of retreat. What □ names, when the language is read against what makes the language coherent, is the structural conditions whose withdrawal is impossible. Necessity is the modal status of T, S, and Φ themselves. What necessity names within that modal status is its reach across worlds: there is no possible world from which T, S, and Φ are absent, because a world from which they were absent would be no world at all. The classical predicate has been pointing, across its formulations, at the modal status of Nature while the doctrine has located that status in a being from which the conditions that constitute it have been removed. Nature has the modal status; the being beyond Nature has none of what the status requires.

### 6.3.2 Eternity {#sec-6-3-2}

Classical theism places God wholly outside time, living all of time "at once." But the things the believer's God does (knowing what is happening now, responding to a prayer, acting at a moment) all need a before and an after. Placing God outside time keeps the word "eternal" but removes what makes those acts possible.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine eternity assembles three reinforcing claims. God is *aeternus* in the strict Boethian sense: *interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio*, the simultaneous and complete possession of unbounded life [@boethius524, V.6]. God is atemporal: outside time, with no before, no after, no succession in the divine being itself [@augustine397, XI; @aquinas1947, I.10; @stumpKretzmann1981]. On the most developed contemporary refinement, the eternal life stands in eternal–temporal (ET) simultaneity with every temporal moment alike, with the eternal *now* equally adjacent to every creaturely *now* [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @rogers2000; @helm2010].

The competing tradition (divine sempiternity, everlastingness, omnitemporality) keeps God within time but extends the divine duration without limit [@wolterstorff1975; @wolterstorff2001; @hasker1989; @mullins2016; @craig2001c; @craig2001b]. Craig combines the everlasting position with A-theoretic tense-realism (the tensed view on which the *now* is ontologically privileged and time genuinely passes) and with the Kalām cosmological argument's reliance on a temporal beginning of the universe ("The Kalam Cosmological Argument" in *The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology* [@craigSinclair2009]); the chapter's engagement with the Kalām's premise that the universe began to exist runs at [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2), where the Kalām cosmological argument is engaged directly, and at Chapter 7, where the structure of the cosmological *beginning* is examined directly. Each move tries to keep eternity from being a feature borrowed from time, with one party preserving transcendence by removing the temporal conditions and the other preserving relation by retaining them.

Hartshorne's dipolar theism [@hartshorne1948; @hartshorne1984] proposes a third line: God's abstract pole (the invariant, necessary, essential nature) is atemporal and immutable in the Boethian sense; God's concrete pole (the cumulative, responsive actuality in which God genuinely experiences and responds to creaturely events) is temporal, successive, and grows with the world's creative advance. The dipolar account is designed to buy classical atemporality for the essential register while preserving genuine temporal responsiveness for the relational register. Q3 (whether duration is coherent without extent) presses the abstract pole. Q4 (whether sempiternity preserves transcendence) presses the concrete pole. Whether the bifurcation itself can be held together is pressed against dipolar theism generally at [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3), where the abstract/concrete pole-relation is shown to be a directed crossing obtaining only within T, S, and Φ.

In its sharpest classical formulation, the doctrine asks for a life whose unboundedness is preserved by removing every dimension along which duration could be tracked.

*What cannot be answered.* Six questions ask of divine eternity what the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning can take up, leaves unanswered. The six pressures run one at the level of the predicate itself, five at the level of the conditions eternity-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *When is a timeless life possessed all at once?* The Boethian formula is the most enduring formulation in the tradition, and it bears more argumentative weight than its length suggests. *Tota simul* (wholly at once) is the move under pressure. Possession-at-once requires a possessor and a possessed; if the possessed is unbounded life, the life in question must have temporal extent, since unboundedness is the modifier of an extent. The eternal *tota simul* possesses an extended life all at once, which is not yet a coherent description until we ask what the *at* anchors. The Boethian defender's primary reply is that the dilemma misreads the doctrine: eternity is not a quasi-temporal manifold but a *sui generis* mode of being whose *at* is not a temporal index. The reply is genuinely available, and the present reading does not insist on a temporal reading of *aeternitas*. The concern reformulates. Even granting the *sui generis* mode, the doctrine wants the eternal life to be in operative cognitive and causal contact with temporal events: to know creatures, to act in history, to respond to prayer, to sustain in being from moment to moment. Each of those predicates requires a determinate asymmetric relation between the eternal pole and the temporal event. If the *at* of eternity supplies that relation, eternity has structural content of its own; if it does not, the *tota simul* preserves co-presence at the cost of losing the operative predicates the doctrine wants the co-presence to carry. Leftow [@leftow1991] develops the most careful contemporary defense; the present reading is that the formula succeeds at marking what the doctrine wants and does not, on either disambiguation, supply the structural relations the predicates downstream require. A parallel concern attaches to the doctrine's principal alternative formulation. The Augustinian–Thomistic phrasing of divine timelessness as *being outside time* (Augustine, *Confessions* XI; ST I.10) trades on a predicate whose ordinary content is spatial-positional: to be *outside* X is to be at a location not enclosed by X, with the relation running along S. The doctrine wants *outside* to do non-spatial work; the classical reply, that the term is meant analogically rather than literally, preserves the verbal gesture by emptying the relation of the structure that gave the term its content. *Outside X* requires X to be a region, the subject to be not-in-the-region, and the not-in relation to track containment; when X is time and the subject is non-temporal, the analogical use preserves the verbal form and reduces the substantive content to *not-temporal*, which is the predicate the formulation was supposed to non-vacuously specify. The objection that *outside* has unproblematic non-spatial uses — outside the set, outside the law, outside the genus — is granted; the point does not rest on the spatial etymology. Take the strongest such reading, on which *outside time* asserts a determinate content: that the divine being is a member of no temporal order and bears no temporal property intrinsically. That reading is not vacuous, but its content is purely privative, and the privation is the difficulty rather than its avoidance. A being that bears no temporal property intrinsically stands in no intrinsic before-and-after relation. Classical eternalists can nevertheless posit extrinsic relations to temporally ordered events and tenseless knowledge of their locations. The burden is to explain indexical knowledge and responsive agency without importing intrinsic succession, not to assume that every such relation is intrinsic. So the contentful reading of *outside* does not escape the first horn; it reaches it by another line: the spatial reading empties the relation of structure, while the privative reading keeps the relation contentful only as a denial, and a denial supplies none of what the downstream predicates run on — that supply is the burden the extrinsic-relations account still owes. *Tota simul* and *outside time* are the doctrine's two principal verbal moves: the first preserves co-presence at the cost of the asymmetric relations the doctrine wants the co-presence to carry; the second preserves transcendence at the cost of the structural relation *outside* implicitly relies on.

**Q2.** *By what shared time is a timeless life simultaneous with a temporal one?* Stump and Kretzmann [@stumpKretzmann1981] define ET-simultaneity as a *sui generis* relation between eternal and temporal entities: the eternal life is simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal, and without the temporal moments thereby being simultaneous with one another. The relation does the structural work the doctrine asks of it: keeps eternal causation, eternal knowing, and eternal love in operative contact with temporal events without temporalizing the eternal pole. The concern is not that *simultaneous with* must mean clock-simultaneity. The defender is right that ET-simultaneity is a defined technical relation, not the ordinary relation. The concern reformulates: a defined technical relation is operatively contentful only insofar as it preserves the asymmetric structure the believer's reports require. The believer's prayer at 3 PM Tuesday was offered after their morning confession and before their evening weeping; the asymmetry is part of what the prayer is. ET-simultaneity can preserve the prayer's place in the creaturely temporal order without reproducing that succession intrinsically in God. The challenge is whether one timeless act can explain different responses to differently located events while remaining simple and unchanged. Leftow's [@leftow1991] formal development sharpens the position, and Mullins [@mullins2016] presses the sustained published case against ET-simultaneity — that the relation either collapses into a temporal mode or fails to secure the asymmetric contact it was introduced to provide; the question the present reading presses is which disambiguation the doctrine takes, not whether the technical relation is well-defined.

**Q3.** *How long is a life that takes no time?* Boethius keeps *life* in the formula. Creaturely life has duration, while the classical doctrine proposes a non-successive mode of life; the coherence of that analogical extension is what must be tested. Aquinas [@aquinas1947, I.10] takes the further step of identifying divine eternity with divine being itself, so that God's being and God's life are the same eternal *now* without succession or extension. The doctrine preserves divine immutability by removing every dimension along which duration could be tracked. The concern here is that what remains is a *now* with no internal differentiation: not the eternal life of a being but the bare instant of an event. An unextended instant is not an everlasting duration. But the eternalist does not identify eternity with a temporal instant; the proposal is a distinct mode of existence, which faces a relation and content burden rather than this simple limiting-case objection. Stump [@stump2003] and Helm [@helm2010] defend the position by treating *now* as analogically rather than univocally applied, and the move is genuinely available; the cost is that the predicate the doctrine wanted (life in its fullest form) now attaches to a mode that has yet to show it can host the conditions life requires.

**Q4.** *How does endless time put a being beyond time?* Wolterstorff [@wolterstorff1975], Hasker [@hasker1989], and Mullins [@mullins2016] develop the alternative tradition: God is everlasting, not timeless. God exists through time, with infinite duration, and the divine being is genuinely affected by, and responsive to, what occurs at each temporal moment. The position preserves the relational vocabulary the doctrine performs ([§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2) takes this up directly) at the cost of placing God within the temporal manifold the classical doctrine had placed God beyond. The concern here is parallel to those raised in [§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3) and [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2): a being within time has temporally located acts and knowledge. This revises strict atemporality but need not surrender every form of transcendence or ultimacy; it shifts the burden to aseity and temporal dependence. The two positions (timeless and everlasting) are best read as the doctrine splitting along a structural incompatibility, with each branch keeping one half of what the unified doctrine had wanted.

**Q5.** *How does a theory of time deliver a being out of time?* Recent defenses of divine atemporality [@leftow1991; @leftow2012; @helm2010] sometimes appeal to the B-theory of time: the tenseless view on which all moments are equally real and the *now* is indexical rather than ontologically privileged. On the B-theory, the move from divine atemporality to divine simultaneity-with-every-moment becomes more tractable: the eternal pole stands in tenseless relation to a tenselessly extended manifold, and the modal asymmetry the A-theory introduces is set aside. The concern here is that the B-theory does not remove temporal structure; it relocates it. Tenseless before-and-after relations are still T, and a being eternally adjacent to a tenseless manifold is still a being whose adjacency requires the manifold to be the manifold it is. Craig's A-theoretic objection presses the dilemma from the other side: if tense is fundamental rather than indexical, divine atemporality has to stand in tenseless relation to a manifold whose primary facts are tensed, and the doctrine's reach for B-theoretic support trades one structural cost (the tenseless adjacency the eternal pole still requires) for another (the disjunction between the eternal pole's tenseless relations and the temporal pole's tensed facts), with the cost on the A-theoretic side sharper than the doctrine's B-theoretic refinements register [@craig2001c]. The B-theory clarifies the doctrine without dissolving the structural difficulty. T's standing on either A- or B-theory is taken up at [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6); the present concern is that whichever theory of time is correct, eternity-talk presupposes the structure rather than transcends it.

**Q6.** *What does "unchanging" add to a being with no time in which to change?* The classical bundle ties eternity tightly to immutability: God is eternal because God does not change, and God does not change because God is eternal. Mullins [@mullins2016] presses the dependency from the inside: the doctrines do not require each other in the form the tradition holds them, and a more relaxed immutability (God's character does not change, though God's relations to creatures do) can survive without strict atemporality. The concern this section adds is that the relaxation removes the motivation for the strongest atemporalist moves: if God can change in some respects, the question why God cannot change in temporal respects becomes a question about which respects rather than about temporality as such. The doctrine of strict atemporality, on the present reading, is the doctrine of strict immutability under a different name, and the contemporary moves that loosen one have already loosened the other.

*What is required.* What the six pressures jointly surface is what *eternal* actually runs on. The Boethian formula keeps *life* in it, and life is the modifier of an extent; remove every dimension along which extent can be tracked, and there is nothing for the modifier to modify. The relational predicates the doctrine asks the eternal life to carry (knowing creatures, acting in history, responding to prayer, sustaining in being from moment to moment) each require an ordering between not-yet and now without which the verbs lack determinate content. *Simultaneous with* is a relation, and a defined technical relation is operatively contentful only insofar as it preserves the asymmetric structure the believer's reports turn on. A temporal moment with no extent is not an everlasting duration, while a proposed timeless mode must be assessed on its own relational semantics. The B-theory clarifies the doctrine without dissolving the difficulty: tenseless before-and-after relations are still T, and a being eternally adjacent to a tenseless manifold is still a being whose adjacency requires the manifold to be the manifold it is. And the classical bundle of eternity-with-immutability does not survive its own loosening: the tradition has held the doctrines as if they entailed each other, and the contemporary moves that relax one have already relaxed the other. Temporal relations structure creaturely events and every everlasting model. A timeless model must explain its contact with that order. This does not by itself identify eternity with T's modal status.

*What is inverted.* The inversion relocates durational continuity and presence-throughout to T. Strict timeless eternity remains a rival proposal whose coherence depends on its account of relation to temporal life. The English *eternal* comes through Old French *éternel* from the Latin *aeternus*, formed on *aevum*: *age*, *lifetime*, *span*; the sense the word carries is durational, presence-throughout. (The further scholastic reading that hears in it *of every age* is lexically contested: *aeviternitas* names the angelic *aevum*, a mode between time and eternity technically distinct from the Boethian *aeternitas*; and the inversion does not rest on it.) The classical tradition reaches for a life that is *interminabilis*, unbounded, and names Nature. Nature has no terminus because it is the condition for there being termini at all. It has the *tota simul* the Boethian formula reaches for, in the only sense the formula can be made to bear: every moment is a moment of the same medium, with Nature present at each as the condition of the moment's being a moment. Presence-throughout is not a duration the divine life possesses but the structural status of T: the condition under which there is any moment to be present at, with no age outside it from which *every* could be a partial quantification. The classical predicate, read against the structure that hosts the predicating, has been naming Nature's durational status under a name the tradition has assigned to a being beyond it.

### 6.3.3 Immutability {#sec-6-3-3}

Immutability is the claim that God never changes in any way. The strain is that the things the tradition also says God does (beginning to create, answering a prayer, becoming incarnate) are all transitions from one state to another. Keeping the action-language while denying God any transition leaves the verbs owing an account of how their direction and contingency arise from an unchanging source.

*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology holds that God is immutable: God does not change, cannot change, and does not undergo any sort of intrinsic variation across time, situation, or relation (Aquinas, *ST* I.9.1; Augustine, *Confessions* XI; Anselm, *Proslogion* XXII).
