The doctrine has Aristotelian roots in the unmoved mover (*Metaphysics* Λ.7) and binds tightly to simplicity ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)), necessity ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)), and pure actuality: a simple, necessary, fully actual being has no potency to be otherwise, and so does not change. Contemporary defenders include Dolezal [-@dolezal2017], Feser [-@feser2017], Weinandy [-@weinandy2000], and Stump [-@stump2003]; the doctrine has been refined into *weak immutability* [@mullins2016; @pawl2020] that distinguishes intrinsic from relational change. The position immutability has traditionally held, fully stated, is that God's intrinsic state (essence, knowledge, will, relations to creatures) is invariant across any possible difference in creaturely state, and that the apparent changes in God's relations to creatures (becoming the creator of *this* world rather than another, becoming incarnate, responding to prayer) are *Cambridge changes* (mere shifts in how God stands related to a changing world, involving no alteration in God) rather than real changes in God.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions confront immutability with what the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning reaches, cannot answer. What underlies the five is structural: the difference between *acting* and *being acted upon* depends on directed transition, and the doctrine's strategy is to deny directed transition of the divine being while preserving the action-language the believer's life rests on.

**Q1.** *How does a being that cannot change begin to create?* Pure actuality (the property of having no unrealized potential) is the metaphysical floor of immutability (Aquinas, *ST* I.3.1). Creation requires a transition in the creature from not existing to existing. Whether it also requires intrinsic transition in the cause is precisely what the classical timeless-causation model denies. The classical reply locates the transition entirely in the creature: God eternally wills the creature; the creature comes to be in time; God does not undergo any change in the willing (Aquinas, *ST* I.46.1; *SCG* II.35). The concern here is that the eternal willing of a temporal creation is the relational structure the believer's prayer life and providence rest on: prayer at t_1 that affects God's relation to the world at t_2. The Cambridge-change reply preserves God's intrinsic invariance by relocating the variance into the creature, but religious language of deliberation and response can suggest intrinsic change. The issue is whether that language is literal, analogical, or accommodated to creaturely perspective; intuition alone does not settle it.

**Q2.** *How does a mind that never changes know that the present has changed?* If God knows that *Caesar crosses the Rubicon* before, during, and after the crossing, the *knowledge-content* differs by tense even if the *fact* is timeless. The classical reply is that God knows the timeless fact and that the tensed truths are creaturely modes of access to the same fact (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.13; [@stumpKretzmann1981; @helm2010]). The concern here is that a being who knows *that Caesar crosses the Rubicon* without knowing *that Caesar will cross* or *has crossed* either lacks information the creature has (in which case omniscience fails) or has the tensed information by some mode the timeless-fact reading does not deliver [@prior1959; @kretzmann1966; @mullins2016]. The Boethian reply (eternal vision of all times at once) preserves immutability by relocating God outside time, which makes the tense-bearing structure of knowing about a temporal world the structural feature the doctrine forecloses.

**Q3.** *How does the maker undergo no transition, when making is the transition?* The creature comes from non-being to being. The classical reply treats the transition as entirely in the creature: it is the creature that transitions; God neither pre-exists the act in any tensed sense (atemporality) nor changes by performing it (immutability). The concern here is that *bringing-into-being* is the paradigm of directed transition ([§2.6.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-2)): the act has a *from* (nothing) and a *to* (the creature), and the directedness is what the act consists in. To attribute the act to an unchanged agent requires an account of how causal direction and contingent effect arise from one invariant intention. It is not semantically empty merely because the transition occurs in the effect. The reply that God is the *terminus a quo* (the starting point *from which*) of the transition without undergoing it makes the *acting* into a structural feature of the world's hosting of the act, not of the agent's performing it.

**Q4.** *How does the unchangeable become flesh?* The doctrine of the incarnation holds that the second person of the Trinity *became* man (*ho logos sarx egeneto*, John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined the union as one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human. The classical reply is that the incarnation is a change in the human nature, not in the divine nature: the divine Word does not become human in the sense of acquiring a property, but human nature becomes the Word's nature in the sense of being assumed (Aquinas, *ST* III.16; Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Unity of Christ*). The concern here is that *assumption* is itself a directed transition: there is a *before* the assumption (in which the human nature does not exist as the Word's) and an *after* (in which it does). The reply that the assumption is eternal in the divine register and temporal in the human register locates the directedness in the human register only, which makes the *becoming* of John 1:14 a structural feature of the human side; the divine side is what *does not become* anything.

**Q5.** *How is a change in God's relations not a change in God?* Pawl [-@pawl2020] and Mullins [-@mullins2016] develop *weak immutability*: God does not change in essential properties or intrinsic state, but does change in accidental or relational properties (e.g., becoming-the-creator-of-this-world, being-prayed-to, becoming-incarnate). The concern here is that *change in relational properties* is what *real change in relations* names, and the classical doctrine's whole strategy has been to deny real relations between God and creatures (Aquinas, *ST* I.13.7; *SCG* II.12). The weak-immutability refinement admits variance back into the divine being's relations, which is what the strong doctrine refused. The refinement is honest about what the believer's intuition requires; the concern here is that what the refinement admits is the directed transition the strong doctrine was preserving against. The temporalist repair pressed from inside the literature (drop strong immutability but keep a temporal, personal God, rather than continue to the dipolar terminus) is the live alternative engaged at [§6.7.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-3) (with the temporality structure at [§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2)); the concern this section presses is that weak immutability's *internal* logic, once relational variance is admitted, runs on to the dipolar assignment Q5 turns to next. Hartshorne's dipolar theism occupies the logical terminus of the weak-immutability move and gives it a principled stopping point: the abstract pole is strictly immutable in the classical sense (no intrinsic change, no relational change, no variance of any kind) while the concrete pole is genuinely responsive, growing with the world's cumulative creative advance and bearing the directed transitions the believer's life rests on (*The Divine Relativity* [-@hartshorne1948]; *Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes* [-@hartshorne1984]). The dipolar account does not blur strong and weak immutability; it assigns each cleanly to a different pole of a single subject. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: the relation between the poles is a directed, asymmetric crossing, and the abstract pole enters a determinate relation with the concrete pole. That creates a differentiation and dependence burden, though a relation need not be a transition undergone by both relata. The crossing obtains only within T, S, and Φ, as [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows; the dipolar assignment relocates the immutability problem into the pole-relation rather than resolving it.

*What is required.* Taken together, the five pressures expose what *immutable* requires. Pure actuality relocates the transition into the creature and construes divine agency through invariant causation. The burden is to explain contingent effects and real causal asymmetry without intrinsic divine change. Tensed knowledge of contingents requires either the tense-bearing structure the doctrine forecloses or a Boethian timeless vision that makes the believer's intuition of God-as-responding to temporal events a feature of the creature's access, not the divine knowing. Creatio ex nihilo is a directed transition in the effect; an immutable-agent account must explain how its source grounds that directedness without undergoing it. The Chalcedonian incarnation requires a *becoming* that the strong doctrine relocates into the human nature, leaving the divine register as the bearer of an action it does not perform. Weak immutability admits relational variance, which is the variance the strong doctrine was preserving against. The five pressures leave a distinction between invariance of character or essence, strict absence of intrinsic change, and invariance of structural conditions. These should not be collapsed into one predicate.

*What is inverted.* Immutability is the structural status of the modal structure. *Does not change*, in the only sense that survives the dilemmas above, names not the invariance of a being but the necessity of a structure: the modal structure □(T∧S∧Φ) is what it is in every possible world because what *possible world* means is *consistent with the structure*. The structure's invariance is not an absence of motion in a being lacking all potency; it is the necessity of the conditions of any motion at all. Immutability's facet of that necessity is specifically temporal: not that the structure holds across every world, but that within any world there is no moment at which T, S, and Φ alter, because succession is something they condition rather than undergo. The action-language the believer's life rests on (creation, providence, response to prayer, incarnation) lives at the level of T, S, Φ: directed transitions of substances within the necessary structure. Those transitions occur within Nature. Calling Nature itself their agent would require an additional theory of agency and should not be inferred from structural hosting alone. The type/token distinction ([§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7)) keeps this exact: it is type-necessary that the structure produce operations of this kind (that there be transitions, agents, and the loop that takes up what Nature contains) while which particular operations occur is token-contingent. *Immutable* names the frame's invariance; that necessity reaches the kind of working the structure must host, not the particular tokens, and the believer's action-language lives among the tokens. Pressed for what makes it coherent, *immutable* names the modal-structure necessity that is the condition of any change at all: not the stillness of a being, but the necessity of the structure within which motion happens.

### 6.3.4 Impassibility {#sec-6-3-4}

Impassibility says God is never acted upon: never moved, never affected, never made to suffer or respond by anything outside. The pressure is that loving someone, hearing a prayer, or suffering on the Cross all involve being affected by another. Removing every trace of "being affected" keeps the words *love* and *mercy* while leaving disputed whether anything responsive remains for them to name.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** Impassibility says God is never acted upon—never moved, never affected, never made to respond by anything outside. It protects God from depending on the world. But look at what the believer's own words need. To love someone, hear their prayer, or grieve with them is to be affected by them: attentive, responsive, changed in your own state by what happens to theirs. Strip out every trace of being-affected and you keep the words love and mercy while removing the responsiveness they name. What's left is the skeleton of love, not its substance—and being affected is just what it is for a persisting thing to bear the events that reach it.

:::


*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology holds that God is impassible: God is not acted upon, does not suffer, does not undergo emotional disturbance, and does not receive anything from creatures (Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1; Augustine, *De civitate Dei* IX.5; Anselm, *Proslogion* VIII). The doctrine binds tightly to immutability ([§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3)), simplicity ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)), and aseity ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)): a being that cannot be acted upon is also one that does not change, has no parts to be moved, and depends on nothing outside itself. The classical reading locates the affective language of Scripture (God's anger, grief, compassion, jealousy) in the creature's relation to God rather than in God's reception of the creature (Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1 ad 2; [@gavrilyuk2004; @weinandy2000]). The twentieth-century *passibilist* turn [@moltmann1974; @fiddes1988; @bauckham1984] pressed in the other direction: a God who does not suffer with creation cannot love it, and the Cross is the central revelation of divine passibility: God's capacity to be affected by, and to suffer with, creation. The position the classical doctrine, fully stated, holds is that God's intrinsic state is invariant under creaturely action: nothing the creature does adds to, subtracts from, or modifies the divine being; God's love, knowledge, and providence are entirely a function of God's own being and not of what God receives.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions reach what the doctrine of impassibility, in the form structural reasoning can take up, cannot answer. Beneath the five runs one structural fact: *reception* is a structural feature of substances persisting through time ([§2.6.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-4)), and the doctrine's strategy is to deny all reception of the divine being while preserving the relational language the believer's life depends on.

**Q1.** *How does a being love what cannot move it?* The classical reading of divine love is that God's love for the creature is the act by which God wills the creature's good, and that this act is identical with God's own being (Aquinas, *ST* I.20). Many accounts of interpersonal love include receptivity and affective response, while classical accounts define divine love primarily as willing the beloved's good. The dispute is substantive: whether perfect love requires intrinsic affective change, not a truth fixed by the concept alone. The classical reply removes the *affected by* component and identifies the love with the willing of the good; the passibilist reply [@moltmann1974; @fiddes1988] is that this is not love but its skeleton, a willing-of-good that proceeds without the responsiveness love names. The concern here is that the skeleton of love is the structural concept *willing* without the substantive content *affected by*; whether the skeleton suffices for what the believer means by *God loves us* is the disputed question, and the dispute has been the central battleground of twentieth-century theology.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** The classical reply is that divine love isn't being moved by us at all—it's God's act of willing our good, identical with God's own being. No reception required, so impassibility stands. Press one question: does willing-the-good, with every trace of responsiveness removed, still name what the believer means by love? A parent who wills a child's good but is never moved by the child's joy or pain has the structure of benevolence without its heart. The later 'qualified impassibility' that lets God be affected without diminishment quietly readmits exactly the variance the strong doctrine refused—and that variance is just persistence bearing what reaches it.

:::


**Q2.** *Who hears a prayer, if nothing can reach the one it is prayed to?* The believer prays to God for the healing of a sick friend. The classical reply is that God eternally wills the friend's healing in response to the eternally-foreseen prayer; the prayer does not move God in time, but figures eternally in the divine plan that includes the healing (Aquinas, *ST* II-II.83). Response to prayer names a counterfactual and explanatory dependence between petition and outcome. In creaturely cases this often involves acts at t_1 and t_2; a classical account instead posits one timeless intention whose effects are temporally ordered. The reply that the figuring is eternal in the recipient relocates the directedness into the petitioner-creature side and leaves the recipient as the *terminus ad quem* (the end point *toward which*) of the figuring without being the *receiver* of the prayer. The believer's intuition that the prayer is *heard* (received by an attending recipient) is what the classical reply replaces with the prayer's *being-figured-in*. What the reply suppresses is not the intuition itself but the structural feature it tracks — reception by an attending recipient, which the eternal-figuring model must either supply in another register or explain away.

**Q3.** *How does an impassible God suffer on the Cross?* The crucifixion of Jesus is, on the Chalcedonian definition, the suffering of the second person of the Trinity in the human nature he has assumed. The classical reply is that the suffering is real in the human nature and that the divine nature does not suffer; the unity of person is preserved by predication-of-the-person rather than by attribution-to-the-nature (Aquinas, *ST* III.46; [@weinandy2000; @gavrilyuk2004]). The passibilist objection is that this preserves impassibility by locating the suffering in a nature distinct from the divine being, which converts the Cross from the revelation of God's love into the dramatic event of a human nature's pain. The concern here is that *the suffering of the person* requires the person to bear what the nature undergoes (to be the *whose* of the *what*) and the impassibilist reading locates the *bearing* without the *being-affected*. What the doctrine performs against here is not only Moltmann's [-@moltmann1974] reading of the Cross as the suffering of God but the central event of Christian revelation that reading interprets. Hartshorne's dipolar account offers a principled reply to Q3: the suffering on the Cross is borne by the concrete pole (the cumulative, responsive divine actuality that is genuinely affected by creaturely events, including the event of the crucifixion) while the abstract pole remains invariant. Moltmann's [-@moltmann1974] intuition that the Cross reveals a suffering God traces its process-theological ancestry to Hartshorne (*The Divine Relativity* [-@hartshorne1948]), whose systematic account of divine receptivity is the direct predecessor of the twentieth-century passibilist revival. The pressure here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: if the single subject suffers, its abstract dimension stands in relation to a temporal event across the pole-relation, and [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows that relation is a directed crossing obtaining only within T, S, and Φ. The concrete pole's reception of the Cross is sustained only by drawing the abstract pole into the conditions it was defined to lack.

**Q4.** *What does a being receive, if it has no potency to receive?* Reception requires the potency to receive. A being that is pure act (with no unrealized potential) has no potency to receive (Aquinas, *ST* I.3.1; [@feser2017]). The concern here is that the doctrine of impassibility is *what pure act entails at the relational level*: a being that cannot be moved cannot be received-from, because reception is being-moved by what is received. The reply that God receives in the order of intention (knowing, willing) without being moved in the order of being (Aquinas, *ST* I.20 ad 2) preserves impassibility by introducing a distinction between intentional and ontological reception. The concern here is that *intentional reception* is what *being affected by what is known and willed* names, and the doctrine's strategy is to keep this in a register that does not modify the being's intrinsic state — which is what the believer's intuition denies the doctrine should keep apart.

**Q5.** *How does God respond to creatures without being acted upon?* The twentieth-century passibilist tradition [@moltmann1974; @fiddes1988; @bauckham1984] has argued that divine love requires divine suffering. The contemporary refinements [@weinandy2000; @gavrilyuk2004; @mullins2016] distinguish *strong impassibility* (no affective variance) from *qualified impassibility* (affective responsiveness without ontological diminishment). The concern here is that *affective responsiveness* is the variance the strong doctrine refused, and the qualified-impassibility move admits the variance the strong doctrine was preserving against. The qualified move is honest about what the believer's intuition requires; the concern here is that what the qualified move admits is the structural feature Φ (substance persisting through events) carries: the persisting substance is the *bearer* of the events, and *being the bearer* is *being modified by* the events as they occur in the bearer. The qualified-impassibilist and full-passibilist positions developed inside personal theism [@mullins2016] are a live destination in their own right (a temporal, personal God genuinely affected by creatures, engaged at [§6.7.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-3) and alongside [§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3)) not merely a way-station to the dipolar terminus; the concern this section presses is that the *internal* logic of admitting affective variance runs on toward that terminus. Dipolar theism is the principled stopping point the passibilist refinements slide toward: Hartshorne's abstract pole is not weakly impassible but strictly impassible, and the concrete pole is not qualifiedly passible but fully receptive, growing with the world's cumulative experience. The abstract/concrete bifurcation is designed to prevent the qualified-impassibility position from being a halfway house: it takes the impassibility/passibility split and assigns it cleanly to two poles of a single subject rather than blurring it across a single nature. The pressure here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: the two poles constitute one subject only through the directed crossing between them, which imports the very structural conditions the abstract pole was supposed to avoid.

*What is required.* Run to their end, the five pressures show what *impassible* finally rests on. Love without intrinsic affective change is the classical proposal; the disputed question is whether willing another's good suffices for perfect love or whether receptivity is essential. Petitionary prayer requires a recipient whose receiving is part of the prayer's structure; relocating the receiving into the eternal-figuring register removes the structural feature *being heard*. The Cross requires a suffering of the person; locating the suffering in a nature distinct from the divine being separates the bearing from the being-affected. Pure act has no potency to receive; the intentional-vs.-ontological distinction preserves impassibility by allowing reception in a register that does not modify the receiver, which requires a clarified distinction between intentional relation and intrinsic alteration. Qualified impassibility admits the variance the strong doctrine refused, which is the variance Φ carries: the persisting substance is the bearer of the events, and being the bearer need not entail intrinsic modification by every relational event. After the five pressures, impassibility remains a claim about the mode and limits of divine receptivity. Φ can describe the persistence of affected bearers, but impassibility is not thereby identical with Φ.

*What is inverted.* The inversion relocates creaturely reception and affective persistence to Φ, the substance/persistence condition. It does not convert the negative divine attribute of impassibility into Φ itself. *Not acted upon*, in the only sense that survives the dilemmas above, names not the absence of reception in a being lacking all potency but the structural fact that the *persisting carrier of events* is what *substance* names: the structural feature of any world in which there is anything *that* is *affected by* anything. The action-and-passion relational structure the believer's prayer life and the Cross rest on lives at the level of substances within Nature: directed transitions of substances within the necessary modal structure, including the substance the second person of the Trinity has assumed. Traced to what it presupposes, *impassible* names Φ: the structural condition of being-the-carrier-of-events, which is the condition of any reception at all. Prayer, creaturely love, and suffering occur through persisting bearers within Nature. Whether God participates in those events passibly, relates to them timelessly, or is revealed through an assumed human nature remains a theological dispute constrained—but not settled—by that structural fact.

## 6.4 Cognition {#sec-6-4}

This cluster gathers the two attributes of divine knowing: awareness ([§6.4.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-1)) and knowledge ([§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2)). The tradition holds that God is conscious of all that is and knows it perfectly, without acquiring, losing, or revising any content.

Pressed, both require the structural conditions of any cognition whatever: to be aware is to stand in a distinction between knower and known, and to know is to carry content across the act of knowing — distinction and carrying-forward that are S and Φ operating, not faculties exempt from them.

### 6.4.1 Awareness {#sec-6-4-1}

Aristotle's phrase still sets the standard: God is "thought thinking itself": consciousness and self-knowledge complete in a single act, taking in nothing from outside. The problem this raises is how one undifferentiated act bears phenomenal and intentional content. Many theories require a subject, perspective, and some self-relation; not all require a temporally extended higher-order registration. Collapse all of that into one changeless point, as the doctrine does, and what is left must show how it keeps the name of awareness without the structure that makes anything aware.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine awareness assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *vita perfecta*, perfect life, with the fullness of self-presence the term implies (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XII.7; Aquinas, *ST* I.18). God is *noesis noeseos noesis*, thought thinking itself: the eternal self-cognition in which knower and known are the same act (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* XII.9; Aquinas, *ST* I.14.2). On the most developed contemporary refinement, divine awareness is sui generis: not a creaturely state of consciousness writ large, but a primitive divine cognition of which creaturely awareness is a faint analogate [@stump2013; @stump2016; @plantinga2000; @alston1991]. Each move tries to keep the qualitative dimension of awareness from being a feature only creatures have. At its most ambitious, the doctrine names a divine being whose self-cognition is one eternal act in which the asymmetry between knower and known has been collapsed into identity at the highest register.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions meet no answer in the doctrine of awareness, taken in the form structural reasoning can engage. What these pressures turn on is the point [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) and [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) develop directly: awareness is reflexive self-relation. A subject is aware when something it bears is held in a relation of taking-itself-as such that the being registers itself in the registering. Self-relation of this kind requires a substantial being (Φ) capable of holding the registration; an interval (T) across which the registering and the registered are distinguishable as the moments they are; and a positional-relational manifold (S) within which the doubled feature (the subject taking itself as object) has somewhere to occur. The classical God is defined as without T, S, and Φ. The five pressures run one at the level of the predicate, four at the level of the conditions awareness-talk runs on.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** Aristotle's phrase still sets the bar: God is thought thinking itself—consciousness and self-knowledge complete in one act, taking in nothing from outside. The trouble is what being aware actually involves. To be aware is for something to relate to itself: a being that holds the awareness, a stretch of time across which it registers, a standpoint from which it's had. Awareness runs on a gap between the registering and the registered. Collapse all of that into one changeless point, where knower and known are the very same act, and you don't get the sharpest awareness—you get a static relation wearing the name of awareness with none of the structure that makes anything aware.

:::


**Q1.** *What relates to itself, where the knower and the known are the same act?* The phenomenal tradition from Brentano [-@brentano1874] through Husserl [-@husserl1900] to recent higher-order theorists [@rosenthal2005; @kriegel2009] treats some form of self-relating as constitutive of awareness, not as a contingent feature of certain awarenesses among others. First-order representational accounts [@tye1995; @dretske1995] can treat awareness as representational content available to a system without a distinct higher-order self-relation. The structural burden therefore concerns determinate subject and content, not one theory of consciousness imposed on every rival. The classical reply is that divine awareness is not analyzable along these lines: God's self-cognition is one eternal act in which knower and known are identical, and the *self-relation* is not a structural condition but a creaturely shadow of the unified divine act (*ST* I.14.2; [@stump2013]). The reply is genuinely available, and it does the work the doctrine asks of it. Its most exact form is Aquinas's *distinctio rationis*: knower and known differ in God by a distinction of reason (a conceptual distinction with no answering distinction in the thing) so the asymmetry awareness seems to need is preserved in our way of conceiving God without importing real composition into the divine act (*ST* I.14.2; I.13.4). The concern this section adds is that a *distinctio rationis* secures the asymmetry at precisely the register that cannot do the structural work. A distinction that holds only for the mind conceiving God, and not in God, leaves the divine act itself with no internal asymmetry between the registering and the registered, and an act with no such asymmetry is not the upper limit of self-relation but its absence. A perfectly identical knower-and-known is not a more vivid awareness than the believer's; it is a static relation with the same name as self-relation and none of the structure that made self-relation phenomenal.

**Q2.** *How does an awareness that never varies attend to one thing rather than another?* For an awareness to be the awareness of *this* rather than *that*, the being must be in a state-of-being-aware-of-this that is distinguishable from the being's state of being aware of something else. Distinguishable contents require differentiation, but they need not occur successively; one awareness can simultaneously include several distinct objects. Aquinas's eternal self-cognition (*ST* I.14) forecloses the registering deliberately: God's awareness is one eternal act that does not modulate as creaturely circumstances change. The doctrine preserves divine immutability. The cost is the same one [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) raises for knowledge and [§6.8.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-2) raises for love: an awareness that does not modulate when its object varies is not a heightened form of attention but a constitutive feature of a static relation. The believer who comes to a moment of grief feels the difference between being-attended-to-in-grief and being-attended-to-in-ordinary-times. Stump's [-@stump2010] second-personal experiential knowledge is the most developed contemporary attempt to preserve modulation while keeping atemporality, and the present analysis registers the position as the most resourceful defense the doctrine has found. The concern raised here is whether the modulation Stump preserves can do the work without the temporal index whose role she has factored out.

**Q3.** *From what point of view is a being aware, if it has no point of view?* The phenomenal tradition treats perspective as constitutive of awareness, but a perspective need not be a metric spatial location; it may be an indexical or subject-relative standpoint. Nagel's [-@nagel1974] bat is aware *as a bat is*, with the perspective doing structural work in what the awareness-of-echolocation is like. The classical reply is that divine awareness is non-perspectival: God's cognition is from no point of view, equidistant from every point of view alike. The concern here is one [§6.8.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-1) raises for presence: *equidistant from every point alike* keeps the language of perspective and removes the contrastive structure perspective requires. An awareness from no perspective is not the most encompassing form of awareness but the limiting case of an awareness with no positional anchor for its content to take hold in. The reply that divine awareness is anchored in divine essence rather than in spatial position [@helm2010; @rocca2004] preserves the term by relocating the anchor; what *anchor* names, on the relocation, is doing primitive work the doctrine has not specified.

**Q4.** *What bears the awareness, if there is no being to bear it?* Self-relation runs on a being. The being holds the doubling, sustains it across the moments of the registration, and is what the registering is *of itself* in the relevant sense. The classical doctrine of divine immateriality denies matter and extension, not metaphysical subsistence; Aquinas explicitly treats God as subsistent being. The pressure is whether such a bearer can host differentiated awareness under simplicity. The doctrine preserves divine simplicity. A defender can press further with Stump's hylomorphic reading of Aquinas [@stump2003]: the divine being is *esse* itself (being itself) and her configurational account of substance offers a bearer that owes nothing to matter or extension, a substance-without-composition fit to hold the self-presence. The concern here is that the bearer this supplies is a substance with exactly the features of substance subtracted: a configuration sustains a doubling only by holding distinguishable elements in a determinate arrangement, and divine simplicity removes the differentiated content any configuration arranges. What remains is not a being with a fuller form of self-presence but a bearer that has yet to show it can hold what *self-presence* names. Stump's second-personal defense is the most resourceful the doctrine has, and it is not the bare positing of a primitive. On Stump's account (*Wandering in Darkness* [-@stump2010]), divine awareness is *knowledge of persons*: the irreducible, non-propositional knowing-by-acquaintance the believer has in mind when they say God *knows* them, distinct in kind from knowledge *that* such-and-such holds. The present analysis registers it as a positively structured knowing rather than a place where analysis stops. The concern here is that second-personal knowledge, taken at the strength Stump gives it, is *more* structurally demanding than the propositional knowing it is contrasted with, not less. To know a person second-personally is to attend to *this* one, as they are, from the standpoint of one present to them: a relation indexed at both poles, running across the interval between the attender and the attended, and borne by a being that sustains the attending as the encounter unfolds. The richness that distinguishes second-personal knowing from propositional grasp is supplied entirely by T, S, and Φ: the temporal index that makes the attending *now*, the positional standpoint that makes it *to this one*, and the substantial bearer that holds the encounter together. Invoked to defend a being without those conditions, the second-personal account does not exempt awareness from the structural requirement; it intensifies it. What the believer means by *God attends to me* is precisely the second-personal relation Stump describes, and that relation, described faithfully, is the structure the classical definition has removed. The defense rescues the believer's intuition only by reintroducing the conditions the doctrine was formulated to deny: the move [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2), Q8 makes for knowledge.

**Q5.** *Once awareness is stripped of all self-relation, what is left to conceive?* The conceivability question for predicates of God in general is taken up at [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3); the present concern is local. Chalmers [-@chalmers2002] registers the relevant asymmetry: conceiving something coherent is some evidence for its possibility, conceiving something with structural self-defeat licenses no such inference. To conceive of awareness without self-relation is, on the analyses surveyed at Q1, to conceive of awareness with the structural condition for awareness removed. To conceive of *vita perfecta* without temporal differentiation, spatial perspective, or substantial being is to conceive of life with the structural conditions of life removed. The reply available to the doctrine is the analogical-and-apophatic one (predicating of God by analogy, or by negation alone; [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3), Q1–Q2): the predicates apply analogically, and the conceivability concern dissolves under the analogical reading. The reply is genuinely available, and [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) takes its measure. What this section adds is that the conceivability concern does not require univocity to apply. Even on the most generous analogical reading, the predicate has to share enough structure with its creaturely paradigm for the analogical relation to obtain, and the structural conditions removed at T, S, and Φ are precisely what the creaturely paradigm consists in.

One classical argument seems to cut beneath all five pressures at once. Avicenna's *Flying Man* [@avicenna1020a] asks you to imagine a person created in an instant, full-grown, suspended in still air, blindfolded, limbs held apart so nothing is felt — no sensation, no perceived body, no world. Even so, the person would affirm *that they are*: self-awareness given with no body to give it, so awareness is no debtor to the structural conditions. Grant the intuition its full force; it still concedes the point. What the scenario subtracts is *outer* sensation and the *perceived* body — not the conditions the self-affirmation runs on. Awareness is not a static having but a registering: to be aware is to be modulated by what one is aware of, to occupy a state that responds to its object and is thereby distinguishable from the states one is not in. If the Flying Man is asked a question, the scenario gains relational content not present in Avicenna's original thought experiment. Even without it, the self-affirmation supplies a minimal subject–content structure; and even with no questioner, his affirming *I am* is the barest form of the same loop, a self registering itself. Feedback of this kind is not one feature of awareness among others; it is what remains when everything else is stripped, and it is already the three structural roles at work: the modulation runs across an ordering (T's role), the registrant stands over against the registered (S's role), and a persisting bearer is what the difference makes a difference to (Φ's role). The tableau concedes as much before the argument begins, suspending him *in air*, creating him *at an instant*, having him *affirm*. The Flying Man supports awareness without outer sensation or perceived embodiment. It supports a bearer and determinate content, but it does not by itself establish temporal duration, spatial placement, or the loaded T/S/Φ types. The intuition that self-presence outlasts the senses is sound; the inference that it outlasts T, S, and Φ removes the very structure the affirmation instances.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** Avicenna's Flying Man seems to cut beneath all this: imagine a person created full-grown in midair, blindfolded, feeling nothing—no body, no world. Even so, they'd affirm that they are. Self-awareness with nothing from outside, so awareness owes nothing to structure. Grant it full force and it still concedes the point. What the scene removes is outer sensation and the felt body, not the conditions the self-affirming runs on. To affirm 'I am' is already a self registering itself: a modulation across an interval, a registrant set over against what it registers, a persisting being the difference makes a difference to. The tableau grants as much before it starts—creating him at an instant, suspending him in air, having him affirm.

:::


*What is required.* Awareness, taken on what the five pressures surface, has a specific structural shape. It begins with an asymmetric self-relation between the registering and the registered; a perfectly identical knower-and-known is not the upper limit of self-relation but its absence. The asymmetry runs in time: states of being aware of *this* are distinguishable from states of being aware of *that* only against a temporal differentiation the doctrine of eternal self-cognition deliberately forecloses, and an awareness that does not modulate when its object varies is the feature of a static relation, not heightened attention. It runs from a perspective: there is a *here* from which the awareness is, and equidistance from every point alike keeps the language of perspective without keeping its content. It runs on a being: self-relation requires Φ to hold the doubling, and relocating *self-presence* to a primitive is where the analysis stops rather than where it deepens. And the analogical defense the tradition leans on requires shared structural scaffolding with the creaturely paradigm to obtain at all: exactly what is conceded at T, S, and Φ is exactly what the paradigm consists in. Awareness is what self-relation does when the relation is doubled across a manifold; the predicate points to a feature Nature has when it loops on itself, not a primitive that bypasses the looping.

*What is inverted.* Awareness is Nature in self-relation. The English *aware* descends through Old English *gewær*, *cautious, watchful*, from Proto-Germanic *waraz*, *attentive, on guard*: the term names a state of standing attentively toward what is there to be attended to, and the standing requires somewhere to stand and something to stand attentive over. This self-relation is developed at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) as an emergent feature of T, S, and Φ at sufficient elaboration, and [§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1) takes reflexive awareness up directly. The classical tradition reaches for a being whose self-presence is more vivid than the believer's, more comprehensive than any creature's, and names a relation that has lost the structure self-presence consists in. The doctrine has been performing the believer's awareness onto a non-being whose conditions for awareness have been removed at every level. The eliminative pressure establishes a determinate subject–content burden. The positive claim that awareness is what Nature does when self-relation develops is deferred to §8 and must be earned there.

### 6.4.2 Knowledge {#sec-6-4-2}

The doctrine of omniscience holds that God knows every truth in one timeless act. The recurring question is how one timeless act bears differentiated, contingent, and temporally indexed content. Knowing requires a knower, content, and epistemic fit; whether it must itself be temporally extended is disputed. A knower with no time of its own can grasp tenseless facts but loses the believer's "you know me, *now*": the very contact the doctrine was meant to secure.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine omniscience assembles several reinforcing claims. God knows every true proposition (Anselm, *Proslogion*; Aquinas, *ST* I.14; [@swinburne1977]): every truth past, present, future, contingent, necessary, modal, and counterfactual. God's knowing is one eternal act of comprehension, not discursive succession (*ST* I.14.7).

On the most developed contemporary refinements, the eternal act stands in ET-simultaneity (a sui generis relation in which the eternal life is cognitively simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal) with every temporal moment alike [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @leftow2012; @rogers2000; @helm2010]. The totality of truths forms a proper class rather than a set, escaping the Cantorian closure pressure [@plantinga1993; against @grim1991]. Divine knowledge is propositional rather than acquaintance-based, deflecting the worry about phenomenal grasp [@jackson1982, applied to omniscience by later defenders]. Divine middle knowledge encompasses every counterfactual of creaturely freedom, dissolving the foreknowledge–freedom dilemma [@molina1588; @flint1998; @craig1987]. Or, on the open-theist alternative, divine knowledge ranges only over what is determinately the case, leaving genuinely open futures genuinely open [@hasker1989; @boyd2001; @mullins2016].

Each move tries to keep omniscience coherent under the doctrine's other commitments. At its most ambitious, the doctrine names a knower whose contact with every truth is held in one comprehensive act and whose scope reaches what creaturely knowers can at best approximate.

*What cannot be answered.* Eleven questions outrun what the doctrine of omniscience, in the form structural reasoning can take up, is able to answer. At bottom the worry is structural. Knowledge is a triconditional relation: a subject (Φ), a holding across time (T) of differentiated content (S), and a fit between the held and the case. The eleven pressures run three at the level of the predicate, eight at the level of the conditions knowledge-talk runs on.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Core concept.** Omniscience says God knows every truth in one timeless act—complete, all at once, taking in nothing. It's meant to be knowing at its maximum. The catch is what knowing involves. To know is to take up what's the case in a way that holds: a knower who bears it, a stretch of time across which the holding lasts, content spread out and told apart. A knower with no time of its own can register tenseless facts, but loses the believer's 'you know me, now'—the very contact the doctrine was built to secure. Push knowing past time, space, and a bearer and you keep the word while removing what lets anything count as knowing at all.

:::


**Q1.** *How does a timeless knower keep contact with every moment, if contact runs through time?* The classical doctrine answers without qualification (Anselm, *Proslogion*; Aquinas, *ST* I.14). God knows every truth in one eternal act, and the *ever* the question places at the verb is, the defender will say, the wrong frame: God knows not at every moment but eternally, in a single act that stands in cognitive contact with each moment alike [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @leftow2012]. The reply preserves the doctrine on its own terms, and the present analysis registers it. The concern is not lexical but structural, and it survives the careful distinction the tradition draws between *aeternitas* (the Boethian *interminabilis vitae tota simul possessio*, the complete and simultaneous possession of unending life) and *sempiternitas*, mere everlasting duration. Grant the strict timeless reading of *aeternitas* in full. The doctrine still wants the eternal knower in comprehensive cognitive contact with every moment alike: knowing what is the case at each time, sustaining each creature through its time, answering each prayer in its time. Contact-with-every-moment is the temporal scope the predicate cannot shed: whether or not the knower is *located* in time, the content known ranges over every time, and the relation of knowing has to reach each of them. The atemporalist retreat relocates the knower out of time without relocating the known out of time, and it is the temporal structure of the known (not a temporal location of the knower) that the section will press. Contact with truths about every moment imports temporal articulation into the content. It does not by itself show that the knower's act is temporally successive; the burden is to explain the content–mode relation.

**Q2.** *When does a timeless knowing itself occur?* The interrogative sharpens the previous question by demanding a temporal anchor rather than a yes-or-no on temporal reach. The defender's available reply is the same atemporal one [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow2012]: God knows in no *when*; the eternal act has no temporal location at which it occurs, and the question's presupposition does not apply. The reply is candid, and the present analysis registers it. The concern is the structural condition the predicate runs on. Creaturely episodes of knowing arise and persist in time. A standing disposition or proposed timeless cognitive state need not take a moment to come into being, so the section cannot assume episodic temporality as part of the predicate. The *when* the question asks for is the temporal anchor at which the holding occurs: not the *when* at which the holding's content is indexed, but the *when* of the holding itself. To answer "in no *when*" is to deny that knowing has a time at which it obtains, which removes the temporal anchor creaturely holdings supply. The doctrine cannot supply a *when* without temporalizing God, and cannot deny one without explaining what does the anchoring instead. The proposal instead owes a positive account of timeless cognitive bearing and epistemic fit.

**Q3.** *How does a knower with no now of its own know the present as present?* The *Kretzmann–Prior puzzle* [@kretzmann1966; @prior1962] raises a question the doctrine has answered with care. The defender will grant that an atemporal knower cannot host the indexical *now* in the first-person way a temporally located knower hosts it, and will reply that an atemporal knower can know all token-reflexive facts as facts indexed to whoever occupies a given temporal location: God knows that *the believer at t says or thinks 'now'*, that *t is Tuesday at 3 PM in the temporal manifold*, and that the manifold contains the moment so indexed. The reply is genuinely available, and the present analysis registers it. The concern reformulates. The believer's confession that God *knows me now* is not the confession that God knows the indexed proposition *the believer at t thinks 'now'*. It is the confession of being attended to *as* the believer is at the moment they are. The devotional vocabulary (*known, attended to, heard, responded to, present with*) turns on a relation that is itself temporally indexed at both poles, not on a tenseless registration of a fact about an indexical token. Aquinas's eternal single act (*ST* I.14) preserves comprehensiveness; what it does not preserve, on the present analysis, is the temporal index that makes the believer's *now* the believer's, in any sense distinguishable from the eternal act's tenseless grasp of every *now* alike.

**Q4.** *From when does a timeless God foreknow?* The question asks for the vantage from which the *fore* operates: a position relative to which the foreknown is later, the cognitive contact prior to the contacted. The available reply on the strict atemporal reading is candid [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @leftow2012]: there is no *from when*; the eternal pole stands outside the temporal manifold and contacts every moment alike. The reply concedes that *foreknowledge* on this reading does not name an antecedent grasp; it names tenseless cognitive contact relabeled. The present analysis registers the concession and asks what the doctrine is left holding. *Foreknowledge* in the tradition's load-bearing uses is not a relation that incidentally involves time. Those uses include Boethius's reconciliation of divine knowing with creaturely freedom (*Consolation* V), Molina's middle knowledge antecedent to creation [@molina1588; @flint1998], and the prophetic literature's *I knew you before I formed you in the womb*. It is a temporally-asymmetric relation in which the knowing is prior to the known and the prior is operative as prior. Strip the asymmetry and the doctrine retains the word and discards the relation it names. The believer who is told that God *foreknew* their prayer is being told that the divine attention to the prayer was anterior to its making. The atemporal defense preserves attention without anteriority. What remains is contact, not foreknowledge.

**Q5.** *What makes foreknowledge "fore," if the knower comes before no moment?* Stump and Kretzmann [-@stumpKretzmann1981] define ET-simultaneity as a sui generis relation in which the eternal life is cognitively simultaneous with every temporal moment without itself being temporal. Leftow [-@leftow1991; -@leftow2012] gives the most careful contemporary development. The doctrine does the work the tradition asks of it: keeps God in operative cognitive contact with every moment without temporalizing the divine pole. The concern here is the one [§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2), Q2 presses: ET-simultaneity is introduced precisely as a cross-mode relation and does not presuppose ordinary shared time by definition. Its burden is whether the technical relation explains cognition and causation without covertly temporalizing God. The believer's prayer at 3 PM Tuesday was offered after their morning confession and before their evening weeping; the temporal asymmetry of the offering relative to the surrounding life is part of what the prayer is. ET-simultaneity preserves God's contact with the prayer by setting the asymmetry aside on the divine side. What remains is contact with a temporally undifferentiated correlate of the prayer rather than with the prayer as the believer made it.

**Q6.** *Where is a knowledge held, if there is no being anywhere to hold it?* The question asks for the locus of the holding: the being in whom omniscience persists. The doctrine answers without spatial commitment. God's knowledge is held *in God*: not in a region, not at a place, but in the divine essence that grounds the knowing without itself being a containing thing (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.4). The reply denies the question's spatial presupposition and relocates the holding from a spatial being to an essential ground. The present analysis registers the relocation and notes its cost. The being the predicate runs on (the Φ among the structural conditions of [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4)) is what stands under the persisting and lets it persist. Bearing knowledge need not require spatial location: minds and abstract informational states are commonly modeled non-spatially. The relevant requirement is a determinate subject or ground of cognitive content, not a literal where. Grounding identifies what makes something the case; it does not perform the holding the predicate names. The divine essence as ground stands as that on which the grasp depends, not as that which stands under it. The doctrine's available answer denies the *where*; whether the essence-as-ground can also stand under the grasp is the open question, and until it is answered what remains is grounding, not holding.

**Q7.** *How does a single act hold all truths at once, if the truths form no whole to be held?* Grim [-@grim1991] raises the *Cantorian difficulty*: the truths form no set, since for any set of truths *K* the power set ℘(*K*) contains more truths than *K*. No unified cognitive grasp of every truth is therefore available as a totality. Plantinga [-@plantinga1993] replies that divine knowledge is proper-class: not bounded by the power-set limit because not a bounded object at all. The reply is the strongest contemporary response to the Cantorian pressure, and it turns on a distinction the present concern has to honor rather than run past: *comprehending* is not *containing-as-totality*. A proper-class grasp can be read distributively (for each truth, that God knows it) without positing a completed whole, *all truths*, that some single act holds as one object. Read that way, Plantinga's reply does not need the totality the Cantorian result denies, and pressing it as though it did would miss it. So the concern is put to the comprehending mode directly. Distributing the grasp truth-by-truth relieves the set-theoretic bound but not the structural condition the predicate runs on: each severally-known truth is still a holding, and the believer's prayer, known severally, is still something that has to be *held* by a knower if *known* is to keep the devotional sense the doctrine trades on. Omniscience is commonly defined distributively — for every truth, God knows it — and need not require all truths to form one set-like object. A separate simplicity question remains about how one act grounds all those differentiated knowledge relations, returning the pressure in the Eleventh interrogation's form: registering a manifold *as* the differentiated manifold it is requires differentiation within the knowing itself ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)). Whether the grasp is read as a totality or as distributive comprehending, the believer who hopes to be known is hoping to be held in mind: not to be a member of a class, and not to be one more value over which their knower's quantifier ranges.

**Q8.** *How does a being that knows everything know what it is like to know nothing?* Jackson's [-@jackson1982] *Mary* distinguishes propositional knowledge from acquaintance: a knower may know every true proposition about red without ever having seen it, and may know every true proposition about pain without knowing what pain is like. Propositional omniscience does not by itself include every phenomenal acquaintance or ability. Whether perfect divine knowledge must include those modes is a theological and conceptual question. The concern invoked by Hebrews 4:15 (NRSVUE) is that the high priest who is *able to sympathize with our weaknesses* is doing more than holding propositions. The pastoral and devotional vocabulary the tradition has performed for two millennia turns on a sense of being known closer to acquaintance than to propositional grasp. Nagasawa [-@nagasawa2008] and Stump [-@stump2010] develop contemporary positions that try to preserve some experiential dimension of divine cognition; the present analysis registers them as the most serious attempts and notes that each preserves the experiential dimension by reintroducing structural conditions the strict atemporalist reading had removed.

**Q9.** *How is a free future act known, before there is any fact of it to know?* The dilemma is ancient (Boethius, *Consolation* V; Aquinas, *ST* I.14.13). If *the believer will pray on Tuesday at 3 PM* is true antecedently, then antecedent truth fixes the action, and the action's freedom in any libertarian sense (the freedom to have done otherwise) is hard to recover. Three positions, each well-developed, address the dilemma. Molinism introduces *middle knowledge* of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom [@molina1588; @flint1998; @craig1987] and faces the grounding objection: what makes the counterfactuals true antecedently to the actions whose ground they are [@adams1977; @hasker1986]? Atemporalism removes the *fore* by removing the temporal location relative to which the foreknowing would be antecedent; the structural concern is Q1's. Open theism [@hasker1989; @boyd2001; @mullins2016] accepts that genuinely open futures are not yet there to be known. Each preserves a different commitment by surrendering another, and each has serious defenders. The present analysis is that the dilemma reflects a real tension in the doctrine, and the three positions are the three ways the tension can be relieved given the classical bundle. None of the three preserves the bundle intact.

**Q10.** *What determines that God determines all facts, if that itself is one of the facts?* The deepest version of the doctrine extends divine knowledge to every modal fact: God knows what is necessary, what is possible, what is impossible. Modal Constitution / S5 invariance ([§2.1.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-3)) and [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) establish that modal status does not vary across worlds and is not a product of any agent's exercise. Divine knowledge of the modal structure is, accordingly, knowledge of a structural fact about how possibility works — not a sovereign reach into a domain the knower has authored. Leftow's [-@leftow2012] modal grounding is the strongest contemporary attempt to make the modal frame a product of divine activity; it is addressed from the necessity side at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q6. The point this section adds is that even granting the comprehensiveness of divine knowledge, what omniscience reaches at the modal level is the structure that conditions any knowing whatsoever: Nature that omniscience operates within rather than over.

**Q11.** *How does a partless knower hold a manifold of truths as the differentiated manifold it is?* The pressure is internal to the classical bundle, where omniscience stands beside divine simplicity ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)): the God of classical theism is without composition, and the divine knowing is not an attribute added to the divine being but is identical with the divine essence (Aquinas, *ST* I.3; I.14.4). The doctrine has a developed answer. God knows the manifold of creatures not by being informed by them but by knowing his own essence as the imitable source from which each derives, so that the multiplicity falls on the side of what is known and not in the simple act or the simple knower (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.5–6; I.15; [@dolezal2011]). The reply is the most developed the tradition offers, and the present analysis registers it in full: a simple knower can know many things, the defender holds, because the manyness is in the objects while the knowing stays one. The question is whether *knowing the manifold as the manifold it is* can be had on those terms. To know every truth is to know, among the truths, that this one is distinct from that: to register the differentiation, not the items alone. A knowing that carries that differentiation has differentiated content within it, which is the composition simplicity was framed to deny; a knowing with no differentiation within it registers the items without their distinctness, which leaves unknown the very truths about distinctness omniscience was framed to include. The eminent-containment move (the essence holds all it knows virtually, in a higher unity that is not composition) is the move [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) runs against classical simplicity directly: either the contained perfections collapse to a single nameless point and the differentiation is lost, or the essence carries the differentiated content the doctrine was built to deny and composition is readmitted. Knowing requires a manifold differentiated enough for what is taken to be the case it is: the condition any knowing whatever must meet, the differentiation (S) among the structural conditions [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4) derives. A partless essence is the one thing that cannot host it. Either simplicity gives, to make room for the manifold the knowing carries, or omniscience gives, to keep the knower partless. The classical bundle cannot retain both.

*What is required.* Across the eleven pressures, what *know* runs on becomes visible. Grant the strict timeless reading of *aeternitas*: omniscience still ranges over temporally articulated content. The scope sits in the known, but it does not follow without further argument that the knower instantiates the content's temporal mode. *Know* also asks for a temporal anchor at which the holding obtains (not the time the holding's content indexes, but the time of the holding itself), and a knower that denies the anchor still owes the positive account of timeless bearing. The believer's *known now* is a relation indexed at both poles; an atemporal grasp of an indexed token reaches the correlate and leaves the index unattended. The *fore* in *foreknowledge* operates from a temporal vantage, and ET-simultaneity preserves the term by setting aside the frame the term presupposes: contact without anteriority is contact, not foreknowledge. The holding needs a bearer: grounding is what makes something the case, and bearing is what stands under the persisting, so relocating the holding from the second to the first preserves the word and not the relation. A unified cognitive grasp differs from both distributive comprehending and open-ended class-membership: the believer hoping to be known is hoping to be held in mind, not to be a truth their knower commands severally and not to be a member of a proper class. Pastoral acquaintance does more than propositional grasp: the high priest *able to sympathize* is doing more than holding propositions, and propositional-only omniscience keeps the word by trading away the experiential dimension the tradition has performed for two millennia. The compatibility of foreknowledge with the freedom of the foreknown is real tension, and each of Molinism, atemporalism, and open theism preserves one commitment of the classical bundle by surrendering another. Modal knowledge operates *within* the modal structure rather than over it: the deepest reach of divine cognition turns out to be Nature, the structure that conditions any cognition whatsoever. And the partlessness the classical bundle prizes is the one constitution that cannot host a differentiated manifold: a knowing that registers the distinctness among truths carries differentiation within it, so either simplicity or the reach of omniscience gives ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)). Knowing, finally, is reflexive in form: taking up what is the case in a way that holds, where the taking requires a manifold differentiated enough for what is taken to be the case it is. Knowing, on the positive account §8 develops, is what Nature does when the loop in it takes up what Nature itself contains, and T, S, and Φ are the conditions under which that taking-up holds.

::: {.column-margin .book-annotation-note}
**Natural worry.** The best modern defense keeps God outside time yet in contact with every moment at once, so nothing is lost. But weigh what the believer means by being known now. Their prayer at 3 PM Tuesday was offered after the morning's confession and before the evening's weeping—that place in the flow is part of what the prayer is. A timeless knower can grasp the tenseless fact that someone prays at that index, but grasping a dated token isn't attending to them as they are, when they are. The contact reaches the correlate and leaves the index unattended. Being known, in the sense the believer lives on, is a relation timed at both ends—which is time doing exactly what the doctrine set out to remove.

:::


*What is inverted.* Knowledge is Nature with the loop in it taking up what Nature itself contains. The English *know* descends through Old English *cnāwan* from the Indo-European *gnō*-, the same root that gives *gnosis*, *cognition*, *recognize*. To know is to *take up* what is the case in a way that holds. Acquired knowledge involves movement from not knowing to knowing; standing or timeless knowledge does not. Every model still requires a bearer, differentiated content, and epistemic fit, while the stronger temporal claim must be argued separately. The positive account is developed in §8: knowledge is what Nature with the loop in it does when the loop's content fits what Nature itself contains. Several of the pressures above are eliminative before they are relocative: the believer's *known now*, the demand for acquaintance, and the anteriority the *fore* in *foreknowledge* requires tell against any knower's supplying them in the devotional sense (the classical God included) and do not, on their own, show that Nature supplies them. That Nature supplies what survives of *know* is the separate, positive claim §8 must earn, not a verdict these pressures deliver by themselves. The classical tradition reaches for a knower whose grasp would be more comprehensive than the believer's, and names a relation whose conditions for holding have been removed at every level. Nature with the loop in it is the one knower-candidate whose conditions remain intact; if §8 earns the positive claim, what the doctrine of divine omniscience has been formulated to track is what Nature with the loop does, not a feature of a being beyond Nature.

## 6.5 Intrinsic Value {#sec-6-5}

This cluster gathers the attributes of divine worth taken in itself: holiness ([§6.5.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-5-1)) and beatitude ([§6.5.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-5-2)), God as set apart in value and as complete in self-sufficient blessedness.

Pressed, each presupposes the structure it claims to transcend: to be set apart is to stand in distinction, and to be complete in beatitude is to be a subject that persists in its own act — distinction and self-maintenance that name S and Φ rather than an intrinsic value floating free of them.

### 6.5.1 Holiness {#sec-6-5-1}

Holiness includes set-apartness, moral purity, and fittingness for worship. The relational analysis bears most directly on the first strand and should not be treated as exhausting the attribute. But being set apart is a relation: you are apart *from* something, standing distinct within some field. A being with nothing to stand apart from and no field to stand in is not supremely set apart; it is simply indistinct, with the word "holy" laid over it.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine holiness assembles several reinforcing claims. Holiness is the attribute under which the others are confessed: the believer's God is holy before it is simple, and the perfect-being maxima are received as the holiness of God made specific. God is *qodesh*: set apart, separated from the common and the profane (Leviticus 11:44–45; 19:2; Isaiah 6:3 NRSVUE, the seraphic *trisagion*). Holiness is the first predicate the worshipper reaches for and the one the liturgy repeats: *hagios, hagios, hagios* (holy, holy, holy), the Sanctus. On the phenomenological refinement, holiness is *sui generis*: Rudolf Otto's numinous [-@otto1917], the *mysterium tremendum et fascinans* (the awe-inspiring and fascinating mystery), a category irreducible to the ethical or the rational, encountered as the *wholly other* before which the creature knows itself as creature. The phrase carries a henological ancestry older than the phenomenology: it descends from the Plotinian One beyond being (*Enneads* V.5; VI.9), whose absolute set-apartness is its philosophical root. Even so, the numinous is no unmediated given: with Katz [-@katz1978], the *wholly other* is itself constituted by the tradition that receives it, not a datum prior to all mediation. In the dogmatic tradition, holiness is God's transcendent separateness as such: Aquinas treats *sanctitas* as purity together with the firmness by which the mind is fixed on God (*ST* II-II.81.8), and the broader scholastic settlement reads divine holiness as the incorruptible separateness of pure act from every creaturely admixture. Barth (*CD* II/1) develops holiness as the form of the divine love that simultaneously gives itself and resists, judges, and sets apart. Contemporary dogmatics [@webster2003] recovers holiness as the mode in which each of the other perfections is God's own. The doctrine carries two strands the tradition holds together: ontological set-apartness (God's categorial separateness from everything creaturely) and moral purity (God's separation from sin and defilement, of which the demand *be holy, for I am holy* is the creaturely echo). At its most ambitious, the doctrine names a being set apart not by degree but by category: the wholly other, separate from all that is not God by the very kind of being it is.

*What cannot be answered.* Four questions find the doctrine of divine holiness, in the form structural reasoning can take hold of, unable to answer them. What underlies them is that set-apartness is a relation before it is a perfection. To be holy is to be set apart, and to be set apart is to stand distinguished from what one is apart from, within a manifold in which the distinction can obtain (S), maintained as the same set-apart being across what would erase the distinction (T and Φ). The classical God is defined without T, S, and Φ. The four pressures run one at the level of the predicate, two at the level of the conditions holiness-talk runs on, and one at the level of what is left to revere when the conditions are gone.

**Q1.** *What is set apart, when nothing stands over against it to be set apart from?* Set-apartness is contrastive: the holy is holy in distinction from the common, as the sacred is sacred against the profane. The contrast requires a field of the not-holy for the holy to be marked off within. The classical reply is that divine holiness is not the relational set-apartness of one item marked off from others but the intrinsic perfection of the divine nature — holiness as the purity of pure act, not a standing-apart from creatures (*ST* II-II.81.8; the simplicity tradition of [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)). The reply is available, and it does the work the doctrine asks. The reply shifts holiness from relational apartness to intrinsic purity. That is a legitimate change of strand; the remaining question is how intrinsic purity is specified and related to moral value. On the relational strand, a wholly other with no manifold to be other within is not supremely distinct but indistinct; the intrinsic-purity reading escapes that verdict only by carrying the specification burden just noted.

**Q2.** *From what does the wholly other stand apart, if it stands in no position relative to anything?* Otto's numinous and Barth's holy God are encountered as *wholly other*, and otherness is a standing-over-against, a positional-relational predicate that requires S, the manifold within which two stand distinguished as the ones they are. The same point is pressed for presence at [§6.8.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-1): a being equidistant from every point alike has no position from which to stand apart. The classical reply relocates the otherness from spatial standing to the analogical transcendence of the Creator–creature distinction. The concern here is the one [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) raises for analogy: the Creator–creature distinction, if it is a real distinction and not a verbal one, is itself a structural relation — directed, asymmetric, obtaining within a manifold that holds the two terms apart. Levinas's absolutely Other [*Totality and Infinity*, -@levinas1961] is borne by the face and indexed to the encounter; strip the indexing and the otherness loses the contrast that made it other.

**Q3.** *How is anything made or kept holy, if both consecration and purity require a being that stands in time to bear them?* Holiness in the scriptural register is verbal before it is adjectival: *qadash* is to consecrate, to set apart, and what is consecrated is then kept pure: the sabbath, the temple, the people are *made* holy and *guarded* holy. Both moments are structural. Consecration is a transition from the common to the set-apart, and a transition requires T, a before and an after across which the same thing is first common and then holy. Purity is the maintained integrity of a being that could be defiled and is not, a property with a bearer (Φ) and a standing across what would compromise it. The classical God is the source of all sanctification yet is immutable, atemporal, and without Φ, and on strong simplicity sustains no real relation to what it sanctifies; its purity, likewise, is the purity of a being with nothing to keep intact and no defilement so much as possible. The classical reply is that God sanctifies eternally and without change in God (the change is in the creature, the immutability settlement of [§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3)) and that divine purity is not the contingent cleanness of a defilable being but the impossibility of defilement in pure act. The concern here is the one [§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3), [§6.4.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-1), and [§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1) reach from their own sides: a sanctifying that terminates on the creature at a moment is a temporally located effect, though a classical theorist can posit a timeless cause. Impossibility of defilement is a modal purity claim, not by itself an ∅-like absence. Both moments take their content (the transition and the maintained integrity) from the temporal side of the relation; the timeless-sanctifier model faces an interface burden there, not yet a semantic failure.

**Q4.** *What is left to revere, once the wholly other is conceived without the otherness that made it holy?* The conceivability question for divine predicates in general is taken up at [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3); the local form concerns reverence. The numinous, conceived without T, S, and Φ, terminates at the point [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) reaches: a referent for which *holy* retains no determinate content, only the affective residue of an encounter the conditions of encounter have been removed from. The reply is Otto's own: holiness is the very category that exceeds conceptual capture, and the demand for determinate content mistakes the numinous for a concept. The concern here is that exceeding conceptual capture is consistent with the set-apartness belonging to the modal structure rather than to a being beyond it. The mystic's silence before the Holy is the honest terminus of refusing to predicate; the worshipper who goes on to address, revere, and stand before the Holy One re-enacts, in every act of address, the positional and relational structure the encounter requires.

*What is required.* The four pressures lay out the structural shape of holiness.
