Holiness, on its set-apartness strand, needs a field of the not-holy for the holy to be marked off within; an apartness apart from nothing is indistinction, not the maximum of distinction. It needs a manifold in which the wholly other can stand over against what it is other than; otherness with no position is the language of distinction without its content. Creaturely consecration involves transition. A timeless sanctifier model retains an asymmetric causal relation while relocating transition to the creature, and therefore faces an interface burden rather than semantic failure. It needs a bearer whose integrity is maintained across what would defile it; purity with no possible defilement and no bearer risks collapsing into ∅'s immunity rather than a being's holiness; the modal-purity reading owes the difference. The set-apartness strand can be analogically relocated to the categorial difference between a modal structure and its occupants: the way Time, Space, and Substance stand to every inhabitant as that which is not itself one of the inhabitants.

*What is inverted.* The inversion relocates categorial set-apartness to Nature. Moral holiness and worship-worthiness are not established by structural difference alone. The English *holy* descends through Old English *hālig* from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz*, bound to *whole* and *hale*: the holy is the whole, the intact, that which is set apart by the integrity that makes it inviolable. The Latin *sacer* and the Hebrew *qodesh* carry the same logic of separation: cut off, consecrated, removed from the common. The tradition reaches for a being set apart from everything creaturely by the very kind of being it is, and names the wholly other. Read structurally, what is set apart from every inhabitant by the very kind of thing it is, is the modal structure: Nature is not one of the things within Nature, and its categorial distinctness from all it grounds is the set-apartness [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) turns on. A being defined without T, S, and Φ cannot be set apart, for it has no manifold to stand apart within and no contrast to be holy against; its purported holiness inverts into *Divine Indistinction*: the limiting case of a holiness with no conditions of distinction left to it. The set-apartness the tradition reveres as the holiness of God is the apartness of Nature itself, which §7 takes up directly.

### 6.5.2 Beatitude {#sec-6-5-2}

Beatitude is God's perfect blessedness: the fullness of self-sufficient joy in which God, lacking nothing, wants nothing it does not already have. The pressure is that the same tradition calls God a lover who wills the good of creatures, a giver whose goodness pours outward, a will that creates what need not have been. Desire and hope ordinarily concern an unattained good, but willing and giving need not arise from lack. The classical distinction between desire and beneficent willing is therefore central rather than something the section may erase. And once God is said to will goods that the world's history may not deliver, a further question opens that the doctrine cannot close: can such a being be satisfied?

*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology assigns God beatitude: the perfect and self-sufficient blessedness of a being that possesses the complete good and so lacks nothing it could want. The doctrine inherits the eudaimonist conception of blessedness as the self-sufficient life (*makária*, the life of one who, having every good, needs nothing further; Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* [-@aristotle1984, I.7, X.6–8]) and locates that life in God as its unqualified instance. Aquinas treats the attribute directly: beatitude (the perfect good proper to an intellectual nature) belongs to God supremely and essentially, one with the act of divine self-understanding, so that God is not made blessed by anything beyond it but *is* its own beatitude, with every other beatitude contained eminently in the divine (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.26]). The doctrine binds beatitude to the attributes the chapter has already examined: a being that is *actus purus*, with no unrealized potential (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.3.1]), and *perfectus* in the sense of *completus*, lacking nothing the having of which would make it greater (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.4]), is a being for which nothing is left to want; its blessedness is not the satisfaction of a desire but the eternal possession of the good it is. Yet the same tradition holds that God loves (wills the good of the creature; Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.20]) and that the divine goodness is diffusive, pouring outward in creation. The contemporary literature divides on whether blessedness so understood survives as a coherent predicate of a personal God. Theistic personalism takes God to be everlasting rather than timeless, a person whose perfect well-being is lived through time [@swinburne1977; @swinburne2004; @mullins2016]; the dipolar tradition assigns invariant blessedness to an abstract pole and a growing, world-enriched joy to a concrete pole [@hartshorne1941; @hartshorne1948]; and the account of love as union and desire for the good of the beloved [@stump2010] makes the beloved's good internal to the lover's own flourishing. The position the classical doctrine, fully stated, holds is that God's blessedness is complete, invariant, and underived: nothing the creature does or fails to do adds to or subtracts from the divine joy, which is God's eternal possession of its own infinite goodness.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions take the doctrine to the edge of what it can answer once blessedness is recast in the form structural reasoning operates in. Underneath them the concern is structural: blessedness, in the sense that distinguishes it from bare self-identity, is the *satisfaction* of a being that could have wanted, and wanting, satisfaction, and the rest that follows attainment are features of substances oriented through Time toward states not yet actual.

**Q1.** *How does a being that lacks nothing desire, will, or hope?* To desire is to be oriented toward a good not yet possessed; a temporal act of willing an end may be directed at a state of affairs that does not yet obtain; to hope is to lean toward a future not yet actual. Each predicate carries, in its ordinary sense, a reference to the not-yet: the structure Time names ([§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4)). The classical reply removes the not-yet: God does not desire the good as absent but possesses it eternally, and God's will is not a motion toward an end but the eternal act by which the end is willed (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.20]). The concern here is that this empties the predicates of the content that made them predicates of a *blessed* being rather than of a bare fact: a timeless will needs an account of contingent objects and effects, but willing another's good need not involve frustrated desire, and joy need not be analyzed solely as desire-satisfaction. The orientation-toward-the-not-yet-actual that *desire* and *hope* name is the structural feature Time carries; the doctrine keeps those words only by removing it, and the non-deficient willing that remains must be specified without them.

**Q2.** *Can a being that lacks nothing want anything — and if it cannot want, can it love or create?* Perfection in the classical sense is *completus*: God has every property the having of which would constitute a greater being, and lacks nothing it could have (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.4]). Pressed from the property-side to the want-side, completeness entails that God lacks no state of affairs it could want, because wanting is the relation of a being to a good it does not have. But a being that is *actus purus* has no potency to be actualized (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.3.1]), and wanting is precisely the potency to be moved by an unattained good. The reply that God *wills* the good of creatures without *wanting* it (willing as pure act, not as desire; Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.20]) preserves plenitude by distinguishing the willing of an end from the wanting of it. The concern here is that the distinction, pressed, leaves creation and love without the feature that made them acts of a blessed will: to will the creature's good and bring about a contingent state requires intentional direction, but it is not therefore wanting under another name. A beneficent agent can choose an outcome without needing it for completion. The dilemma is therefore conditional: either God wants the goods it wills, and is not complete, or the willing is non-deficient beneficence, in which case the doctrine still owes an account of why *this* outcome is chosen that never borrows the orientation wanting supplies.

**Q3.** *Can God be satisfied?* Three commitments the tradition holds together generate the question. First, God loves universally — wills the good of every creature (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.20]). Second, on orthodox eschatology, not every creature attains the good God wills for it; some are finally lost. Third, God's blessedness is complete, invariant, and impassible — not added to or diminished by what creatures do ([§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3), [§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4)). Add the contestable value-theoretic premise that divine love includes a desire whose satisfaction contributes to divine well-being. Classical theorists reject that premise, and traditions also differ over whether God wills every creature's final salvation in the same sense. The three commitments and the premise cannot all hold. If some willed good is finally unattained, a being whose blessedness tracked its loves would not be fully satisfied, but the doctrine says God is fully blessed. If God is fully satisfied regardless of whether its loves attain their goods, then the willed goods are not goods God wanted attained, and universal love is emptied. And if the divine satisfaction varied with the world's history (full where its loves are attained, less than full where they are not), beatitude would change, which immutability and impassibility forbid. The trilemma therefore arises only under a desire-satisfaction model plus a specific account of universal salvific will; it is not internal to every doctrine of beatitude. The trilemma is the beatitude-register form of the composition pressure [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) develops: perfect love, perfect blessedness, and invariance do not compose without relaxing one of them.

**Q4.** *Which commitment gives way?* The tradition's resources for the trilemma are systematic, and each resolves it by relaxing one of the three commitments. The atemporal-eternalist holds that God's beatitude is timeless, so there is no before-and-after of satisfaction to vary, but this relaxes the sense in which God wills goods *for* a history whose outcomes are not yet actual, the pressure of Q1. The pure-act Thomist holds that *satisfied* and *unsatisfied* apply to God not univocally but only analogically, but this concedes that beatitude-as-enjoyment is not literally predicated, and the analogical move faces the homonymy-or-univocal-core dilemma [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) presses (Q1). The open theist and the theistic personalist hold that God's blessedness genuinely tracks the world and can be less than it would otherwise be [God grieves what is lost; @swinburne1977; @swinburne2004; @mullins2016], but this relaxes immutability and impassibility ([§6.3.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-3), [§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4)) and concedes a temporal, affected God. The dipolar theist assigns invariant blessedness to the abstract pole and world-tracking joy to the concrete pole [@hartshorne1941; @hartshorne1948], but, as [§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4) and [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) press, the two poles are one subject only through the directed crossing between them ([§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3)), which imports the structural conditions the abstract pole was meant to escape. The Reformed-Edwardsian holds that God's last end is the manifestation of its glory [@edwards1765], so that the finally lost manifest divine justice and no willed good goes unattained, but this relaxes universal love, narrowing what God wills the good of. The Aristotelian-Thomist returns beatitude to its eudaimonist root: God's blessedness is the self-contemplation of its own goodness, *makária* in the strict sense, and does not consist in the attainment of any creaturely good, but this relaxes the diffusiveness of the good and the love of Q2, severing blessedness from the willing of creaturely goods altogether. Every exit pays in one of the three commitments; none holds all three.

**Q5.** *By what is God blessed — by its own goodness, or by the attainment of what it wills?* The eudaimonist root makes blessedness self-sufficient: God is *autarkēs*, blessed in the contemplation of its own complete goodness, needing nothing outside itself. The relational commitments make blessedness include the good of what God loves: a God whose joy is wholly indifferent to whether its loves attain their goods does not love them in the sense the believer's life rests on. If blessedness is self-sufficient, then creation, love, and the creature's good add nothing to it, and the diffusiveness of the good is a giving that costs and returns the giver nothing: beatitude sealed off from the history it is said to govern. If blessedness includes the attainment of willed goods, then it depends on what is received and brought about (on states of affairs realized through Time, in Space, by the persistence of substances) and is conditioned by the structure the doctrine placed beatitude beyond. The concern here is that *blessed* is either self-sufficient, in which case it names not a relation to any good but the completeness of a structure that has no outside, or relational, in which case it is conditioned by T, S, and Φ. The doctrine wants both: the self-sufficiency of a being that needs nothing and the responsiveness of a being whose loves are answered.

*What is required.* Carried through, the five pressures bring out what the predicate *blessed* actually depends on. Desire and hope are ordinarily oriented toward the not-yet-actual, while will can be construed as non-deficient intention; a beatitude that removes the orientation keeps the words only if joy can be specified apart from desire-satisfaction, and that specification is still owed. Wanting is the potency to be moved by an unattained good, which pure act excludes; plenitude and the diffusiveness of the good compose only through a non-deficient willing whose account of directed choice remains open. The satisfaction-trilemma, under its desire-satisfaction premise, cannot be answered while all three commitments stand: universal love, complete blessedness, and invariance then do not compose, and every classical exit relaxes one of them. And blessedness is either self-sufficient (in which case it names the completeness of a structure with no outside to want) or relational, in which case it is conditioned by Time, Space, and Substance. What survives is a disputed distinction between non-deficient self-sufficiency and relational joy. Structural completeness may illustrate the first, but it does not itself possess joy.

*What is inverted.* The inversion relocates self-sufficiency to Nature at the structural level; it does not establish that Nature is a blessed subject. *Blessed* (*makarios*, *beatus*, the predicate of a life that lacks nothing and needs nothing outside itself) names, in the one sense the dilemmas above leave standing, not a subject enjoying its own completeness but the modal completeness of the structure that has no outside: □(T∧S∧Φ) exhausts the field of real possibility, so there is no possibility beyond Nature that Nature could lack, want, or be oriented toward. The eudaimonist tradition fixes the mark of blessedness as *autarkeia*, self-sufficiency: the blessed life is the one that, possessing every good, depends on nothing further. What is genuinely *autarkēs*, depending on nothing outside itself because there is no outside, is not a being among beings but Nature, the structure within which every good, every want, and every attainment occurs. The classical doctrine reaches for a being whose joy needs nothing the world can add and fears nothing the world can take, and locates it in a subject that, to be blessed, has to be lifted out of the Time, Space, and Substance through which anything is ever wanted or attained. Viewed within the structure that hosts it, *blessed* names the self-sufficiency of Nature: not the rest of a will that has stopped wanting, but the completeness of the modal structure that has no beyond. Desire, satisfaction, and the rest that follows attainment belong to the configurations within Nature whose wanting is the felt form of the modal pressure running through the whole ([§8.1](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-1)); blessedness, the predicate the tradition reserved for the being beyond all wanting, belongs to the whole within which all wanting moves. The aseity [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) returned to the modal self-grounding of Nature and the perfection [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) returned to its necessity meet here: what depends on nothing and lacks nothing is the structure that is the condition of dependence and lack, not a being exempt from them. The result is carried forward at [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10).

## 6.6 Life {#sec-6-6}

The tradition calls God *the living God*, not merely existent but supremely alive, life in its highest instance. The difficulty is what *life* has meant since the tradition's own founding texts: to be alive is to move from within, to act of oneself, to be the source of one's own activity rather than a thing merely held in being. The classical God, though, is pure act without potency, immutable, outside time: a being that passes from no state of activity to any other. The predicate that was to mark God as most alive turns out to require the very self-movement the surrounding attributes deny.

*What the tradition holds.* Scripture's God is *the living God*, and the philosophical tradition makes life a divine attribute of the first rank. Aristotle's unmoved mover is itself life: the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality. The divine life is the eternal self-contemplation of *noēsis noēseōs*, thought thinking itself (Aristotle, *Metaphysics* [-@aristotle1984, XII.7, XII.9]). Aquinas systematizes the attribution: life belongs to God most properly of all, because those things are most properly called living that move themselves. Life is immanent self-activity, operation that proceeds from the agent and remains within it, and God, as pure act, is the highest instance of such immanent operation, the act of self-understanding (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.18.1–4]). To live is the highest grade of being; God, as the fullness of being, is alive in the fullest sense: *vita Dei*, the life identical with the divine essence. The doctrine keeps the God of the covenant from collapsing into an inert principle by binding life to actuality: God is most alive because most fully in act.

*What cannot be answered.* Four questions ask of the doctrine what it cannot answer once *life* is required to carry its own content. The pressure beneath them is that the tradition's own definition of life (immanent self-movement) names the transition the classical attributes forbid.

**Q1.** *If to be alive is to move oneself, and God cannot change, what makes God living rather than inert?* Aquinas defines the living as the self-moving (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.18.1]): self-movement is a passage from one state of activity to another effected by the thing itself. The classical God is immutable and timeless: it undergoes no transition, effects no change in itself, passes from no state to any other. A being in which nothing moves satisfies the definition of the inert, not the living; the tradition's own criterion for life is the one the classical God is built to fail. The reply that divine "movement" is metaphorical (activity without change) either keeps the content of *self-movement*, and immutability is lost, or drops it, and *living* no longer marks anything off from a static principle.

**Q2.** *If God's life is the pure actuality of self-understanding, what does that understanding do that bare being does not already do?* Aristotle and Aquinas locate the divine life in contemplation: the changeless act of thought thinking itself. The Thomist anticipates the obvious pressure (that an act which never passes from considering to considered is an act in name only) and blocks it on the doctrine's own terms: *life* and *operation* are predicated of God not univocally but analogically (Aquinas, *ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.13]), naming *immanent operation*, activity that remains wholly within the agent and needs no transition, in a mode proper to the divine being. It is the strongest reply the doctrine has here, and it has to be met where [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1) meets it. Analogical predication earns its content only if the predicate tracks a real correlate in the divine subject, standing in the appropriate proportion to its creaturely instance ([§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1)); a predicate that tracks no such correlate is not analogical but empty. Ask what the correlate of *operation* is. The Thomist denies at the outset that divine understanding is a taking-up that runs from understanding to understood: in God knower and known coincide, the operation remaining wholly within, with no interval to cross and no order to run. Grant exactly that. The pressure is not that God's self-understanding *must* be a directed crossing, but that it must be *something* if it is to be operation at all: an exercise the divine subject performs, tellable apart from the bare standing of its essence. And [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) fixes what any such exercise costs: an interval across which it runs (S), an order in the running (T), and a substantial carrier in which it originates and terminates (Φ). The dilemma is therefore not whether the divine act crosses an interval the Thomist has already denied, but whether, stripped of every such condition, anything is left that *operation* still names. The horns are the ones [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1) draws for *actus purus*: either the divine operation is a genuine way of being-in-act, and it carries the conditions any way of being decomposes into, or it is no way at all (an act with no exercise, no relatum, no passage) and then it is indistinguishable from the bare standing of the essence, and *life* has added nothing to *existence*.

**Q3.** *If God is alive only by being responsive to what happens, how can the living God be the ground of happening rather than a participant in it?* The process tradition presses exactly this: the immutable, impassible God is *dead* (affected by nothing, responsive to nothing) and only a God who genuinely changes with the world is alive [@hartshorne1948]. The dipolar God is alive because responsive. But [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) has shown what responsiveness costs: to receive and respond is to stand in a directed crossing that runs through T, S, and Φ, and a being alive by such crossing instantiates the structural conditions rather than standing beyond them. Life bought by responsiveness is life on the structure's terms. The horns are fixed: an unresponsive God keeps aseity and forfeits life; a responsive God secures life and forfeits aseity.

**Q4.** *If God's life, knowledge, will, and being are one undivided act, what does calling God living add to calling God existent?* On divine simplicity ([§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1)), God's life is not distinct from God's understanding, willing, or being: God *is* the divine life, without composition. But then *living* marks no feature that could be present or absent, and [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1) has traced where that leads. Either *life* picks out a determinate content distinct from bare existence, an operation tellable apart from the mere standing of the essence, and the simplicity that forbids all internal differentiation fails; or it picks out nothing distinguishable, and *the living God* says no more than *the existing God*, the predicate emptied of the vitality it was asserted to carry.

*What is required.* The four pressures together isolate what *life* depends on. Life, on the tradition's own definition, is immanent self-movement, and self-movement requires a before-and-after of the moving (T), differentiated states between which the living thing passes (S), and a substantial agent that persists as the source of its own activity across the passage (Φ). Contemplation counts as life only where it is exercised, and an exercise stripped of interval, order, and carrier has yet to show what *operation* still names. Responsiveness counts as life only at the cost of embedding in the structure the response crosses. And life predicates something of its bearer only where it is distinguishable from bare existence, which requires the composition simplicity denies. What *life* survives as, once the pressures have run, is not a grade of being a static essence could hold but the structural fact of a carrier in directed activity among its states.

*What is inverted.* Life is the self-activity of Substance in time. *Living*, in the only sense that survives, names a carrier (Φ) undergoing directed transition (T) among differentiated states (S) from an internal principle, which is to say, it names Nature in act. Aristotle sees it exactly: the actuality of thought is life, and actuality, as the argument has shown, is the instantiation of the structural conditions, not their negation. The tradition reaches for *life* to say that God is no inert abstraction but the living source of all activity; traced honestly, the same vocabulary finds that what is alive is what moves itself through time, and what moves itself through time is Nature, not a being defined by the denial of motion. The living God is the life of Nature, named as though it stood outside the only thing that lives. The predicate is inverted from within: *the living God* is a being specified by the absence of everything living things do.

## 6.7 Agency {#sec-6-7}

The active arm opens with agency: the attributes of divine doing: power ([§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1)), causality ([§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2)), interaction ([§6.7.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-3)), and sovereignty ([§6.7.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-4)). Each says that God acts: brings about, causes, engages, and governs.

These are the chapter's clearest carriers of the second master result, the directed-crossing analysis of [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3): any act that brings something about must cross from cause to effect along an asymmetric ordering, through distinct relata, with an agent that persists across the doing — which is to say it runs on T, S, and Φ. A being defined as lacking Time, Space, and Substance cannot perform an act; an agent that acts already instantiates all three, and with them the Conditions they bear.

### 6.7.1 Power {#sec-6-7-1}

Omnipotence is "all-powerful," but the same tradition calls God "pure act": without any unrealized potential. Those pull against each other, since power is usually the capacity to do what is not yet done. And whatever power comes to, exercising it (creating, sustaining, intervening) is an act, and acting runs through time, place, and substance. The section presses both seams.

*What the tradition holds.* Theists call God omnipotent and gloss the word as *all-powerful*. *Omnipotens* is *omnis* + *potentia*: all-potency, every capacity. But in the Aristotelian frame the tradition inherits, potency is the unrealized side of act: the capacity not yet exercised, what could be otherwise but is not yet. And the same tradition defines God as *actus purus*: pure act, entirely without potency. Aquinas is explicit that in God there is no potentiality, no unrealized capacity, no movement from what is not yet actual to what is (ST I.3.1–2; I.9.1). The central attribute is therefore held in two directions at once. The standard Thomistic resolution distinguishes active power from passive potency: God has unlimited active power without unrealized passive potency (ST I.25.1; [@stump2003; @dolezal2017]), so that the gloss *all-powerful* reads *omnipotens* against active power rather than against unrealized capacity.

Around this resolution the classical doctrine assembles a set of reinforcing claims about how that power operates. God created the universe *ex nihilo*, with no antecedent matter, time, or space (Aquinas, ST I.45; cf. Genesis 1:1 NRSVUE). God conserves all things in being moment by moment (ST I.104). And God concurs with creaturely action, so that creaturely causation occurs through divine causation rather than alongside it (ST I.105; [@flintFreddoso1983]). God also acts in history through miracles, in which divine causation overrides ordinary causal regularity [@hume1748; @swinburne1970; @larmer2014]. Ash'arite occasionalism (the view that God is the sole genuine cause, creaturely events being only the occasions of God's acting) is the parallel development in the Islamic tradition (Al-Ghazali, *Incoherence of the Philosophers* XVII; [@frank1992; @griffel2009]).

The tradition then refines the scope of the power itself. On Aquinas's canonical refinement, omnipotence is the capacity to bring about whatever does not involve contradiction (ST I.25; with @mavrodes1963 and @frankfurt1964 on the stone-paradox). On Geach's reading, the more theologically traditional term is *almighty* [@geach1973]. Wierenga [-@wierenga1989] develops the contemporary analytic account. And on the most ambitious reading, divine power extends to the modal structure itself [@leftow2012]. Taken at that most ambitious reading, the doctrine names a being whose power is comprehensive enough to author what is possible, sustained moment-by-moment in everything that obtains, and unrestricted by any condition external to itself.

*What cannot be answered.* Six questions open onto what omnipotence, in the form structural reasoning can take up, cannot account for. The structural pressure here has two layers. First, the active-power refinement preserves the gloss but not the work: active power is power-*to*-actualize-this-rather-than-that, and what divine power is asked to do (create, conserve, govern, intervene, answer) has its content in the actualization of one determinate state rather than another. Without a contrast between the state actualized and the state not actualized, the verb *actualize* loses determinate content; the doctrine of pure act, taken strictly, removes that contrast and leaves the term *power* without the modal contrast power consists in. Second, causation, on the analyses [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) develops in detail, is the carrying of influence forward by a being (Φ) through an interval (S) in a temporal direction (T), and the classical God is defined as without any of the three. The six pressures run one at the level of the predicate, five at the level of the conditions causation-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *How does creation cause a world, if there is no state it brings the world out of?* *Creatio ex nihilo* holds that God brought the universe into being with no antecedent matter, time, or space. Aquinas (ST I.45) develops the doctrine carefully: creation is not a change, since change requires a subject that undergoes the change, and prior to creation there is no subject. Creation is the production of being itself, with nothing antecedent for the production to occur in. The reply preserves the doctrine against the classical objection that nothing comes from nothing. The concern here is the cost of the preservation. Causation, on the analysis given, is a transition from a state in which the effect does not obtain to one in which it does. If creation is not a transition (if there is no antecedent state for the transition to be from) then creation, on the classical reading, is not a case of the structural relation the analysis examines. The classical reply is that *cause* applies to creation analogically rather than univocally, and the analogical application preserves what the term performs. The reply is genuinely available, and [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) takes its measure. The point this section adds is that what *create* names, on the doctrine fully stated, is closer to a primitive of divine doing than to an analyzable case of causation, and the difference is precisely the structural conditions the doctrine has placed beyond divine being. There is a further pressure on the modal side. If creator-status is essential to God (if God is necessarily a creator) then in every world where God exists, God creates; if God exists necessarily, creation is necessary. The Thomist's standard distinction between God's act-considered-in-itself (necessary) and the act's *terminus ad extra* (its outward effect toward creation, which is contingent) requires a real ground for the distinction in God, which strict simplicity disallows. Mullins [-@mullins2013; -@mullins2016] and Tomaszewski [-@tomaszewski2019] press this from inside the literature. The doctrine has wanted necessary creator-status and contingent creation simultaneously, and these are two commitments joined only by the term *one act*. Pruss and Rasmussen's necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction (*Necessary Existence*, -@prussRasmussen2018, ch. 5) offers the canonical middle position: God necessarily creates *some* world (creator-status is essential), but creates this particular contingent order among alternatives (the necessity attaches to the creator-status, not to the specific creation). In the power register, the distinction deflects the modal-collapse concern by locating contingency in the terminus of the creative act rather than in the act itself. The concern for the Pruss/Rasmussen reply at Q1 is whether the selection among contingent termini itself requires the directed-act structure creation-as-power consists in: the being must be positioned to select (S), must transition through the selection (T), and must be the substantial bearer of both the creator-status and the selecting act (Φ). The necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction shifts the modal-collapse concern from the level of creator-status to the level of selection, where the chapter's structural analysis applies at full force.

**Q2.** *How does power make a thing possible, when making it already takes its being possible?* Aquinas (ST I.25.3) restricts omnipotence to what is logically possible: God cannot make a square circle, not because divine power is limited but because *square circle* names no possibility for power to range over. Descartes (Letters to Mesland 1644) takes the opposite turn: God's power extends to the eternal truths themselves, including logical and mathematical necessity. The contemporary mainstream sides with the Thomistic restriction [@swinburne1977; @wierenga1989; @flintFreddoso1983]. The modal-frame question is worked from the necessity side at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) and from the logic-grounding side at [§5.1.9](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-9); the concern returns here in the form [§3.4](convergence.html#sec-3-4) revisits. The Thomistic restriction either makes logical necessity a condition on divine power, in which case the deepest modal facts are not products of divine activity ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)), or extends divine power to the modal structure itself [@leftow2012], in which case the conditions any exercise of power presupposes are themselves the products of an exercise. The first horn keeps coherence by surrendering scope; the second keeps scope at the cost of self-grounding the doctrine has not made structurally tractable.

**Q3.** *What is unlimited in a power confined to possibilities it never authored?* Frankfurt [-@frankfurt1964] raises the puzzle in its sharpest form: can God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? The Thomistic resolution is well-developed [@mavrodes1963; @plantinga1967]: omnipotence is the capacity to bring about logically possible states of affairs, and a stone too heavy for an omnipotent being to lift is not a logically possible state of affairs. The resolution is correct as far as it goes. The concern this section adds is what it reveals: omnipotence is defined relative to a modal space whose status is what [§3.2.6](convergence.html#sec-3-2-6) has put in question. The paradox dissolves under the Thomistic restriction; what the restriction leaves is a doctrine of omnipotence indexed to the modal structure, with the being's authorship over the modal structure either denied (collapsing scope) or affirmed (collapsing the structure). The pattern generalizes. The *stone paradox* is one of three structurally analogous cases the tradition treats under the same restriction: the immovable stone (Φ-logic), the square circle (S-logic), and the past-altering act (T-logic). The three are analogous rather than identical (the immovable stone fails by modal-conceptual necessity, the square circle by geometric necessity, the past-altering act by temporal-logical necessity) but the Thomistic restriction dissolves each the same way, by declaring it not a possibility for power to range over; what the restriction concedes, taken across the three together, is that what *power* can do is indexed to the three structural logics [§2.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-10) isolates: the modal structure any exercise of power presupposes. The limit the theist concedes so readily in logic, that omnipotence reaches neither the immovable stone nor the square circle nor the altered past, was a limit of structure all along: what logic forbids in the three cases is what the structural logics of substance, extension, and succession forbid. The paradox is a symptom; the concern is the condition the symptom registers.

**Q4.** *How does a cause come before its effect, if it stands at no time at all?* Causation runs in a temporal direction: the cause precedes or is simultaneous with the effect, and the effect does not precede the cause. The analyses [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) develops are explicit on this point, and even the most permissive contemporary accounts [@lewis1973a; @salmon1984; @dowe2000] preserve the asymmetry as constitutive. The classical God, defined as atemporal, has no temporal location relative to which the *from*-state of any causal act is before and the *to*-state is after. The doctrine of eternal causation (God's act of creation, conservation, and governance is one eternal act) addresses the difficulty by setting aside temporal direction [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @leftow2012]. The concern here is the one [§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2) presses for eternity and [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) for knowledge: setting aside the temporal asymmetry preserves the term *cause* and removes the structure that distinguishes causation from a static relation between abstracta. A logical entailment between premises and conclusion does not *cause* the conclusion in the sense the doctrine of providence trades on. The doctrine wants the relation between God and creation to be more than logical entailment, and the more is precisely T.

**Q5.** *By what power does a being produce the very conditions its power runs on?* Q2 raises the modal-scope question; Q5 returns to its sharpest form. The deepest version of the doctrine extends divine power to the conditions any exercise of power presupposes: God authors what is possible, not merely what is actual [@leftow2012]. The concern here is the one [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2) will press at the level of agency: to author the modal frame is to do something whose conditions appear to require T, S, and Φ: a transition between not-having-authored and having-authored, a position from which the authorship is exercised, a substantial being through which the activity runs. The pressure runs equally on the target side. Creating X presupposes that X is possible to create, since *create* names the actualization of what is antecedently possible: the verb has no determinate target where the target has no antecedent modal standing, and the actualization-relation runs from a possibility into an actuality of that possibility. The classical reply that divine creation establishes the possibility-of-X in establishing X itself preserves the doctrine by making the conferral of possibility and the conferral of actuality one act, and the move is genuinely available; what it does not preserve is the difference between *create* and *be*, since the verb's content depends on the modal contrast its target carried before the operation. To create-the-possibility-of-X simultaneously with actualizing-X is to perform two operations whose ordering the doctrine has flattened: the first supplies the modal range the second operates within, and the simultaneity preserves the verb at the cost of the structure the verb's intelligibility runs on. Agent-side and target-side conditions converge on the same modal field: the field that hosts the act and the field that supplies the target are one field, and a field that hosts and supplies the exercise of power cannot be the exercise's product. To preserve *author* while removing those conditions is to keep the verb and lose the structure that gave it its content. Pruss [-@pruss2011], Mullins [-@mullins2016], and Mullins and Byrd [-@mullinsByrd2022] raise structural concerns from inside the literature. The point this section adds, from the side of power specifically, is that the most ambitious version of the doctrine (omnipotence over modality) names what Nature is and locates it in a being beyond Nature. Nature is what underwrites possibility because Nature is what possibility is the modal status of. Pruss's PSR pressure runs symmetrically against the inversion. If Nature underwrites possibility because it is the necessary modal structure, the PSR demand returns at the level of Nature itself: what grounds Nature's having the specific structural conditions it has (T, S, Φ in their particular constitutions) rather than other conditions or none (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason*, -@pruss2006; *Infinity, Causation, and Paradox*, -@pruss2018)? The section's terminus (*Nature has them as a necessary fact*) is what Pruss identifies as the PSR-violating move: treating brute structural necessity as the terminus of explanation without asking what grounds the necessity's specific character. The asymmetry the inversion requires (that Nature's structural necessity is less explanatorily objectionable than a God's) depends on a reply to Pruss's PSR demand that the book's positive account carries at [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) (resting on [§2.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-8)).

**Q6.** *How can a creature do otherwise than God moves it to do?* If divine causation conserves all things in being moment by moment (ST I.104) and concurs with all creaturely action (ST I.105; [@flintFreddoso1983]), the question is whether creaturely actions retain the not-being-determined-by-divine-causation that libertarian freedom requires. The Banezian–Molinist debate (Báñez vs Molina, 16th–17th c.; [@garrigouLagrange1936; @flint1998]) is the classical site. Banezian physical premotion holds that God moves the will to its act in such a way that the act remains genuinely the creature's own; Molinism holds that divine concurrence operates through middle knowledge of what the creature would freely do. Both positions are serious; both face well-developed contemporary objections: the grounding objection against Molinism, the question of how physical premotion preserves freedom against Báñez. The concern here is parallel to those raised at [§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4) and [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2): the doctrine wants comprehensive divine causation and genuine creaturely freedom, and the standard refinements partition the explanatory contributions in ways that preserve the verbal predicates without resolving the underlying tension.

*What is required.* The six pressures, considered together, reveal what the predicate *power* commits to. Power consists in actualizing this rather than that, and active power without a this-rather-than-that for the act to be the actualization of preserves the term while removing the modal contrast power consists in. *Creation* read as production without transition is closer to a primitive of divine doing than to the analyzable causal relation *cause* names, and the analogical defense registers the distance from causation rather than closing it. The carrying of influence runs through a bearer; a divine essence as ground stands as what exercise depends on, not as what performs the carrying. It runs across an interval, since without spatial extension between agent and patient there is nowhere for the influence to travel. And it runs in a temporal direction: eternal causation preserves the term *cause* while removing the structure that distinguishes causation from logical entailment, while the doctrine of providence requires the relation between God and creation to be more than entailment. At the deepest layer the doctrine reaches, power that authors the modal structure is power exercising the conditions it authors, and the structure does not survive the recursion; the comprehensive-providence/creaturely-freedom partition preserves the verbal predicates without dissolving the underlying tension. *Potens*, read against the conditions of its application, is the capacity Nature has to issue its potency into act; T, S, and Φ are what makes the issuing possible.

*What is inverted.* Power is what Nature does when Nature actualizes what its structure permits. The English *power* descends through Old French *poeir* from the Latin *posse*, *to be able*. The verb's root, *potis-*, names *capable, having the capacity to*. To be powerful is to have, in the being, the structural conditions for potency to issue into act: a substantial being the capacity is of (Φ), an interval the influence traverses (S), a temporal direction along which the actualization runs (T). What the doctrine of omnipotence was reaching for is the full actualized capacity of Nature: not a being outside Nature with its potency stripped, but Nature itself with its potency intact. Omnipotence requires potency; pure actuality forecloses it; the two doctrines cannot both be true in the same sense. Spelled out in full, the predicate's conditions describe Nature.

### 6.7.2 Causality {#sec-6-7-2}

Scripture's God acts: a true agent who wills, chooses, and intervenes in history. An act, examined, needs a real alternative it picks out (this done *rather than* that) and a path from not-yet-done to done. A single eternal act with no unactualized alternatives is not the most concentrated agency; it is indistinguishable from a static fact that simply follows from God's nature. The believer's "let this cup pass" asks for a difference such an act has none of.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine agency assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *actus purus*, pure act, with no potency, no transition, no movement from could-be-willing to is-willing (Aquinas, *ST* I.3, I.19). God's willing is identical with God's being; the willing and the willed are one eternal act (Augustine, *De Trinitate* XV; Aquinas, *ST* I.19). God acts in history (election, exodus, incarnation, resurrection) and answers prayer, and works miracles in which divine causation overrides ordinary causal regularity [@hume1748; @swinburne1970; @larmer2014].

On the most developed contemporary refinements, the eternal divine act stands in ET-simultaneity (eternal-temporal simultaneity: the relation by which an eternal being is present, in full, to every temporal moment alike) [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991; @leftow2012]. Divine causation is *primitive* rather than a special case of structural causation [@mccann2012; @stump2016]. Divine sovereignty extends to the modal structure within which acts are intelligible at all [@leftow2012]. Open theism takes the reverse turn and pulls God back into time, allowing genuine response to creaturely action [@wolterstorff1975; @hasker1989; @mullins2016].

Each move tries to keep agency from being a creaturely capacity writ large. At its most ambitious, the doctrine names a being whose every doing is one eternal act, whose sovereignty extends to the modal structure within which doing is intelligible at all, and whose creatures' acting is held within the divine causing without compromising its being theirs.

*What cannot be answered.* Seven questions ask of divine agency what, in the form structural reasoning can take up, it cannot answer. What lies beneath them is the structural analysis the section's argument depends on. An act is the actualization of one determinate state rather than another: the hand reaches rather than not-reaching; the reaching is the agent's; the not-reaching is a real alternative until the reaching displaces it. Agency, on this minimal description, has a modal-structural profile before it has a temporal one. There must be a contrast between actualized and unactualized alternatives (done and not-done, this rather than that) for the resulting state to be an act rather than a static fact. Where the contrast is realized in time, agency runs through a transition (T) between not-yet-having-acted and having-acted, an interval (S) across which the doing is launched and at which it lands, and a substantial being (Φ) in whom the doing originates and through which its influence runs. The deeper condition is the modal contrast itself: an act is intelligible only against an unactualized alternative. The same analysis explains why freedom cannot mean unconstrained origination. An act is free only where there is a live alternative for the agent to model and a persisting agent able to participate in which alternative becomes actual. At the instant of reaction, agency contracts into embodied response; with distance from the action, the agent can hold more alternatives in view, compare consequences, revise impulse, and reshape the field in which later acts will occur. Freedom, on this analysis, is the degree to which a self-modeling agent can participate in the selection of one live possibility among alternatives. The seven pressures run two at the level of the predicate, five at the level of the conditions agency-talk runs on. [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) takes up the analogical and apophatic replies in the form they have in the literature.

**Q1.** *How does God intend this rather than that, if there is no "that" left undone?* For an intention to be the intention to do *this* rather than *that*, there must be a real alternative: a determinate state the agent does not actualize, set against the determinate state the agent does actualize. The contrast is constitutive: an intention is the agent's selection of one alternative over another, and where there is no unactualized alternative there is no selection. *Actus purus* (Aquinas, *ST* I.19) forecloses the contrast deliberately: in God there is no potency, no unrealized alternative, no movement from could-be-willing-otherwise to is-willing-this, only the single eternal act in which willing and being are identical. The Thomist's standard reply is that the worry conflates active power with passive potency: God has unlimited active power without unrealized passive potency. The reformulation does not turn on Aristotelian potency. It turns on modal contrast. Active power is power-to-actualize-this-rather-than-that. Strip the contrast (remove every unactualized alternative) and what remains is not a more concentrated form of agency but a static eternal fact, indistinguishable from a logical entailment between the divine essence and what follows from it. The believer who prays "let this cup pass" is asking for a difference between an actualized and an unactualized alternative; the eternal act with no internal contrast has no such difference to give. Stump [-@stump2003] and Dolezal [-@dolezal2017] defend the position by treating *intention* analogically; the present analysis registers the move and presses the cost: the analogical reading preserves the term by removing what the term tracks.

Hartshorne's dipolar account addresses Q1 by locating agency in the concrete pole: the concrete pole's acts are genuine intentional acts, involving directed transition, modal contrast, and responsive selection among the open alternatives creaturely co-creation supplies. The abstract pole provides the invariant structure within which the concrete pole's agency runs; the concrete pole provides the modal contrast Q1 requires. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses, in the local form of an agency dilemma: if the composite subject's acts belong to the concrete pole, the concrete pole is a temporal, T-instantiating being whose acts have all the structural features Q1 identifies; if the concrete pole's acts are not the composite subject's acts, the abstract pole bears an acting subject at one remove across the pole-relation: the directed crossing [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows obtains within T, S, and Φ. Either way the agent the doctrine's predicates are about instantiates the structural conditions rather than escaping them.

**Q2.** *What does God choose in willing the best, if the best leaves nothing else open to will?* For a willing to be a choice rather than a computation, the willing must be undetermined by the inputs that supply its content: the ranking over options must permit divergence, the selection rule must not return a single output, or the agent must have a remainder to contribute that goes beyond what the ranking and the option set already fix. The classical doctrine fixes all three. The ranking is the divine nature, identified with the good (Aquinas, *ST* I.19.1; Augustine, *De Trinitate* VIII). The option set is the modal landscape, fixed independently of the willing ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1); [§2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-3)). The selection rule is *wills what is best*, formalized in Leibniz's principle that God selects the *best of all possible worlds* (*Théodicée* 1710). The structural concern is what this preserves of *choice*. A selection determined by a fixed ranking over a fixed option set with a deterministic selection rule is the output of a function, not the act of an agent: the verbs *chooses* and *computes* become interchangeable without remainder. Spinoza recognizes that the doctrine, taken in its strongest form, collapses Leibnizian optimism into necessitarianism, the view that nothing could have been otherwise and whatever is the case is so necessarily (*Ethics* I, prop. 33), and the contemporary literature has not closed the line: Adams [-@adams1972], Rowe [-@rowe2004], and Kraay [-@kraay2010] develop the no-best-world variant, in which the selection rule has no determinate output to track, the theological form of *Buridan's ass*: a rational will offered options among which its own rule fixes no unique winner, and so unable to select without selecting arbitrarily; Aquinas himself concedes the possibility (*ST* I.25.6, ad 1). The compatibilist reply (divine freedom is action from one's own nature without external constraint) preserves the term *free* by removing what the term tracks. A thermostat acts from its own nature without external constraint; the compatibilist reading factors out of *free* any sense that distinguishes choosing from executing. Hartshorne proposes an aesthetic-creativity alternative to the Leibnizian best-world framework: God necessarily exemplifies the highest aesthetic order (abstract pole), but the specific content of the best is not pre-fixed: it is the creative synthesis of what creaturely agents have contributed, so that the concrete pole's willing is always the best responsive integration of the world's actual creative advance rather than a selection from a pre-specified menu (*Man's Vision of God*, -@hartshorne1941; *Creative Synthesis and Philosophic Method*, -@hartshorne1970). The concern for the aesthetic-creativity alternative is whether the concrete pole's responsive best-making constitutes a live selection among alternatives or whether the abstract pole's necessary exemplification of the highest aesthetic order determines the concrete pole's response given any world-state, restoring the function-output structure Q2's analysis finds objectionable.

A Frankfurt-style reply might seem to blunt Q1 and Q2 together: if genuine agency does not require live alternate possibilities at all (§E.1.4 develops the point for creaturely freedom via Frankfurt cases [@frankfurt1969]), then the mere absence of an unactualized alternative should not by itself disqualify the will's act from counting as a choice. The reply does not reach this case, because it trades on a resource *actus purus* does not supply. Frankfurt cases hold the actual sequence fixed: a reasons-responsive process runs from an antecedent state to the act, and it is that process, not the presence of a live alternative, that does the work of grounding responsibility; the counterfactual intervener is idle precisely because the actual mechanism already suffices. Pure act removes the mechanism along with the alternative: there is no antecedent state, no transition from could-be-willing to is-willing, for any actual-sequence theory to locate a process in, since willing and being are numerically one eternal act rather than the terminus of an unfolding history. The objection this section presses is accordingly the stronger of the two available forms it could take. It is not that God lacks alternatives the willing could have gone another way among; it is that God lacks the actual sequence that any theory of freedom, alternate-possibilities or actual-sequence alike, requires an act to issue from.

**Q3.** *From where does an act reach one target rather than another, if the agent is nowhere in particular?* For an act to be directed at a target (for an effect to land on this object rather than that one) there must be a real spatial relation between the agent and the target. The classical reply is that God is omnipresent: present everywhere alike, requiring no specific position to act from. [§6.8.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-1) presses the structural concern with that reply at the level of presence; the present concern is closer in. Action identical at every point appears to lack directional structure. The act either has a directional structure, in which case some position from which the direction is reckoned seems required, or it does not, in which case it is hard to see how the act takes hold on one target rather than another. Inman [-@inman2017] and Hudson [-@hudson2009] develop the most careful contemporary attempts to preserve directionality without position; the present analysis registers them as the strongest moves available and notes that each preserves directedness by relocating the directional resource to a primitive of divine intention. The relocation keeps the verb and shifts the locus of the difficulty.

**Q4.** *Through what does the influence travel, if there is no medium for it to cross?* For the influence to reach its target, there must be a medium that carries it forward. The classical God, defined as immaterial, is defined as having no medium through which to act. The reply that God acts directly, without intermediate causes, addresses the requirement by relocating it. A direct cause still has a structural relation to its effect. McCann [-@mccann2012] presses the contrary view: divine causation is genuinely primitive, not a special case of ordinary causation but a category of its own. Pruss develops the parallel analytic-Catholic treatment in *Actuality, Possibility, and Worlds* [-@pruss2011]: primitive divine causation is read as the limit case of immediate causation more generally, with the cause-effect relation retained at the level of metaphysical dependence rather than at the level of any intermediating medium. The reply is available and serious. The concern here is what makes primitive divine causation a case of *causation* rather than a homonym. Whatever makes the primitive case a case of the genus depends on retaining enough of the structural relation between cause and effect for the term to apply, and the structural relation is precisely what the doctrine of immateriality has placed beyond God. The reply preserves the term by leaving its application to a primitive whose work the analysis cannot examine.

**Q5.** *What difference does an unchanging, unmoved cause pass on, if it has none of its own to give?* Causation, on the analyses [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) develops, is the transmission of difference forward through a medium: the cause undergoes a state, and the effect undergoes the corresponding consequent state. A cause that does not itself change has no differential structure to distinguish causing from not-causing; a mover that does not itself move has no motion of its own to transmit. The doctrine meets this difficulty at both ends of its history. At its Aristotelian origin, the Prime Mover (*Metaphysics* XII) is unmoved and yet causes the motion of the celestial spheres, drawing them as the object of desire and final cause; Aquinas absorbs the structure into the First Way (*ST* I.2.3), where the regress of changers-themselves-changed terminates in a first cause that moves without being moved, and the picture has supplied Western theism with its account of divine causation ever since. The desire-as-final-cause solution preserves the asymmetry by relocating the dynamism to the moved party (the spheres move themselves toward the Prime Mover), but appears to do so at the cost of leaving it unclear, in any operative sense, what the first mover *does*: the aspirational object is not the aspiration's cause but its target.

At the contemporary end the same pressure recurs as the bare requirement that a cause bear differential change. Wolterstorff [-@wolterstorff1975] gives the alternative its canonical form: God is everlasting, not timeless; Hasker [-@hasker1989] and Mullins [-@mullins2016] extend the move into open theism. The repair responds to the concern (a God who undergoes states has differences to transmit), but at the cost that a being who exists through time instantiates T, and a being instantiating T at the moment of acting is one whose acting is an event in time, with the structural commitments that follow. The two replies mark the doctrine splitting along a single structural incompatibility: *actus purus* keeps the changelessness and forfeits the difference there is to transmit, while divine everlastingness keeps the transmissible difference and forfeits the changelessness, relocating God within the conditions the classical doctrine had defined God against. Generalized from the spheres to a creator of the universe, an answerer of prayer, a worker of miracles, the difficulty is the same at both ends: an unchanged source has no difference of its own to pass forward, and a source that has acquired difference enough to pass forward is no longer unchanged.

**Q6.** *What does an eternal act do at any moment, if it occurs at no moment at all?* The atemporalist cascade attempts to preserve divine action without taking on temporal structure. Boethius (*Consolation* V.6) describes eternity as the simultaneous and complete possession of unbounded life. Stump and Kretzmann [-@stumpKretzmann1981] refine this into ET-simultaneity. Leftow [-@leftow1991; -@leftow2012] sharpens the metaphysics; Rogers [-@rogers2000] and Helm [-@helm2010] defend the framework. The concern here is whether ET-simultaneity preserves the act in a sense stronger than the term. The single eternal act does not occur at 3:14 PM on a Tuesday; it stands eternally alongside that moment without the moment's *at* being operative for the eternal agent. Any particular act of intervention has a *when*, and the *when* appears to be part of what the act is. ET-simultaneity preserves causal contact by setting aside the temporal relation that, on the structural analysis, is constitutive of an act's being the act it is. The believer who reports a moment of grace at a specific moment is reporting something whose specificity ET-simultaneity has factored out for the divine pole.

**Q7.** *What does an act author in the realm of the possible, if the possible already holds across every world?* The deepest version of the doctrine extends sovereignty to the modal space itself: God authors what is possible, not merely what is actual. To author the possible, however, is to bring about a state in which what was not possible becomes possible: a transition between modal states. Transitions require T. Modal invariance (§[§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)–2.1.5) sets out the structural difficulty: modal status does not vary across worlds. Leibniz (*Théodicée* 1710) tries to thread this by having God *select* among possibles rather than author them: the best of all possible worlds is chosen, not made. The selection still appears to require sovereignty exercised within a modal structure God did not generate. Leftow [-@leftow2012] develops the most ambitious contemporary attempt to ground modality in God; [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q6 and [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1), Q5 engage it from the necessity and power sides; the present point is that the modal structure appears to function as a condition on God's action rather than as a product of it. The pressure runs in the opposite direction as well. If God is necessarily creator (if creating belongs to God essentially rather than accidentally) then in every world where God exists, God creates; if God exists necessarily, creation is necessary. The Thomist escape distinguishes God's act-considered-in-itself (necessary) from the act's *terminus ad extra* (its term in the external created order, contingent), but on strict simplicity the distinction has no real ground in God: God's act is identical with God's being. Mullins [-@mullins2013; -@mullins2016] and Tomaszewski [-@tomaszewski2019] press this from inside the literature. Either creator-status is essential and creation is necessary, in which case the act loses the modal contrast agency requires; or creator-status is contingent and the doctrine has surrendered the necessity of God's being-creator, on which providence and revelation were supposed to rest. The modal result carries the necessity of any essential predicate to whatever the predicate really commits to. The classical doctrine has wanted necessary creator-status and free creation at once. But free creation requires live alternatives, and a being whose essential creator-status necessarily issues in a sustained order lacks the relevant contrast. If the sustaining relation is necessary, Nature is necessary with God; if it is contingent, creatorhood is not necessary in God. The doctrine must choose which claim to surrender. Pruss and Rasmussen's necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction addresses the dichotomy directly (*Necessary Existence*, -@prussRasmussen2018, ch. 5): God necessarily creates *some* world (creator-status is essential) but creates this particular contingent order among possible alternatives; the necessity attaches to the creator-status, not to the specific creation. The distinction preserves necessary creatorhood without necessitating any particular creation. The concern for the Pruss/Rasmussen reply at Q7 is that the selection among contingent termini is itself a modal-contrast act: what determines which contingent order is actualized? The selection requires the same live-alternative structure Q1 identifies as constitutive of any act, and exercises that structure through a substantial agent (Φ) across an ordering of alternatives (T, S). The necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction moves the chapter's agency concerns from the level of creator-status to the level of the selection, where they apply at full force.

The same pressure appears when creation is considered as a whole. A creator who brings about a reality genuinely other than itself must stand in a determinate relation to the created term. If created reality is external to God, creatorhood is a real outward relation — the directed relation the preceding questions analyze. If created reality is within God, creaturehood becomes a differentiation or modification in divine reality, pressing against simplicity and the Creator–creature distinction. If the relation is real only on the creature's side, the remaining question is what makes *God creates* a determinate explanatory claim rather than a formula for creaturely dependence. The point is not that creatures make an infinite God quantitatively larger; infinity is not a quantity. It is that a genuinely other creation cannot be related to a simple, atemporal God without either restoring a structural relation or withdrawing the positive content of creation.

*What is required.* Seven pressures yield, between them, the structural commitments of *act*. An act is the actualization of one determinate state rather than another, and an act with no transition has no difference for any petition or selection to address; the analogical reading of *intention* preserves the term while removing what the term tracks. The willing has to be undetermined by its inputs for the willing to be a choice rather than a computation; a fixed ranking over a fixed option set with a deterministic selection rule returns the act as the function's output, and the compatibilist redefinition of *free* preserves the term by removing what it tracks. Where the act lands depends on directional structure: action identical at every point lacks the asymmetric agent-target relation along which influence is reckoned, and relocating directedness to a primitive of intention keeps the verb while shifting the locus of the difficulty. The act runs through a structural relation between cause and effect: primitive immaterial causation either retains enough of that relation for the term to apply or leaves the application to a primitive whose work the analysis cannot examine. The cause has to bear differential change: a cause that does not itself change has no difference to transmit, and the open-theist response preserves responsiveness by relocating God within the very conditions the classical doctrine had defined God against. The act has its *when*: the believer's reported moment of grace has a specificity ET-simultaneity factors out on the divine pole, and the *when* the act has appears to be part of what the act is. It runs on a doer, a substantial being in whom doing originates and through which influence travels; the unmoved mover that does not itself change leaves unclear what operative role it plays in the moving the doctrine wants it to do, and a final cause is not the act it is the target of. And the modal structure the doctrine wants to author functions as a condition on action rather than as a product of it: sovereignty that authors the conditions any exercise presupposes is sovereignty exercising the conditions it authors, and the doctrine faces a structural dilemma: either creator-status is necessary and creation is necessary, or creator-status is contingent and the doctrine surrenders the necessity it claimed. T, S, and Φ are the structural conditions any act runs on.

*What is inverted.* Agency is what Nature does when its motion takes hold on its own further configuration. The English *agent* descends through Latin *agere*, *to do, to drive, to lead*. To act is to drive a transition forward, to lead from not-yet to now. The doing requires a doer, an interval to drive across, a doer-being the doing is *of*. [§8.9](expanding-the-field.html#sec-8-9) develops the positive account of agency as directed change of just this kind. The classical tradition reaches for an agent whose acts would be more comprehensive than any creature's, and names a relation whose structural conditions have been removed at every level. The doctrine has not preserved an agent whose reach exceeds the creaturely. It has performed the verb *act* onto a non-being with none of the structure acting consists in. Agency belongs to Nature. What *God acts* names, on the classical predicate read for the structure its own application requires, is a feature of Nature, driving its own further configuration forward, in the only structural relation the verb *act* names.

### 6.7.3 Interaction {#sec-6-7-3}

Interaction is the back-and-forth the scriptural story is full of: God speaks, Israel answers, God responds. But interaction needs both sides to be in it: sequence, give-and-take, two parties that persist through the exchange. The classical doctrines put every one of those features on the creature's side only, which leaves a one-sided relation that is not really *inter*-action at all.

*What the tradition holds.* The doctrine of divine interaction holds that God acts upon, communicates with, and is responsive to creatures while remaining timeless, immutable, impassible, and absolutely simple. Aquinas treats the relation as one of pure asymmetry: creatures are really related to God, but God is only logically related to creatures (*Summa Theologiae* I.13.7), so that what scripture calls God's "turning toward" or "drawing near" is a change in the creature rather than in God. Boethius secures the same point through eternity-as-*tota simul*: God's act of providence is a single, undivided gaze on the whole temporal order, and what appears to us as sequential response is, in him, one timeless willing (*Consolation* V.6). Anselm and the Reformed scholastics inherit this picture and harden it: the impassibility tradition (Augustine, *City of God* IX.5; Aquinas, *ST* I.20.1 ad 1; Turretin, *Institutes* III.xi) treats every scriptural ascription of grief, anger, or change-of-mind as anthropopathism: accommodation to creaturely modes of speech rather than literal predication.

Yet the same tradition affirms that Yahweh struck Egypt, spoke from Sinai, walked the wilderness with Israel, took flesh in the womb of Mary, ate fish on a shore, wrote in the dust, and at every point bilaterally engaged particular creatures at particular times. The doctrine, then, is double-handed: God interacts, but every feature of interaction (sequence, responsiveness, persistence of relata, affect, mind-change, physical contact) is denied of the divine side and located only in the creature.

*What cannot be answered.* The interrogation of interaction asks how a being defined by timelessness, immutability, impassibility, and simplicity can be the subject of any of the predicates that make scriptural narrative legible as encounter.

**Q1.** *How can a being whose life is one timeless, immutable act be the subject of sequence — acting, then being acted upon, then acting again?* The back-and-forth is constitutive of interaction, not incidental to it. Boethius's *tota simul* eternity collapses this sequence into a single timeless act. Stump and Kretzmann's ET-simultaneity [-@stumpKretzmann1981] attempts to recover bilateral structure within timelessness, but the recovery requires that distinct temporal beats register as distinct in God, which is what the doctrine of immutability was meant to deny: the objection Mullins develops at length in *The End of the Timeless God* [-@mullins2016]. Mullins [-@mullins2016], Wolterstorff [-@wolterstorff1975], and Hasker [-@hasker1989] argue that the scriptural picture (Moses pleading, God relenting, the conversation continuing) is unintelligible without temporal sequence in God himself. Tradition's reply preserves the doctrines by emptying the narrative of any feature that could make it interaction rather than monologue.

**Q2.** *How can a being that is acted upon by nothing be bilaterally responsive, as interaction requires?* The wilderness account is structured by call and answer: Israel cries, God responds; Israel rebels, God grieves; Moses intercedes, God turns. Impassibility [@weinandy2000; cf. @helm2010] denies that God is acted upon. Open theism [@pinnock1994; @boyd2001; @sanders1998] accepts the bilateral structure and surrenders the doctrine. The classical tradition retains the doctrine and reads the bilateral structure as unilateral accommodation, but accommodation is a mode of divine action, not of divine *inter*-action, and the *inter* is what the predicate names.

**Q3.** *How can interaction hold between relata that persist across time on both sides, when divine simplicity grants real relation only on the creature's side?* The forty-year engagement with Israel is not a series of unrelated acts but a continuous relation. Divine simplicity [@dolezal2017] holds that there are no real relations in God — every relation is in the creature side only. But a relation that is one-sided is not, in the ordinary sense, a relation; and an interaction whose relata persist only on one side is not interaction.

**Q4.** *How can an impassible being track engagement affectively, as the wilderness narratives mark it?* The wilderness narratives mark engagement by registers of divine feeling: grief at the calf (Exodus 32:14 NRSVUE), kindled anger at Kibroth-hattaavah (Numbers 11:33), the heavy-with-glory *kābēd* response at Korah (Numbers 16:42). Impassibility [@helm2010; @dolezal2017] reads each of these as anthropopathism; open theism [@pinnock1994; @sanders1998] reads them as literal divine affect. Tradition cannot have both the literal text and the doctrine: it must subtract one.

**Q5.** *How can an immutable being change his mind, as the texts repeatedly say God does?* *Nāḥam* (to repent, to relent, to grieve into a different course) is used of God at Exodus 32:14 (Moses talks Yahweh out of destroying Israel), Genesis 6:6 (Yahweh regrets making humanity), 1 Samuel 15:11 (Yahweh regrets making Saul king), and Jonah 3:10 (Yahweh relents from destroying Nineveh). Each is the verbal form whose literal sense is a turning. The impassibility tradition reads each as anthropopathism, but the texts are not merely emotive: they record a different downstream course of divine action contingent on a creature-side act. Either the divine course is genuinely contingent on the creature-side act (and immutability fails) or the contingency is illusory (and the text is false at its surface).

**Q6.** *How can an incorporeal being engage the physical world by contact, as interaction with it appears to require?* The doctrine of omnipotence [@mavrodes1963; @plantinga1967; @wierenga1989; @hoffmannRosenkrantz2002] holds that God can do anything logically possible. But interaction with the physical world appears to require physical contact: the burning bush burns, the pillar of fire heats, the Red Sea parts, the dust-written word is written *in dust*, the fish is broken and eaten. Drawing in particular requires a substrate, a hand or hand-analogue, and a temporal stroke. Can a non-physical being draw at all? The doctrine of incorporeality says no. The text says yes.
