Tradition's reply (that these are instrumental acts mediated through created causes) concedes that *God does not himself interact physically*; he occasions physical events from outside the physical, which is not the picture the texts present.

**Q7.** *How can petitionary prayer be efficacious — God's act depending on the petition — when immutability and timelessness forbid that dependence?* The tradition [@stump1979; @murrayMeyers1994; @davison2017] treats petitionary prayer as efficacious: God answers, sometimes by granting, sometimes by withholding, in a way that depends on the petition having been made. But efficacy requires that God's act be contingent on the creature's act, which immutability denies; and the contingency must be temporally located, which timelessness denies. The doctrine of efficacious prayer is functionally interactionist while the metaphysical doctrines forbid the interactionism that would underwrite it.

**Q8.** *How can the incarnation, the paradigm of interaction, be the act of a God who as God does not interact, the deepest form of the problem?* The two-natures doctrine [@hick1977; @morris1986; @crisp2007; @pawl2016; @pawl2019] holds that the Logos took on a complete human nature without ceasing to be God. But the human nature interacts — eats, sleeps, tires, weeps, dies — and the divine nature does not. Either the interactions of Jesus' human nature are interactions of God (in which case God interacts, and the doctrines of impassibility and immutability fail at the deepest possible level: at the very being of the Word) or they are not interactions of God (in which case the incarnation is a juxtaposition of two beings rather than a single subject, and Chalcedon fails). The tradition wants both: God interacts as the man Jesus *and* God does not interact as God. It is at the incarnation, more than at any other point, that the doctrinal structure and the narrative structure of interaction cease to be reconcilable.

*What is required.* Eight pressures, taken together, surface what *interact* depends on when the term is examined against the conditions of its application. The doctrines of timelessness, immutability, impassibility, and simplicity, taken together, leave no room for *inter* (for between, mutual, sequenced, contingent driving) on the divine side of the encounter. Each pressure names a feature constitutive of interaction (sequence, responsiveness, persistent relata, affective tracking, mind-change, physical contact, contingent efficacy, incarnational unity-of-subject) and at each point the tradition saves the doctrine by relocating the feature entirely to the creature. But interaction is precisely the predicate that requires the feature on *both* sides: one-sided sequence is not sequence, one-sided responsiveness is not responsiveness, one-sided contact is not contact. This is the precise respect in which interaction differs from the asymmetric relations the tradition is content to grant God. A ground can stand wholly outside what it grounds (Aquinas's pure asymmetry, the creature really related and God only logically related, is built for exactly that) but interaction is the one relation that cannot be run from outside: to drive *between* two relata is to stand among them, within the conditions across which the driving passes. The very asymmetry that leaves grounding intact is what disqualifies interaction: a subject withheld from T, S, and Φ may be called the ground of what bears them, but cannot be one of the relata between which the action runs. Each of the eight features runs on the same structural conditions. Sequence and mind-change require a transition between before and after (T); persistent relata and physical contact require an interval across which the parties stand distinct and meet (S); responsiveness, affective tracking, contingent efficacy, and incarnational unity-of-subject require a substantial bearer in whom the engagement registers and is sustained (Φ). What the doctrine relocates to the creature is not an incidental residue but the whole modal structure interaction runs on. The Modal Convergence Theorem and the Subsistence definition (developed in Chapter 8) supply the technical equipment for relocating that structure as a modal-structural property Nature bears in property mode, rather than as the action of a being upon Nature. What *interaction* names, when its referent is examined, is the bilateral driving Nature carries on between its own constituents (process engaging process, system responding to system, history bearing the marks of mutual constraint all the way down) within the conditions T, S, and Φ supply. The addressed, affective character the narratives carry (grief, anger, relenting, encounter rather than mere causal traffic) is not subtracted in the relocation but routed to where it is derived rather than presupposed: the first-person register of a self-modeling life within Nature (Chapter 7), under which subject-on-subject maintenance reads as benevolence and address ([§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1)). The same cluster the chapter has met at every attribute reappears: the feature the doctrine cannot seat in God is the feature Nature bears at every level.

One rival to this relocation must be met before the inversion is secured, because it grants the eight pressures and halts one step short of the conclusion. Divine temporalism, in both its bare and its open-theist forms [@wolterstorff1975; @hasker1989; @mullins2016; @pinnock1994; @sanders1998; @boyd2001], concedes that the timeless, immutable, impassible God cannot bear the *inter* of interaction and repairs the doctrine not by relocating interaction away from God but by putting God in time: a personal agent with genuine before-and-after in the divine life itself, who responds, relents, and is really related to what creatures do. The repair reaches this section's destructive result and stops at its constructive one, and that step is where the disagreement turns. To restore interaction the temporalist must grant that the interacting subject bears succession in its own being: before and after in God, not merely in the creature. But succession borne by the agent is T borne by the agent; the responsiveness so recovered still requires the interval across which the parties stand and meet (S) and the substantial bearer in whom the engagement registers and is sustained (Φ). The temporalist has not found an interacting subject outside the conditions; he has moved the subject inside them and kept the name. And a subject that takes on T, S, and Φ in order to interact is, by [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), no longer a candidate for the modal status the doctrine reserved for God: necessity is the modal status of the modal structure T∧S∧Φ and does not transfer to a being that bears the modal structure's conditions (modal invariance, §[§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)–2.1.5; the transfer result, [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)). Such a subject is a denizen of the conditions Nature supplies, however exalted, not the ground beyond them, and the ground it was meant to be is necessary, hence uncreated, so there is no act of creating or altering it left for any agent, temporal or timeless, to perform. Re-timing is therefore not an alternative to the relocation; it is the relocation, carried halfway and halted at the word *God*. What survives the repair is not a rival to the inversion but a residual question internal to it (whether the bearer of T, S, and Φ is a person or Nature) and that question is taken up where personhood and address are derived rather than presupposed (Chapter 7), not by stationing a personal agent at the threshold. The single remaining foothold, that divine "metaphysical time" is mere topological succession rather than the metric time Nature instantiates [@padgett1992; cf. Swinburne on topological and metric time], collapses into the same fork: any succession thick enough to constitute the divine person's responding *after* the creature acts is T enough to count among the frame's conditions, and any "time" too thin to be that is too thin to host the genuine response the repair was introduced to secure.

*What is inverted.* Interaction belongs to Nature. The Latin *interagere* is built from *inter* (between) and *agere* (to drive, to act, to do); the predicate names a mutual driving, a between-ness that requires both sides to bear the action. The Greek ἐνεργέω (*energeō*), to work upon, to be active in, preserves the same shape: ἐν (in) + ἔργον (work), an in-working that lodges in the medium it touches. Hebrew has no single verb for *interact*; the relational structure is carried by *‘āsāh* (to do, to make) governed by *‘im* (with), *‘āsāh ‘im*, God *does-with* his people. In each tradition the predicate is bilateral at its root: between-driving, in-working, with-doing, and the bilaterality requires Nature: two relata sharing T, S, and Φ in the structural sense that lets the action run both ways. The doctrinal package built around timelessness, immutability, impassibility, and simplicity strips precisely the bilaterality the etymology preserves: what remains is unilateral action from a side that cannot itself be moved or moved-toward: action without between, work without in-, doing without with-. Nature bears interaction (bilaterally, sequentially, contactfully, mind-changeably) at every level at which the doctrines forbid God to bear it. The structural inversion is this: the predicated subject cannot be moved or moved-toward, and so cannot bear the very between-driving its predicate requires: the being whose interactivity the tradition was meant to underwrite turns out, on its own doctrinal terms, to be the one being in the system that cannot interact. What *God interacts* names, once the classical predicate is examined for what its application takes, is the bilateral driving Nature carries on within itself, between constituents that share its conditions. The doctrine of divine interaction, however formulated, locates that mutual driving in a subject beyond Nature rather than in Nature itself.

### 6.7.4 Sovereignty {#sec-6-7-4}

Sovereignty is God's rule over everything: providence, election, the eternal decree. To govern a domain you have to have a grip on it: to know it and to act on it. So sovereignty inherits all the difficulties the knowledge and power sections already raise, now at the level where God is said to rule. The eternal decree and its unfolding in history add a further strain on a God who is supposed never to change.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine sovereignty assembles several reinforcing claims. God is king (Psalm 47, 93, 96; Isaiah 6; Revelation 4–5 NRSVUE), with kingship the central political-theological metaphor for divine authority. God exercises providence, ordering all things to their proper end (Aquinas, *ST* I.22), and governance, the execution of providence in time (*ST* I.103). God elects: God has chosen some creatures for salvation, with the choice grounded in divine sovereign will rather than in any feature of the creatures (Augustine, *De Praedestinatione Sanctorum*; Aquinas, *ST* I.23; Calvin, *Institutes* III.21–24). Reformed scholasticism develops the architecture of decree theology: a single eternal decree determines every event in creation [Turretin 1679–85; Owen 1647; @helm1993; @feinberg2001]. On the most developed contemporary refinement, divine sovereignty grounds the modal structure itself: not merely what is actual but what is possible [@leftow2012]. Each move tries to keep divine governance from being one regional jurisdiction among others. At its most ambitious, the doctrine reaches for a king whose decree is meticulous, eternal, and comprehensive, whose election constitutes those it falls upon, and whose reach extends to the modal structure within which any decree is intelligible at all.

*What cannot be answered.* Six questions ask of divine sovereignty what the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning can pursue, cannot answer. What drives them is local to sovereignty and cumulative across the chapter. Governance, on the analysis given, is the holding of a domain under determinative authority such that what occurs within the domain occurs by the authority's decree. The holding requires a jurisdictional being whose grip on the domain is structural, and grip is what [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) (Knowledge) and [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) (Power) have already pressed. If the conditions for divine knowing and divine causing have been hard to reconcile with the doctrine of divine simplicity-and-atemporality at every step, the conditions for divine governing inherit those difficulties at the level where governance is exercised through knowing and causing. The six pressures run one at the level of jurisdictional grip, five at the level of the conditions sovereignty-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *How does a being keep its hold on a world it is no part of?* For a jurisdiction to extend, the being who holds the jurisdiction must stand in some real relation to what falls under it: must be able to know the domain, hold it within a determinative frame, and effect what the jurisdiction decrees. Helm [-@helm1993], Feinberg [-@feinberg2001], and Leftow [-@leftow2012] develop the most rigorous contemporary defenses of comprehensive divine governance. The concern here is that the difficulties run together: [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) raises whether the conditions of divine knowing are coherent with the doctrine of divine simplicity-and-atemporality; [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) raises the parallel question for divine causing. Sovereignty exercised through knowledge and power inherits both. The reply that divine governance is direct rather than mediated by knowledge and power is the reply McCann [-@mccann2012] develops as primitive divine causation; it preserves grip by leaving its mode unanalyzed. The present analysis registers the move and presses the cost: a primitive grip whose conditions cannot be examined is not a more thorough grip than the structural one but a different relation that has inherited the term.

**Q2.** *What does history add to a decree already complete in eternity?* Reformed scholasticism holds that the divine decree is one eternal act in which God determines every event that will ever occur (Turretin 1679–85; Owen 1647). The execution of the decree unfolds in time. The concern here is the relation between the two. If decree and execution are one act, the temporal unfolding adds nothing the decree did not already contain, and the temporal world is a representation of an eternally complete decision. If decree and execution are distinct, divine immutability is pressured: God's decreeing is eternally complete, but God's executing is temporally extended. Stump and Kretzmann's [-@stumpKretzmann1981] ET-simultaneity addresses the difficulty by treating decree-as-eternal and execution-as-temporal as eternally simultaneous. The structural concern with the relation is pressed in other contexts at [§6.3.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-2), Q2 and [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2), Q2. The point this section adds is that decree-and-execution is the doctrine's signature pairing, and the pairing is intelligible only if both terms have determinate content. Eternalizing the decree preserves immutability; temporalizing the execution preserves history; the doctrine has wanted to do both at once, and these are two commitments joined only by the term *one act*.

**Q3.** *How does God choose some over others, with no one yet there to be chosen?* The doctrine of election holds that God has chosen some creatures for salvation, with the choice grounded in God's sovereign will rather than in any feature of the creatures (*De Praedestinatione*; *Institutes* III.21). For election to discriminate, the elector must stand in a position from which the elected can be picked out and the unelected passed over. The classical reply is that God's election is not a temporal choosing-among but an eternal act in which the elect are constituted as such (Aquinas, *ST* I.23). The concern here is whether constitution-without-position is the form the doctrine of election asserts. If God's eternal decree constitutes who counts as elect, the elect are not picked out from a prior class but defined by the decree; the doctrine preserves the believer's sense of having been chosen by setting aside the *from-among* the choice ordinarily presupposes. Barth's (*CD* II.2) reframing of election as universal in Christ and Stump's [-@stump2018] narrative reading register the difficulty from inside the tradition; the modal reading agrees that the difficulty is a real one and locates it in the constitution-without-position move the classical position depends on. Stump's [*Atonement*, -@stump2018, ch. 6] narrative-relational reading of election offers a richer alternative: election is not primarily the selection of individuals for a soteriological status (a standing with respect to salvation) by an eternal decree, but the irreducibly particular character of God's second-personal relating to Israel-in-Jacob-and-his-descendants in a narrative whose particularity is what makes it election rather than general divine benevolence. On Stump's account, the *from-among* the classical doctrine needs is not secured by a positional distinguishing act but by the thisness of the relation: what it is in the relating, not in a prior act of positional picking-out. The concern for Stump's narrative election is whether the *thisness* of a second-personal relation has individuating content in the absence of spatial and temporal distinguishability: a narratively irreducible relation between God and Israel requires that the relata be distinguishable as the relata they are, and relational thisness at the narrative level trades on the same structural conditions of individuation the chapter has found constitutive of any relation at all.

**Q4.** *How does God decree what is possible, if decreeing already needs the possible in place?* The deepest version of the doctrine extends divine sovereignty beyond the actual world to the modal space within which actuality is selected. Leftow [-@leftow2012] develops the position that what is possible is grounded in divine activity: there are no possibilities prior to God for God to range over. The position is engaged from the necessity side at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q6, from the power side at [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1), Q5, and from the agency side at [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q7. The point sovereignty adds is that the deepest version of *governance* extends to the conditions any governance presupposes. To govern a domain is to exercise authority within structural conditions the domain provides. To govern the conditions themselves is to exercise authority over what makes any exercise intelligible. Modal invariance (§[§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4)–2.1.5) presses the same difficulty from the opposite direction: modal status is not a product of any agent's exercise. The modal account agrees that the deepest structural facts are not subject to anyone's decree. The doctrine that places them under decree, when its predicates are read in the structure that supports them, is reaching for the modal status of Nature and naming a sovereign beyond it. The same difficulty runs through the doctrine of necessary creator-status: if creating belongs essentially to God, then in every world in which God exists God creates; if God exists necessarily, creation is necessary. And creation, if coherent, can only be creation of an order instantiating T, S, and Φ (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance). The dichotomy is binary, not gradient. Whatever God could be said to create either has temporality, spatiality, and substantiality, or it has none. In the first case, the creature is Nature or part of it. In the second case, there is no duration over which the creature persists, no location at which it stands distinct from its creator, and no being that carries the property of having been created. The second branch does not describe a different kind of creature. It describes the absence of any feature by which a creature could be there to have been created. There is no third option. Sovereignty over a necessarily sustained domain is therefore not the elective decree the doctrine performs but the structural status of Nature itself. The modal-collapse concern is developed from the sides of power and agency at [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1), Q1 and [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q7; the same concern surfaces here as the pressure on sovereign election. Pruss and Rasmussen's necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction [*Necessary Existence*, -@prussRasmussen2018, ch. 5] carries to the sovereignty register: God necessarily creates *some* order (essential sovereign creator-status), but the content of the order is contingent on God's free selection among possible orders (the necessity attaches to the creator-status, not to the specific created order). On this reply, the dichotomy between necessary-creator-status-with-necessary-creation and contingent-creator-status-with-free-creation is dissolved. The concern in the sovereignty register is that the selection among contingent orders is itself a sovereign act: it requires a being positioned to select among alternatives (S), a transition through the selection (T), and a substantial sovereign who is the bearer of both the creator-status and the act of selection (Φ). The necessary-creating/contingent-order distinction preserves sovereign freedom at the level of what is created; the chapter's structural conditions of sovereign action apply at the level at which freedom is now located.

**Q5.** *How does a creature freely do what God decreed it would do?* The Augustinian-Calvinist tradition holds that God's eternal decree determines every event, including every creaturely free action. The Pelagian, Arminian, and Molinist traditions develop alternative positions on which creaturely freedom remains genuinely libertarian [Arminius 1608; Molina 1588; @flint1998]. Compatibilist positions [Edwards 1754; @helm1993] hold that determined actions can be free in a sense compatible with moral responsibility. Libertarian positions [@plantinga1974b; @flint1998] hold that genuine freedom requires alternative possibilities the decree must not foreclose. The concern here is parallel to [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2), Q9 (foreknowledge) and [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1), Q6 (concurrence) at a different level: [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) asks whether divine knowing fixes the future; [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) asks whether divine causing leaves room for creaturely doing; the present question asks whether divine *decreeing* can determine creaturely action without precluding it. Each of the three positions (compatibilism, libertarianism, Molinism) preserves one commitment at a price the doctrine had been holding the others against. None preserves the full classical bundle.

**Q6.** *What does a creature add, if God decrees the falling of every leaf?* Meticulous providence is the most thoroughgoing version of the doctrine: every event, down to the falling of every leaf, is decreed by God [Calvin, *Institutes* I.16; @helm1993]. The concern here is whether the doctrine leaves room for any genuinely creaturely contribution to what occurs. If every event is meticulously decreed, creaturely action is at best the executed expression of a decree creatures had no part in making. The classical reply is the concurrence-and-secondary-causation move [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1), Q6 engages: divine sovereignty operates *through* creaturely agency rather than around it. The concern here parallels the earlier ones: whether the through-not-around relation has determinate content on a non-analogical reading, or whether the relation is doing primitive work the doctrine asks of it. Pruss [-@pruss2013] and Furlong [-@furlong2019] develop contemporary attempts to give the relation more determinate content; the modal reading registers them as the most serious attempts and notes that each preserves the through-not-around relation by reintroducing structural conditions the doctrine of strong simplicity had removed. Hartshorne's process alternative presses from the other side: divine sovereignty is persuasive rather than coercive, the concrete pole genuinely responsive to the creaturely contributions meticulous providence cannot accommodate [*The Divine Relativity*, -@hartshorne1948], and the coherence of that responsive sovereignty is pressed against dipolar theism at [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) and [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q1.

*What is required.* Six pressures bring the structural commitments of *governs* into view. Governance has to grip its domain: sovereignty exercised through knowing and causing inherits the difficulties pressed in the two preceding sections, and a primitive grip whose mode cannot be examined is a different relation that has inherited the term. Decree and execution have to be a determinate pair; eternal-decree-with-temporal-execution wants both terms with full content, and the *one act* terminology holds them together verbally rather than structurally. Election has to discriminate from-among: the constitution-without-position move sets aside the choosing-among the doctrine of election asserts, and the believer's sense of having been chosen depends on a prior class from which the elect were picked. The modal frame functions as a condition on governance rather than as its product: the deepest structural facts are not subject to anyone's decree, and the creator-status dichotomy collapses any necessarily sustained domain to Nature or to no creature at all. Decree and creaturely freedom have to be compatible without flattening either, and each of compatibilism, libertarianism, and Molinism preserves one commitment of the bundle by surrendering another. Through-not-around concurrence has to be more than a verbal predicate; meticulous providence preserves the verb by relocating the through-relation to a primitive whose work the doctrine has not specified. What *governs* picks out when its referent is examined is the structural condition under which jurisdictional grip obtains: T, S, and Φ in their lawful invariance, which is the modal status of Nature itself.

*What is inverted.* Sovereignty is the modal status of Nature. The English *sovereign* descends through Old French *soverain* from the Latin *super*, *above*. To be sovereign is to stand above the domain governed: to hold it under one's authority by virtue of a position that is not itself a position within it. The classical doctrine extends this *above* to its limit: God is above creation in every dimension, with no creaturely standing for divine sovereignty to be located within. The modal reading agrees that what is sovereign over the domain is not a domain-located being. What is sovereign over what occurs within T, S, and Φ is the structure of T, S, and Φ themselves: the lawful invariance that holds across every moment, position, and instantiation. Nature reigns over what occurs within it, not as a domain-located ruler, but as what makes the occurring lawful occurrence in the first place. Sovereignty's facet is self-rule: not merely that T, S, and Φ hold invariantly, but that nothing stands above them to govern the holding. The structure is not law-abiding but lawmaking; it answers to no higher frame, because there is no frame above the frame. The doctrine of divine sovereignty, however the tradition has framed it, locates this lawful invariance in a sovereign beyond Nature rather than in Nature itself.

With sovereignty inverted, it is worth marking what has now happened across four of the attributes, because the convergence is not an accident of exposition. Necessity, immutability, sovereignty, and perfection have each, run to completion, landed on the same structural fact under a different description: necessity on the structure's reach across every world, immutability on its constancy across all time, sovereignty on its answering to no higher law, perfection on its lacking nothing. These are four angles on one feature, the modal standing of T, S, and Φ, not four separate perfections of a being. That four of the tradition's greatest divine attributes collapse into facets of a single structural fact is not a redundancy in the argument; it is the inversion thesis showing its hand: the classical engine multiplied names for what is structurally one feature, and distributed them across a being, precisely because the feature seen whole is the modal character of Nature rather than the property of any bearer.

## 6.8 Reach and Contact {#sec-6-8}

This cluster gathers the attributes by which God reaches and is reached: presence ([§6.8.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-1)), relatability ([§6.8.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-2)), describability ([§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3)), and revelation ([§6.8.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-4)) — being present to, standing in relation to, being truly described by, and disclosing itself to creatures.

Each is a contact-attribute, and each requires a two-way crossing: to be present is to occupy a standpoint relative to another, to be related and described is to be distinguished and carried in thought, and to reveal is to transmit across an interval. The reach the tradition assigns to God is the reach T, S, and Φ make possible, and it cuts in both directions, the severing the chapter runs throughout.

### 6.8.1 Presence {#sec-6-8-1}

Omnipresence is God's being wholly present everywhere at once, present to every place while occupying none. The two halves pull apart: "present at every point" quantifies over places, but "no spatial extension" denies there are any places for God to be at. A presence that cannot tell here from there is not a more intimate presence; it is the loss of the very contrast the word "present" depends on.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine omnipresence assembles three reinforcing claims. God is present everywhere by being everywhere intimately and substantially: *Deus est in omnibus rebus*, God is in all things, by power, by presence, and by essence (Aquinas, *ST* I.8.3). God is present *totus in toto et totus in qualibet parte*: wholly in the whole and wholly in every part (*ST* I.8.2; Augustine, *Confessions* I.3). On the most developed contemporary refinement, presence is an act in which God is operatively present at every point alike, with no point favored over any other [@wierenga1989; @hudson2009; @inman2017]. The doctrine preserves the believer's intuition that God is here and not absent at any *there* by extending the *here* without limit. It does so, on the doctrine fully stated, in a being defined as having no *here* of its own. Pressed to its limit, the position holds that divine presence is unrestricted precisely because the being has nowhere of its own from which any restriction could be a restriction *from*.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions expose what the doctrine of omnipresence, in the form structural reasoning takes up, cannot answer. The difficulty beneath the five is structural, the conjunction of two of the doctrine's strongest commitments: God is wholly present at every spatial point, and God has no spatial extension. *Wholly at every point* is a quantifier over points; *no spatial extension* is the negation of a manifold over which the quantifier could range. The doctrine wants the universal of presence and the negation of position at once. The five pressures run one at the level of the predicate, four at the level of the conditions presence-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *At what place is a placeless being present?* The classical doctrine treats omnipresence as the universal of position: God is at every point. Hudson [-@hudson2009] develops the contemporary defense by treating divine presence as *occupation* of every spatial region, with the divine being filling space without being divided by it. Inman [-@inman2017] argues for a *grounding* construal: God is present at a region by grounding what occurs there. Wierenga [-@wierenga1989] and Hoffmann and Rosenkrantz [-@hoffmannRosenkrantz2002] treat presence as a function of divine knowledge and power: God is wherever God knows and acts. The concern this section adds is that each construal trades positional content for something else: occupation without division, grounding without location, knowledge-and-power without where. The believer's *here* is positional. *Wholly at every point* is positional. Treating divine presence as non-positional preserves the universal at the cost of removing what the *at* in the universal was supposed to track. To say God is present-by-knowledge-and-power is to say something true about what knowledge and power require (as [§6.4.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-4-2) and [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) develop); on the doctrine taken in its strong form it is to substitute one predicate for another and claim the substitution is a clarification.

One test disposes of the non-positional construals together, and it does not assume what the defenders deny. Grant each its own terms: occupation without division [@hudson2009], grounding of what occurs at a region [@inman2017], presence-by-knowledge-and-power [@wierenga1989]. Each is still the claim that God is present *at this region rather than that one*: present at the burning bush in a way God is not present at the next shrub on Sinai, present at A in whatever way occupies or grounds or knows A and not identically at B. Strip that out and the construal no longer yields omnipresence but a single undifferentiated relation to everything at once, and the nearness and directedness the doctrine insists on (the fourth and third questions below) go with it. So the construal must individuate presence-at-A from presence-at-B. But to individuate A from B is to hold them apart as distinct positions standing in relational non-identity, and a manifold of positions held apart by relational non-identity is what S is ([§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7)). The defender's *at every region* is a quantifier, what it ranges over is a field of mutually distinct locations, and a field of mutually distinct locations is not an alternative to spatial structure but an instance of it. Occupation, grounding, and knowledge-and-power do not remove S from presence; they presuppose S as the manifold across which their *at* is indexed.

One construal does not trade position away, and so does not fall to the disposing test as stated: *ubiquitous entension* [@hudson2005; @hudson2009]. The entension theorist concedes location rather than substituting for it: God is *wholly* located at every region and at every subregion alike, an extended occupant present in its entirety at each part of what it occupies and divided by none. This is the contemporary cash-out of *totus in qualibet parte*, and it meets the disposing test head-on: it does not preserve the universal of presence by removing the *at*; it affirms the *at* at full strength and denies only that being wholly-located-at-each entails being partitioned. The test above assumes the defender purchases omnipresence by trading position for occupation-without-division, grounding, or knowledge; the entension theorist refuses the trade, so the construal must be met on its own ground. Grant entension everything it claims: an undivided whole wholly located at every region and subregion. It remains that the regions it is wholly located *at* are many, and many *as positions*: the occupant is wholly at A and wholly at B only if A is a position distinct from B and held apart from it, so that being-wholly-at-A is not already being-wholly-at-B. Entension does not dispense with the manifold of mutually distinct positions; it is *defined over* it: *wholly at each* is a quantifier whose field is a plurality of locations held apart by relational non-identity, and that plurality is what S is ([§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7)). The occupant is not thereby identified with the manifold (that would help itself to the section's thesis rather than earn it) but the entended occupant cannot so much as state its *wholly at each* without presupposing the manifold as the field across which the *each* is indexed. Entension locates the predicate *present* in S all the more firmly for affirming location instead of trading it away: it needs the differentiated field of positions in order to have anything for its undivided whole to be wholly at.

This is why the aspatial defender's most ambitious move (that God is present to creation in a manner needing no spatial structure at all) does not relocate presence to a higher register but dissolves it: a relation that cannot tell *here* from *there* is not a more intimate presence than the believer's, but the negation of the contrast the word *present* names. The differentiation of positions is not an imperfection in creaturely presence that divine presence improves on; it is the condition under which there is any *there* for God to be present *to*.

**Q2.** *How is a being with no extension wholly present at every point?* *Totus in toto et totus in qualibet parte* is the formula at its sharpest. To be wholly in the whole is one claim; to be wholly in every part of the whole is another; to be both at once, when the whole has parts and the parts are spatially distinct, is to be reduplicated at every part without thereby being divided. The classical reply is that divine non-extension makes the reduplication unproblematic: only an extended being could be divided by being placed in extended regions. The concern here is that *wholly at* presupposes spatial location for whatever is wholly at the place, since *wholly* contrasts with *partly* and the contrast is positional. A non-extended being is not wholly at any point in the contrastive sense the formula trades on. *Totus in qualibet parte* keeps the language of part-by-part presence and removes the structure that makes part-by-part presence different from no-part presence. The formula performs the doctrine's deepest work by deploying terms whose ordinary content has been suspended.

**Q3.** *In what direction does a being act, if it is no nearer one point than another?* For an action to be directed at a target (for a divine intervention to land on this object rather than that one, on this body rather than the body next to it) there must be a structural relation between the agent and the target along which the action runs. [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2) presses the question for agency; the present concern is closer in. If God is at every point identically, with no point preferred to any other, the divine standing-at-A-and-not-at-B that would distinguish acting on A from acting on B is unavailable. The reply that divine action is mediated by divine intention rather than by spatial direction is the same one [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2) examines: it preserves directedness by relocating it from a structural relation to a primitive of will. The concern this section adds is that omnipresence in its strong form removes the spatial asymmetry directionality requires, and the doctrine's preservation of directedness through divine willing imports a structure the doctrine had been preserving God from importing. The two commitments of the doctrine are in structural tension at the point of contact between presence and act.

**Q4.** *How is a being near to one place, if it is no farther from any other?* Scripture and devotional theology repeatedly emphasize divine nearness in particular places and moments: the burning bush (Exodus 3 NRSVUE), the tabernacle (Exodus 40), the holy of holies (1 Kings 8), the incarnation as the *tabernacling* of the Word (John 1:14), the indwelling of the Spirit in the believer (Romans 8). Each presupposes a contrast between *here in this place* and *not-here in some other*. The classical reply distinguishes ordinary presence (everywhere alike) from special presence (here-and-now in a way that elsewhere is not), with special presence understood as a heightened mode of divine action rather than as a positional difference. The reply preserves the devotional vocabulary by treating *nearness* analogically (Aquinas, *ST* I.8.3 ad 1; [@pruss2013]). The concern here is that the analogical reading preserves the term by removing the contrast the term tracks. Nearness is a positional contrast; the divine special presence at the burning bush is *not at* every other shrub on Sinai in the sense that mattered for Moses to remove his sandals at this one. Omnipresence-in-its-strong-form leaves no resource for reading the contrast structurally, and the analogical reading registers the cost.

**Q5.** *Can panentheism, panpsychism, or pantheism make God present without giving God a place?* The contemporary literature has pressed alternatives that retain the spatial intuition while modifying the doctrine. Panentheism [@clayton2004; @cooper2006; @pfeifer2016] holds that the world is in God without being identical with God, preserving immanence by giving God a quasi-spatial relation to creation. Panpsychism in its theistic forms [@goff2017; @mathews2003] treats consciousness as ubiquitous in nature, with divine consciousness as the unifying fact about the manifold. Pantheism (Spinoza, *Ethics* I; [@levine1994; @buckareffNagasawa2016]) identifies God with the world. Each move concedes some classical commitment to preserve another. The present analysis agrees that the doctrine of strict transcendence-with-omnipresence is unstable, and treats the contemporary alternatives as registering the instability rather than resolving it. What each alternative reaches for, in different directions, is a way of relocating the *here* of divine presence into the structure that makes *here* a coherent predicate at all. The relocation, taken to its limit, is the analysis the present chapter offers: presence is what S is; Nature is the being the doctrine has been reaching for.

*What is required.* The five pressures together mark out what *present* actually depends on. The *at* of presence has positional content, and substituting occupation, grounding, or knowledge-and-power for location clarifies what the doctrine commits to while trading what the *at* was holding for something else. The contrast between *wholly at* and *partly at* is positional in the only sense that lets *totus in qualibet parte* mean part-by-part presence rather than no-part presence, which requires an extended spatial manifold for the contrast to obtain across. Directed action presupposes spatial asymmetry: a being identically at every point lacks the standing-at-A-and-not-at-B that distinguishes acting on A from acting on B, and the move that relocates directedness to a primitive of will already imports the structure the doctrine had been preserving God from importing. Nearness is a contrast as well: special presence at the burning bush is *not at* every other shrub on Sinai in the sense that mattered for Moses to remove his sandals, and the analogical reading registers what removing the contrast costs. The believer's *here* is positional, and presence-everywhere is the universal of position rather than its negation. The contemporary pan- alternatives have been registering the destination from different directions: each reaches for the same structural relocation of the predicate into the manifold that makes *here* a coherent term at all. S is what each of these conditions requires; the predicate the tradition has been performing on God is the modal status of S itself.

*What is inverted.* Presence is the structural status of S itself. The English *present* renders the Latin *prae-esse*: to be *before* in the sense of *in front of*, to be at a place where one can be addressed and met. The etymology only illustrates a point the five pressures established without it: the content of *present* does not survive having position removed. What *omnipresent* names, when the predicate is read against the structure that supports it, is the universal of S: the spatial manifold that is at every point of itself, by being the condition of any *at* whatsoever. Nature is *totus in qualibet parte* in the only sense the formula can be made to bear: every part of S is a part of the same S, with the same medium present at each as the condition of the part's being a part. Space is what is everywhere by being at every point of itself: the universal of position the tradition has been performing onto a being defined as having no *here* of its own. This is an inversion of the predicate, not a pantheist identification: the claim is that *omnipresent*, read for what it requires, names S, not that God is the spatial world; [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2) takes up the *deus sive natura* identification on its own terms.

### 6.8.2 Relatability {#sec-6-8-2}

Religion lives on a God who can be related to: one who loves, hears prayer, and draws near. The classical safeguard is the "mixed relation": creatures are really related to God, but God is related to creatures only in our way of speaking, with nothing added on the divine side. The trouble is that a relation real on only one end is not, in the ordinary sense, a relation, and the believer's "God loves me" reports exactly the two-sided structure the doctrine removes.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine relation assembles several reinforcing claims. God loves creation (1 John 4; Romans 8 NRSVUE); God is present to the believer (Psalm 139; Matthew 28:20); God hears prayer (Psalm 65; Matthew 7); God grieves and rejoices over creaturely action (Genesis 6; Luke 15). At the same time, God is immutable (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17), impassible ([§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4); Aquinas, *ST* I.9), aseitous ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q4; *ST* I.4), and simple (*ST* I.3): lacking parts, dependencies, or any feature whose obtaining requires anything outside God. Aquinas's resolution: the relations between God and creatures are not mutual. The creature has a *real* relation to God, grounded in the creature's actual ontological dependence; God has only a *relation of reason* to the creature, a relation that obtains only from the creature's side and adds nothing to the divine being [*ST* I.13.7; cf. *ST* I.28; for contemporary defenses, @stump2003; @dolezal2017]. On the most developed contemporary refinements, divine simplicity entails that God's loving the creature, knowing the creature, and creating the creature are all identical with God's being and add nothing relational to it [@pruss2008; @bergmannBrower2006; @dolezal2011]. Open theism, process theology, and panentheism take the reverse turn and grant God real relations at the cost of immutability and aseity [@hartshorne1948; @wolterstorff1975; @hasker1989; @pinnock1994; @mullins2016]. Each move tries to keep the believer's experienced relation to God from collapsing. Pressed to its limit, the position holds a relation in which the creature's real dependence on God is meant to preserve the believer's experiential reports while the divine end remains untouched by what the creature is or does.

*What cannot be answered.* Six questions ask of the relational predicates what the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning can examine, cannot answer. What presses here is structural — local to the relational predicates and explicit in the tradition's own concession. Two things stand in a relation when something obtains *between* them: the cup is on the table; the child loves the parent; the planet orbits the star. In each case the relation has two relata and a structural connection that holds them in the configuration named, and to be related is to be jointly determined by the connection: a change at one end registers, in the appropriate way, at the other. The classical tradition reaches for a relation between God and creation that exceeds any creaturely relation in depth and intimacy, and reaches, simultaneously, for a doctrine of divine immutability and aseity on which the deeper end of that relation contributes nothing to the divine being. The two reaches pull against each other, and the doctrine of *mixed relation* (Aquinas, *ST* I.13.7) is one of the most explicit concessions in the history of metaphysics: the classical tradition resolving the tension by sacrificing one of the two reaches. On the analyses [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) develops, a relation is a structural connection between relata that share the conditions of relation: minimally, the conditions for one relatum's state to make a difference at the other. The classical God is defined as standing in no condition the creature shares. The six pressures run two at the level of the relational predicates themselves, four at the level of the conditions relation-talk runs on.

**Q1.** *Can a relation of reason do the structural work?* Aquinas's *mixed relation* (*ST* I.13.7) is the central resource: the creature is really related to God, but God is related to the creature only by *relation of reason*, a relation that obtains in our concepts and predicates rather than in the divine being. Stump [-@stump2003], Dolezal [-@dolezal2017], and Bergmann and Brower [-@bergmannBrower2006] defend the doctrine carefully. The concern here is what the relation of reason is positioned to do. The believer who reports being loved by God is not reporting a relation that holds only in the believer's concepts of God; the believer is reporting a relation in which God is the lover and the believer the beloved, with the loving running from God to the believer. The doctrine of mixed relation preserves divine immutability by relocating the divine end of the relation from the divine being to the creature's concepts of the divine being. What this preserves is the term *love*; what it surrenders is the structure on which the believer's report depends: the running-from. The Thomistic doctrine is honest about the cost in a way the contemporary refinements often are not: Aquinas does not pretend the doctrine leaves the believer's experiential reports unchanged. The present analysis registers the candor and presses the cost.

**Q2.** *Does God love the world, and can the unaffected love?* The believer's confession that God loves the world (1 John 4:8) is among the most central claims of the tradition, and the relational reports that surround it (of being loved, heard, attended to, grieved over, rejoiced over) are reports of an affecting relation: God's state is held to be partly determined by the believer's state. For loving to be the relation the confession reports, the lover must respond to the beloved: the loving must take its character, in some structural sense, from what the beloved is and what the beloved does. Two classical commitments foreclose this together. On love, the reply is that God's love is wholly active rather than responsive; it bestows rather than receives; it is identical with God's being and is therefore eternal, immutable, and unaffected by what the beloved does (Aquinas, *ST* I.20), the position Nygren [-@nygren1932] gives its sharpest classical form in the *agape*-vs-*eros* contrast. On affection, impassibility holds that God cannot be acted upon by anything outside God ([§6.3.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-4); *ST* I.9), and the *real-but-not-mutual* doctrine has God affect the creature without the creature affecting God (Lewis [-@lewis1940]; Stump [-@stump2003; -@stump2010]; Helm [-@helm2010]). The concern is whether love-without-response, or asymmetric affection, is the relation the believer's reports name. A love that does not respond to the beloved is not, in the structural sense, a relation between two relata; it is a one-sided pouring whose target's state makes no difference to the pouring. An affecting relation that runs from one relatum to the other but not back is, in the structural sense, half of a relation: the half on the divine pole is what the doctrine preserves, and the half on the creature's side is what the believer's reports require but the doctrine does not give. The doctrine preserves divine immutability by relocating the responsive structure from God to creation; the believer who reports having been heard in a moment of distress is reporting a responsive structure factored out at the divine pole. The mystical literature (Eckhart, *Sermons*; Teresa, *Interior Castle*) is full of reports the present analysis is not positioned to dismiss; the question is what the reports presuppose about the structural conditions of encounter. Stump [-@stump2010; -@stump2018] and Wolterstorff [-@wolterstorff2015] develop the most serious attempts to preserve the responsive structure within the classical frame, and each does so by reintroducing structural conditions divine immutability had removed. The dipolar account is the principled terminus of those attempts. Hartshorne's *The Divine Relativity* [-@hartshorne1948] proposes that divine love is genuinely bipolar: the abstract pole's love is the invariant, bestowing, formal commitment to the creature's good and is strictly impassible, the creature's state making no difference to it; the concrete pole's love is constitutively responsive and fully receptive, growing with the beloved's joys and sufferings. The two sides of love (bestowing and responsive) and the two sides of affection (impassible and receptive) are assigned to two poles of a single subject, supplying the bidirectionality the reports require while the abstract pole keeps the aseity the classical doctrine demands. The concern here is the one [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) presses: the abstract pole and the concrete pole are one subject only through the relation that unites them, and [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) shows that relation is a directed crossing obtaining within T, S, and Φ. The unity of the loving agent is purchased by installing the structural conditions between its poles, and the half-relation the classical doctrine was accused of offering reappears as the abstract-pole half of the dipolar composite's own pole-relation.

**Q3.** *Where do the relata meet?* Two relata stand in a structural connection only if they share enough conditions for the connection to obtain. The cup and the table share spatial position; the child and the parent share temporal extension and embodied presence; the planet and the star share the gravitational structure of the solar system. The classical God shares none of T, S, or Φ with the creature. The relation between God and creature must therefore obtain across a difference at every structural level. The classical reply is that divine relation is *sui generis*: a relation of a kind no creaturely relation matches, holding between God and creature in a way no creaturely framework can capture (Pseudo-Dionysius, *Mystical Theology*; Aquinas, *ST* I.13). The apophatic non-relation strategy originates with Plotinus: in *Enneads* VI.9 the One is related to nothing and to no one, since relation presupposes a dyad and the One precedes all dyadic structure; Pseudo-Dionysius transmits the Plotinian strategy to Aquinas via the Neoplatonic inheritance. [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3), Q5 and [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2), Q1 trace the apophatic ancestry more fully. The reply is honest. The concern here is what makes the *sui generis* relation a relation in the structural sense the relational predicates trade on. Whatever connects God and creature, on the doctrine fully stated, lacks the shared conditions that make creaturely relations relations. The term *relation* is doing work the doctrine has not specified.

**Q4.** *Can the believer be heard?* Petitionary prayer presupposes that the believer's request reaches God and that God responds. For the request to reach God, there must be a structural channel (a configuration of T, S, and Φ) along which the request travels. For God to respond, there must be a difference between God's not-yet-having-responded and God's having-responded; that difference is a transition; transitions require T. The classical reply is that God's response is eternally complete in a single act, and what unfolds in time is the temporal expression of that eternal act [Aquinas, *ST* I.23; @stumpKretzmann1981]. [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q6 presses the concern with the relation between an eternal act and a particular temporal *when*; the present concern is closer in. The believer in distress at 3:14 PM on a Tuesday is asking for a difference between the world before 3:14 and the world after; ET-simultaneity preserves the divine end of the answering by setting aside the temporal asymmetry that, on the structural analysis, is constitutive of an act's being a response to anything in particular.

**Q5.** *Can the Trinity be a relational solution?* The doctrine of the Trinity gives the classical tradition a resource: God is internally relational (the Father loves the Son in the Spirit) without depending on anything outside God. Trinitarianism preserves divine relationality without compromising aseity [Augustine, *De Trinitate*; Boethius, *De Trinitate*; Aquinas, *ST* I.27–43; for the contemporary social-vs-Latin debate, @plantinga1989; @swinburne1994; @cross2002]. The concern here is what the divine processions are, on the doctrine fully stated. If the relations within God are real relations (each Person's being depending on the relations to the others) the Persons are individuated by relational properties, and those properties require structural conditions for relation. The Latin tradition since Augustine has worked to give the relations content without giving the Persons separable being; the Cappadocian tradition has worked the converse problem. Both run on relational structure that, on the present analysis, requires the conditions T, S, and Φ supply. The doctrine of immanent Trinity buys internal relationality at the cost of locating relational structure within the simple, atemporal divine being, which is precisely the structural difficulty divine simplicity was intended to foreclose.

**Q6.** *What does *immanence* relate?* The contemporary panentheist and process traditions, with Hartshorne [-@hartshorne1948] the systematic process progenitor, developed by Cobb and Griffin [-@cobbGriffin1976], Clayton [-@clayton2004], and Peacocke [-@peacocke2007], attempt to preserve the relational depth the believer's experiential reports require by placing creation *within* God or treating God and creation as mutually constitutive. This panentheist *creation-within-God* must be distinguished from Plotinian emanation: in emanation the One's procession reaches even matter without the One being *within* what proceeds from it ([§5.3.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-2)), so the source keeps its non-relational transcendence, whereas panentheism surrenders exactly that transcendence to secure mutual constitution. The move responds to the concern. The cost is symmetrical to the open-theist cost [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2) names: a being whose relations to creation share creation's structural conditions is a being who instantiates those conditions. Panentheism preserves relationality by relocating God within the modal structure the classical doctrine had defined God against. The two positions (mixed relation and panentheism) are best read as the doctrine splitting along a structural incompatibility. One preserves the predicate by relocating its referent; the other preserves the structure by surrendering the referent.

*What is required.* Taken in sum, the six pressures show what *related* depends on once the term is held to the conditions of its application. Two things stand in a relation when their states are jointly determined by a structural connection between them, and the relation of reason preserves the term while surrendering the running-from on which the believer's report of being loved depends. Love runs through responsive structure: love-without-response is a one-sided pouring whose target's state makes no difference to the pouring, and the doctrine of divine immutability factors that responsive structure out at the divine pole. Relata meet by sharing structural conditions; the *sui generis* relation lacks what creaturely relations have, and the term *relation* is doing work the doctrine has not specified. Prayer reaches God along a temporal channel: ET-simultaneity preserves the divine end of the answering by setting aside the temporal asymmetry constitutive of being a response to anything in particular. Affecting relations are bidirectional: asymmetric affection is half of a relation, and the half the believer's reports require is precisely what the doctrine does not give. Internal relationality cannot be bought in simplicity-incompatible coin: the Trinitarian resource buys internal relations at the cost of locating relational structure within the simple, atemporal divine being, which is the structural difficulty simplicity was intended to foreclose. And the panentheist preservation of structure pays for itself by surrendering the referent the classical doctrine was defining God against. Each option splits the doctrine along the same structural incompatibility rather than holding it together. T, S, and Φ are the conditions of bilateral connection; relation is the structural shape Nature takes when it carries one relatum's state back to another within itself.

*What is inverted.* Relation belongs to Nature. The English *relation* descends through Latin *relatio*, *a carrying back, a referring*. A relation carries back: the obtaining of one relatum's state to the other, and the other's to the first. The carrying back requires Nature. To be related is to share Nature with another relatum, in the structural sense that lets the obtaining of one's state make a difference at the other. The classical God is defined as standing outside the conditions T, S, and Φ the creature shares. The classical doctrine of *mixed relation* is honest about the consequence: the divine end of any relation between God and creature obtains only from the creature's side. The present analysis agrees that the doctrine is honest and presses what it costs. What is jointly carried back, between any creature and any other element of Nature, is what Nature *is*: T held in common, S held in common, Φ held in common. Nature is what makes carrying-back possible. The classical tradition reaches for a deeper relation than any creaturely relation to anything within Nature, and names a relation across a difference at every structural level. What love, presence, hearing, and being-heard *are*, on the classical predicates weighed against what their application takes, are the structural ways Nature carries one relatum's state back to another within itself. The doctrine of divine relation, however formulated, locates those carryings-back in a relatum beyond Nature rather than in Nature itself.

### 6.8.3 Describability {#sec-6-8-3}

The standard reply to everything before it is that words like *knows* or *good* were never meant to apply to God in the plain, ordinary sense: they apply by analogy, or only by negation. But even the gentlest analogy has to share *some* structure with the everyday meaning to count as analogy at all, and that shared structure is the very time, space, and substance the doctrine was trying to avoid. Negation and analogy relocate the problem; they do not dissolve it.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical tradition assembles several reinforcing positions on religious language. *Univocal* predication (the term means the same in *God is good* and *Socrates is good*) is rejected by Aquinas (*ST* I.13.5); Scotus (*Ordinatio* I.3) defends a restricted version. *Equivocal* predication (the term means something altogether different in the two cases) is rejected by both. *Analogical* predication, the middle path, holds that divine and creaturely predicates share content via a structured proportion: God's goodness stands to God as creaturely goodness stands to creature, with the *as* doing structural work the merely equivocal lacks [*ST* I.13.5–6; with refinements by Cajetan 1498; @mcinerny1996; for contemporary discussion @burrell1986; @rocca2004; @white2016].

*Apophatic* or negative theology (we know what God is not, not what God is) was developed by Pseudo-Dionysius (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1) into the central method of mystical-theological reflection, taken up by Maximus, Eriugena, and Eckhart, and continues in contemporary form [@marion1991; @turner1995]. The method's philosophical origin lies with Plotinus: *Enneads* V.3 (*On the Knowing Hypostases and That Which Is Beyond*) and VI.9 (*On the Good, or the One*) develop the ascent-through-negation procedure in its first systematic form: the One is beyond intellect, beyond being, beyond any predicate that would make it an object of thought; what can be said of the One is said by stripping away every determination, and the stripping terminates in silence. Pseudo-Dionysius transmits the Plotinian method into the Christian theological tradition; from Pseudo-Dionysius it passes to Maximus, Eriugena, Eckhart, and the contemporary apophatic forms Marion and Turner develop. The citation gap is not merely genealogical: what Plotinus names as *the One beyond being* is the philosophical ancestor of the Pseudo-Dionysian *cloud of unknowing*, and naming the ancestor changes the doctrinal assessment at Q5.

Maimonides's negative theology in the *Guide for the Perplexed* [I.50–60; @seeskin2000; @stern2013] is the parallel Jewish-tradition development; the doctrine of attribute-by-attribute negation receives its sharpest classical form there. *Perfect-being theology* holds that God is the being than which none greater can be conceived (Anselm, *Proslogion* 2–3), with each attribute the perfection of its kind; it supplies the methodology for deriving the classical attributes [@morris1987; @leftow2012; @speaks2018].

Each tradition tries to keep divine description from being either flat creaturely projection or empty piety. The meta-doctrine, at its most disciplined, asks for a register in which divine predicates are neither univocal projections from creaturely experience nor empty equivocations, and in which the apophatic, analogical, and perfect-being resources together preserve the believer's confession against both flattening and dissolution.

*What cannot be answered.* Seven questions ask of the meta-doctrine what it cannot answer once reduced to the form the analysis can engage. What surfaces beneath them is the reply this chapter has been deferring through eleven sections. Eleven sections of pressing the classical attributes have so far proceeded as if the predicates *exists*, *is one*, *is necessary*, *is eternal*, *is present*, *is aware*, *knows*, *can*, *acts*, *governs*, *relates* applied to God in the same sense they apply to anything else. The classical tradition itself has not made that assumption. Aquinas's doctrine of analogy (*ST* I.13.5) is one of the most carefully developed theories of religious language in the history of philosophy, and the Pseudo-Dionysian tradition of apophasis is older still. The believer who confesses that God is good is not, on the classical position, predicating goodness of God univocally with the goodness of a friend or a deed; nor is the predication merely equivocal, with no shared content between the divine and creaturely cases. The third option, *analogy*, has done the work of making divine description intelligible for the better part of a millennium. The full reply is that every structural pressure the chapter has registered concerns the predicates read univocally, and the classical tradition has been telling its readers since at least Aquinas not to read them that way. The concern is not whether analogy and apophasis are coherent doctrines of religious language; they are. The concern is what they preserve when their preservations are added up. The eleven preceding sections have argued that the classical attributes, taken at face value, presuppose structural conditions T, S, and Φ the doctrine has placed beyond divine being. The doctrine of analogy responds: the predicates were never meant to apply at face value. The doctrine of apophasis responds: the predicates negate creaturely limitations rather than affirm divine features. The doctrine of perfect-being theology responds: the predicates are derived from the very property of being maximally great, which neither structural analysis nor creaturely experience constrains. Each reply preserves the doctrine by relocating where its content is carried. The seven pressures ask what is left when the relocations are taken seriously and the structural conditions the predicates have shed are tallied up: one at the level of the doctrine of analogy (Q1), four at the level of the conditions divine description runs on (Q2–Q5), and two at the level of competing doctrines of religious language (Q6 univocity, Q7 revelation).

**Q1.** *How is God's goodness like ours, if in God there is nothing for goodness to belong to?* Aquinas's doctrine of analogy (*ST* I.13.5–6) holds that divine and creaturely predicates share content via a structured proportion: God's wisdom stands to God as creaturely wisdom stands to creature. The doctrine is one of the most carefully developed theories of religious language in the history of philosophy. The concern here is what the proportion preserves. For *as* to do structural work, the two sides must share something the proportion can be a proportion *of*. The doctrine of *analogy of proper proportionality* (Cajetan 1498) holds that the shared content is the constitutive relation between attribute and bearer; the doctrine of *analogy of attribution* holds that creaturely attributes are derivative from divine ones. McInerny [-@mcinerny1996] and Rocca [-@rocca2004] develop contemporary refinements. The concern here is that the doctrine of strong divine simplicity (*ST* I.3) entails that there is no real distinction in God between the attribute and the bearer, and the *as* of the proportion requires precisely that distinction on the divine side. The doctrine of analogy preserves the predicates by appealing to a constitutive relation that the doctrine of simplicity has eliminated at the divine pole. White [-@white2016] acknowledges the difficulty and develops the most careful contemporary defense; the present reading registers the defense and presses the cost. Feser's act/potency grounding [*Aquinas: A Beginner's Guide*, -@feser2009, ch. 4] offers the most rigorous contemporary defense of the causal-grounding side of Q1's second pressure. On Feser's account, the analogical proportion is primarily a metaphysical grounding relation rather than a semantic proportion between predicate-tokens: creaturely perfections are *participated* forms of an act that God, as *ipsum esse subsistens*, subsistent esse (the act of being) itself, possesses without any act/potency composition. The esse/essence distinction in creatures (esse is real and distinct from essentia) grounds the asymmetry: in God esse and essentia are identical, so God's perfections are possessed eminently and without restriction, and the proportion tracks metaphysical participation rather than linguistic similarity. The concern for Feser's grounding is that *participation* is itself a structural relation: for the creature's participated act to be grounded in God's subsistent act, the creature must stand in the reception-relation to a source, and that relation is a directed, asymmetric, structural dependence (T, S, Φ) of the participated in the subsisting source. Feser's reply is that esse is not a temporal-causal relation but the metaphysical grounding of participated-being in being-itself; the concern here is whether the grounding relation (*creature receives esse from God*) requires the structural conditions of any reception, including those of direction, distinction, and substantial bearer.

A second pressure on the analogy doctrine runs through its grounding rather than its compatibility with simplicity. Aquinas's own grounding of analogical predication (*De Potentia* q.7 a.7; *Summa Contra Gentiles* I.34) takes the semantic fact of analogy to rest on a metaphysical fact: a real causal relation between Creator and creature, in which creatures derive their perfections from God as effects from their source. That causal relation is structurally constituted. Production is asymmetric (T), cause and effect are distinct relata (S), and the productive act is carried across the distinction it spans (Φ). These are the structural roles, and they carry to Time, Space, and Substance in type by the upgrade earned at [§3.5.3](convergence.html#sec-3-5-3) (on the realizer biconditionals whose anti-Finean necessity is discharged at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10)). The doctrine that was supposed to insulate divine predicates from the structural conditions enlists those conditions at the level of grounding. The two analogy concerns are complementary: the first locates the cost at the divine-pole side of the proportion; the second locates it at the metaphysical grounding the proportion rests on. Both press in the same direction.

A third resource within the analogy family locates the shared content not in the proportion but in the manner of signifying. Aquinas's distinction between the *res significata* and the *modus significandi* (*ST* I.13.3) holds that a perfection-term (*good*, *wise*, *living*) said of God signifies a perfection, the thing signified, that belongs to God properly and indeed pre-eminently, while the creaturely *mode* of signifying it (the way the perfection is held by a composite, dependent, time-bound knower) is what falls short and is not affirmed of God. On this account the predicate's determinate content survives on the side of the *res significata* even as its creaturely mode is set aside; the difficulty is supposed to lie only in the mode, not in the thing signified. The concern is what the *res significata* retains once the *modus* is subtracted. The perfections the believer predicates are given as determinate only in a mode: goodness as a settled orientation among alternatives, wisdom as the holding-together of a differentiated manifold, life as a duration. Subtract the mode and the move forks. Either the thing signified keeps a determinate content (in which case it keeps the structural conditions the mode was carrying, the orientation, the manifold, the duration, and the perfection lands on a subject that instantiates T, S, and Φ after all) or the subtraction takes the content with the mode, and the *res significata* thins to the bare *is* that [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) finds without individuating content and that Q2 and Q5 below reach as the apophatic terminus. The distinction draws the line in the right place; it does not relieve the pressure, because the conditions that made the perfection determinate are exactly what the *modus significandi* supplied and the divine pole is required to shed.

**Q2.** *What is left to confess, once every word for God has been negated?* The Pseudo-Dionysian tradition of negative theology (*Mystical Theology* 1; *Divine Names* 1) holds that we know what God is not, not what God is. The doctrine has been the central resource of mystical theology for fifteen centuries [Maximus, *Ambigua*; Eriugena, *Periphyseon*; Eckhart, *Sermons*; for contemporary form @marion1991; @turner1995; @davies2008]. The concern here is what the negations leave for the believer's confession. *God is not finite*, *God is not temporal*, *God is not embodied*, *God is not changeable*: each negation rules out one structural condition the corresponding affirmative predicate would have required. When the negations are summed, what remains is a being defined by the absence of every structural condition affirmative predication has been found to require. The Pseudo-Dionysian tradition is honest about this: the *via negativa* terminates in the *cloud of unknowing*, in silence, in the surrender of every conceptual handle on the divine. The present reading agrees that the apophatic tradition has been more honest about its terminus than the cataphatic (affirmative) refinements that build atop it. The question this section adds is what *God exists* affirms when every structural condition for existence has been negated. The honest answer the apophatic tradition itself gives is: not what *exists* affirms in any case the structural analysis examines.

**Q3.** *What is the greatest possible power, if it has no conditions left to be powerful within?* Anselm's perfect-being methodology (*Proslogion* 2–3) derives the classical attributes by taking each attribute as the perfection of its kind: God is most powerful, most knowing, most good, with each *most* taken to its limit. Morris [-@morris1987], Leftow [-@leftow2012], and Speaks [-@speaks2018] develop contemporary versions. The concern here is the projection. To project an attribute to its limit is to extend a creaturely scale beyond any creaturely instance. The scale extends within the structural conditions of the attribute: powerful-within-T, knowing-within-T-and-S, good-within-relations-with-other-bearers. To extend the scale beyond any creaturely instance while removing the structural conditions of the scale is not to find a maximal point on the scale; it is to leave the scale. The doctrine projects the predicate beyond the modal structure the predicate is intelligible within. The result is not the predicate at its maximum but a being defined by the predicate's having no modal structure to be at any value within. The methodological reply is that perfection just means *unlimited by structural conditions*. The present reading registers the reply and presses what is left of the predicate when its structural conditions are *the limitation* perfection negates.

**Q4.** *How does calling something a mystery make a contradiction cohere?* The classical tradition has long held that the divine nature exceeds creaturely comprehension and that the limits of creaturely comprehension entail no limit on divine being. The doctrine of *mystery*, properly understood, is not the surrender of reason but its acknowledgment of the bounds of analogical predication [Pseudo-Dionysius, *Mystical Theology*; Aquinas, *ST* I.12.7; @wittgenstein1921; for contemporary defense @plantinga2000; @stump2010]. The concern here is what mystery accommodates and what it excludes. A doctrine that contains apparently incompatible commitments (say, divine immutability and divine response to prayer) can preserve coherence by appeal to mystery: the apparent incompatibility holds only at the level of creaturely understanding, not at the level of divine being. The reply is genuinely available; the structural reading does not exclude it. The question this section presses is what mystery is positioned to do. Mystery, properly understood, is the recognition that creaturely concepts may not capture divine reality.
