It is not the recognition that contradictions cease to be contradictions when applied to a sufficiently elevated subject. The concern here is that the eleven preceding sections have not turned on creaturely conceptual limits; they have turned on structural conditions the doctrine has placed beyond divine being. Whatever mystery accommodates, it does not accommodate the running-of-predicates outside the constitutive modal structure the predicates require for application.

**Q5.** *If God is beyond every word, what have the words been describing all along?* The deepest version of apophasis [Eckhart, *Sermons* 22, 52; @marion1991] takes the negations to their limit: God is beyond being, beyond goodness, beyond every category, beyond beyond. The position is not nihilism but the most rigorous form of theological humility. The present reading registers the position and notes its symmetry with the conclusion the chapter has been pressing. To say of God *exists*, *is one*, *is necessary*, *is eternal*, *is present*, *is aware*, *knows*, *can*, *acts*, *governs*, *relates* (with every predicate qualified to remove the structural conditions of its application) is to terminate at the same point as Eckhart's *abyss beyond God*: a referent for which no predicate the believer would recognize has determinate content. The mystical tradition arrives at this terminus by faithfulness to the apophatic method; the present chapter has arrived at it by faithfulness to the structural conditions of predicate application. The two paths converge. The Plotinian origin makes the convergence structurally intelligible. In *Enneads* VI.9, Plotinus's ascent terminates in the One *epekeina tēs ousias* (beyond being) which is beyond intellect, beyond goodness as a property, beyond every predicate that would make it an object of thought. The present chapter arrives at the same terminus from the structural side: the predicates applied to God, when their structural conditions are removed, no longer have determinate content. The Plotinian mystic arrives there by faithfully stripping predicates; the structural analysis arrives there by faithfully examining what makes predicates contentful. The question the convergence raises is which path has been tracing the right referent: the Plotinian One-beyond-being, or the structural conditions whose removal the negations name. The question is what the convergence shows. On the apophatic reading, what the predicates have been reaching for is the divine being itself, beyond all categories. On the present reading, what the predicates have been reaching for is the structural conditions of any reaching at all.

The convergence does not leave the two readings symmetrically poised. The Plotinian One is the honest terminus of *refusing to predicate*: the ascent ends in silence, and silence is consistent with the One-beyond-being precisely because no predicate is asserted of it. But the believer's God is not silent. The tradition does not stop at the *cloud of unknowing*; it goes on to confess a God who creates, knows, loves, judges, and answers. Every such confession is an act of predication, and an act of predication is governed by the conditions of predication this section has been tracing. The apophatic terminus is therefore available only to a theology willing to follow it all the way down into silence: to surrender the acting, relating, worshipped God along with the predicates. The theology that keeps predicating has already declined the One-beyond-being; what it is left reaching for, every time it predicates, is the structural conditions any predicate requires. The referent the *continuing* predications track is Nature, not the silence beyond being. The One-beyond-being is what is left when predication stops; Nature is what predication, when it goes on, has been about.

**Q6.** *If "being" means the same for God as for us, how is God's being not structured like ours?* Duns Scotus, against Aquinas, holds that *being* (*ens*) applies univocally to God and creatures: the same concept of being, with the same content, predicated in the same sense across the Creator–creature divide [*Ordinatio* I.3; @cross2005; @williams2005]. The semantic motivation is sharp: if creaturely concepts shifted in meaning when applied to God, theological speech could not refer at all. Univocity of being is what makes theological discourse contentful. Grant the position in full. Univocity does not flatten God into a being among beings; the formal distinction [@cross2005, ch. 4] preserves the qualitative gap between infinite and finite being while keeping the concept of being itself constant across the divide. The Scotist Creator is still uniquely sovereign, uniquely necessary, uniquely the source. The cost surfaces at the level of what the constant concept *is*. If *being* applies univocally to God and creatures, then whatever being is for creatures it is also for God. Creaturely being is structured being — being-in-Time, being-extended-in-Space, being-as-what-bears-its-own-persistence. Univocity preserves theological speech by paying for it in the coin of structural commitment: the feature that makes God-talk contentful for Scotus is the feature that places God within structure. The Scotist Creator–creature distinction is real, but it is now a distinction *within* structure, not a distinction between structured being and something outside it.

Scotus's is the medieval form of the position; its most developed contemporary form is Swinburne's [*The Coherence of Theism*, -@swinburne1977, ch. 4, "The Words of Theology"]. Swinburne grants neither full univocity nor analogy but a controlled stretching of ordinary-language terms: a word keeps its ordinary meaning while the conditions of its application are loosened just far enough to reach the divine case without importing the creaturely limitations. The motivation is Scotus's (speech that does not refer is not speech) but the mechanism is meant to preserve reference at lower structural cost than univocity of being. The concern here is what the stretching can loosen without losing the term. Either the loosened conditions still include the structural frame the predicate runs on, in which case the controlled stretch imports T, S, and Φ exactly as univocity did, only less visibly; or the stretching loosens the structural conditions themselves, in which case it has not stretched the term's content but cut it loose from what gave the term determinate application, sliding toward the equivocity Swinburne means to avoid and the apophasis Q2 has already weighed. Controlled meaning-stretching preserves reference only on the first branch, and the first branch is univocity's structural commitment under a softer name.

**Q7.** *How does the hidden God become the disclosed God without changing?* Karl Barth [-@barth1932, I/1; cf. @mccormack1995; @hunsinger1991; @webster2004] refuses analogy in favor of revelation: we know God not by extending creaturely concepts upward, but only in the act in which God reveals Godself. That act is dialectical (*Realdialektik*): in revealing Godself, God remains hidden, disclosed as the One who is not exhausted by what is disclosed. Barthians press this as the move that protects God's transcendence without giving up theological speech. A dialectic between hiddenness and disclosure that is *real*, and not just a conceptual contrast, requires three things: a distinction between what is hidden and what is disclosed (S), an act in which the one becomes the other (T), and one and the same God who is both the hidden one and the disclosed one (Φ). The Barthian rejoinder (that revelation is not a worldly event but God's eternity breaking into time) restates the point in stronger language without removing it. Eternity that breaks *into* time still has direction. Hiddenness that endures *through* disclosure still has a being. Transcendence revealed *as* immanent still has relational structure. The *Realdialektik* is the act in which T, S, and Φ operate at maximum intensity, not the act in which they are left behind. Between univocity (Q6), equivocation (rejected by both Aquinas and Scotus), and analogy (Q1), no semantic option preserves a Creator outside structure. Revelation as the alternative to analogical predication preserves it by *enacting* T, S, and Φ rather than predicating them.

*What is required.* The seven pressures register the structural conditions divine description depends on. Analogy requires a constitutive relation between attribute and bearer on the divine side for the proportion to be a proportion *of*; the doctrine of strong simplicity has factored that relation out at the divine pole. The causal grounding the analogy rests on is itself structurally constituted (production asymmetric in T, cause and effect distinct in S, productive act carried across the distinction in Φ) so analogy preserves the predicates by enlisting at the level of grounding the very structure it tries to set aside at the level of the proportion. Apophasis, summed, removes every condition affirmative predication has been found to require, and the tradition's terminus in *cloud of unknowing* and *abyss beyond God* is honest about what its method leaves standing. Perfect-being theology projects creaturely scales past the limit of their own modal structure; extending an attribute beyond any creaturely instance while removing the structural conditions of the scale is leaving the scale, not finding a maximal point on it. Mystery accommodates conceptual humility, but it does not accommodate predicates running outside the structural frame their application requires: the eleven preceding sections turned on structural conditions, not on creaturely conceptual limits. Mystical apophasis and the present chapter's structural reading converge on the same referent for which no recognizable predicate retains determinate content; the question is which referent the predicates have been reaching for. Univocity preserves theological-speech content but pays for it in the coin of structural commitment: if *being* applies univocally to God and creatures, whatever being is for creatures it is for God, and creaturely being is structured being. Revelation as the alternative to predication enacts T, S, and Φ at maximum intensity rather than transcending them: hiddenness through disclosure has direction, hidden-and-disclosed needs a being, and *Realdialektik* is the act in which the structural conditions operate at full force, not the act in which they are left behind. What divine description names, when its referent is examined, is the activity of marking out a contour Nature supplies.

*What is inverted.* Description is the marking of a contour the description follows, and the contour requires Nature. The English *describe* descends through Latin *describere*, *to write down, to copy, to mark out*. To describe is to mark a contour the description follows. The contour requires a subject of contouring: something the marking is *of*. The classical doctrine of analogy, apophasis, and perfect-being theology, in each of its formulations, has worked to preserve the marking while qualifying it past the conditions of contouring it would otherwise require. The qualifications have been carried out with extraordinary care over fifteen centuries; the concern this chapter presses is not that the qualifications fail at what they were designed to do, but what they leave standing for the believer to hold onto. That question does not turn on a univocal reading the classical tradition has not endorsed; the eleven preceding sections depend instead on the predicates retaining enough determinate content for the believer's confession to mean what it has been taken to mean. Analogy, apophasis, and perfect-being theology each preserve the predicates' grammatical role in the believer's confession by qualifying their structural content past the point where the structural conditions of application obtain. What the doctrines preserve, when their preservations are added up, is the inheritance of the verbal forms; what they have qualified away, in the same accumulation, is the structure that gave the forms determinate content. The chapter does not press an argument against the doctrines; it presses an account of the cost. The cost is what this section names. In ordinary terms: silence may be a coherent religious posture, but it cannot also supply the positive claims that God knows, acts, loves, creates, or relates.

### 6.8.4 Revelation {#sec-6-8-4}

Revelation is the claim that God has made himself known (at Sinai, in Christ, in scripture) and made himself known sufficiently, for everyone. The actual deliveries, though, are local in time and place, stamped with the culture that produced them, and spread along the ordinary routes of trade and conquest. They look exactly like human productions, which is hard to square with a disclosure from a source outside all of that, and the case for that conclusion runs as a weight-of-evidence pattern, not a strict proof.

*What the tradition holds.* The doctrine of divine revelation holds that God has made himself known (his nature, his will, his redemptive purpose) through specific historical disclosures (Sinai, the prophets, the incarnation of the Word, the apostolic witness) and through the standing testimony of creation and conscience. The medieval and Reformed traditions distinguish *revelatio specialis* (special revelation: scripture and incarnation) from *revelatio generalis* (general revelation: the natural order and the *sensus divinitatis* implanted in every human being). Aquinas treats the specially-revealed articles as suprarational truths necessary for salvation (*ST* I.1.1; cf. Romans 1:20 NRSVUE and the Five Ways for the naturally-knowable preamble), and Calvin grounds the *sensus* in *Institutes* I.iii.1 as a universal seed of religion. The Reformed scholastics tighten the structure: scripture is self-authenticating (*autopistia*) and clear in the matters necessary for salvation (*perspicuitas*); the natural knowledge is sufficient to convict but insufficient to save (Turretin, *Institutes* I.iv). Barth's twentieth-century reformulation collapses the special–general distinction by treating *all* revelation as the dialectical event of the Word's own self-disclosure (*Church Dogmatics* I/1), so that natural theology is rejected as a category-mistake. Across these formulations the tradition holds two claims jointly: that God has made himself genuinely known, and that the knowing is sufficient: sufficient for assent, sufficient for salvation, sufficient as ground for the worship and obedience God's standing in the order of being requires.

*What cannot be answered.* The question revelation must answer is whether the actual deliveries of the tradition can bear the universal and decisive load the doctrine ascribes to them. But *sufficient* is not a single demand. The doctrine needs the deliveries sufficient at once on several independent fronts: reaching every rational creature, distributed as widely as the claim is universal, intelligible to those it reaches, clear enough to ground the assent it asks, and decisive enough to carry the evidential weight it is given. These come apart, so a gain on one front is no answer to a shortfall on another; granting the historical case at its strongest, as Q6 does, leaves the questions of delivery, reach, and clarity standing where they were.

**Q1.** *How can a disclosure delivered at a single time bear the universal weight the doctrine assigns it, reaching every temporal cross-section of the rational creation?* Sinai occurred at one place in one millennium; the incarnation occupied a thirty-year window in a single Roman province; the Quranic recitations span twenty-three years of seventh-century Arabia. A being whose nature is to-be-known by every temporal cross-section of the rational creation cannot deliver his self-disclosure at a temporal point and expect the disclosure to bear universal weight. Either the disclosure is for that location only (and the universal claim fails) or it must be re-delivered to each location (and it has not been).

**Q2.** *How can a disclosure confined to one place, and spread only along the ordinary routes of human culture, be the universal self-disclosure of an omnipresent God?* Sinai is in the Sinai; the incarnation in Galilee and Judea; the Quran in the Hijaz. The actual propagation pattern of each tradition follows the contours of empire, trade-route, migration, and conquest, that is, the contours of human cultural diffusion. The pattern of dissemination is indistinguishable from the pattern any merely-human cultural production would exhibit. If revelation were sourced in the omnipresent ground of being, we would expect its distribution to look unlike, not exactly like, the distribution of human cultural artifacts.

**Q3.** *How can a disclosure that bears the cultural fingerprint of its producing era at every level have a source standing outside Φ, the space of human production?* The texts are written in the literary genres of their period; they encode the cosmologies, legal institutions, and rhetorical conventions of their producing cultures; the variants and redactional layers track the practices of the scribes who transmitted them. @ehrman2005 [-@ehrman2009], @allison2010, @walton2009, and @collins2006 document the pattern in detail. A revelation issued by a being whose standing is outside Φ would not bear Φ's fingerprint at every level of its delivery; one issued from inside Φ would. The deliveries we have bear the inside-fingerprint.

**Q4.** *Even granting a genuine source, how can a written text be the right instrument for a disclosure meant for every person?* Scripture reaches anyone only across a chain of human relays (composition, transcription, canonization, transmission, translation, interpretation) and each link is a point of loss, open only to the literate, the linguistically matched, and the textually trained. Paine presses the structural form: a revelation fixed in writing and carried by human hands is, after its first hearer, no longer revelation but report: testimony about a revelation, with no more reach than the fallible chain that conveys it [@paine1794]. A source whose standing is universal would not entrust its universal message to the least universal of media; one working from inside human culture would have nothing else to use. The deliveries use exactly what a from-within-Φ production would use, and nothing a from-outside-Φ source could distinctively command.

**Q5.** *Setting the question of error aside, why does a disclosure supposedly from outside human culture never carry content its era could not yet have reached?* A source from outside Φ has every opportunity to exceed its century; none of the deliveries does. Where the deliveries speak of nature, law, or history, they speak with exactly the reach, and exactly the limits, of the era that produced them: the otherwise-inaccessible truth a from-outside-Φ source could supply, and a from-within-Φ source could not, never appears. The point is not that the content errs, which Q8 takes up, but that it never exceeds its century: a clean predictive miss, since a genuinely external source has every chance to include what its age could not author, and the deliveries decline it every time.

**Q6.** *How can the deliveries bear the evidential load the doctrine needs, once sufficiency-of-delivery is distinguished from sufficiency-of-evidence?* The tradition often equivocates between the two: between *God has made himself available* and *what God has made available is decisive*. @habermasG1996 [-@habermasG2003], @habermasLicona2004, @licona2010, @wright2003, @craig2008, and @davis1997 press the historical case for the resurrection as a sufficient evidential ground for the central claim: not merely *some witnesses reported X*, but a cumulative case from early testimony, transformed communities, explanatory fit, and the claimed irreducibility of the resurrection to ordinary legendary development. Pressed that far, the case is not dismissible as naïve evidentialism. The concern here is narrower and sharper: even if the historiographical case is granted at its strongest, the inference from historically serious testimony to *this is the load-bearing public ground for cosmic moral allegiance* runs through a probabilistic gap that the doctrine of sufficient revelation cannot tolerate without supplementation by the very *sensus* or interior witness it was meant to supply from outside.

**Q7.** *Why does the distribution of revelatory clarity fail to track the distribution of sincere openness, as a loving discloser would seem to require?* @schellenberg1993 [-@schellenberg2007; -@schellenberg2015] formalizes the divine hiddenness problem: a perfectly loving God would ensure that no capable, non-resistant rational creature is, by their own lights, without sufficient ground for relationship with him; many such creatures are, by their own lights, without such ground; therefore no perfectly loving God exists. @howardSnyderMoser2002 collect the responsive literature, and @hick1966 offers the epistemic-distance defense. But the defenses retain the explanandum: that the actual distribution of revelatory clarity does not track the distribution of sincere openness. The revelation is delivered, on the tradition's own terms, less clearly than its purpose appears to demand.

**Q8.** *How can deliveries marked at every turn by the empirical errors of their era have a source outside that era?* Genesis 1's cosmology, Joshua 10's stayed sun, Luke 2's Quirinian census, the Matthean and Lukan birth narratives' incompatible geographies, the genealogical disagreements, the parallel-pericope contradictions in the synoptic record: each is documentable, and each is the kind of artifact a delivery from within Φ would exhibit and a delivery from outside Φ would not. @ehrman2005 [-@ehrman2009], @allison2010, @walton2009, and @collins2006 catalog the artifacts. The tradition's reply (that these are accommodations to the original audience's idiom) concedes the data and relocates the burden onto a doctrine of accommodation strong enough to absorb anything the texts contain, which is to say strong enough to absorb falsifying content.

**Q9.** *How can a single source deliver, as the content of revelation, pairs of claims one of which entails the negation of the other?* Mary's location at the tomb (Matthew 28 vs. John 20), the death of Judas (Matthew 27 vs. Acts 1), the genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1 vs. Luke 3), and the timing of the crucifixion (synoptic Passover vs. Johannine Preparation) cannot all be true on any reading that respects Aristotelian non-contradiction (*Metaphysics* Γ.3) or its scholastic inheritance (Aquinas, *ST* I.85.5). The accommodation move available for empirical errors is structurally unavailable for contradictions in revelation's own content: a being who delivers revelation cannot deliver, as the content of revelation, a pair of propositions one of which entails the negation of the other.

**Q10.** *If revelation is reframed as a self-disclosure that carries its own veiling within it, what surface feature of the delivery could still count for or against its having occurred?* Barth's dialectical move [@barth1932, I/1; @mccormack1995; @hunsinger1991; @webster2004] attempts to absorb these pressures by reframing revelation as the event of God's self-disclosure that bears within itself its own veiling: a *Realdialektik* in which the Word makes himself known precisely by remaining hidden in his disclosure. The move is theologically powerful but evidentially evacuating: if the dialectical structure is internal to revelation, then no surface feature of the delivery (clarity, accuracy, distribution, evidential adequacy) can count for or against revelation having occurred, which is to say no feature can count.

**Q11.** *Can general revelation patch what special revelation cannot deliver, or does it inherit the same Φ-fingerprint problem?* Romans 1:20, the Five Ways, Paley's *Natural Theology* [-@paley1802], and Plantinga's *sensus divinitatis* [-@plantinga2000] furnish standing creaturely access to God that does not depend on a particular historical delivery. But each construal of general revelation either runs against the same Φ-fingerprint critique (the natural theologies are themselves cultural artifacts of particular philosophical traditions) or relocates the work to an interior faculty whose universality is empirically contested.

**Q12.** *Why does the properly-basic belief Reformed epistemology describes track the religious tradition of the believer's birthplace rather than the truth of the propositions believed?* Reformed epistemology [@plantinga2000] treats Christian belief as properly basic (justified without being inferred from other beliefs) when produced by a properly functioning *sensus* in a congenial environment with the truth-aimed cognitive design plan of the IIHS (Internal Instigation of the Holy Spirit). The epistemic system is internally coherent, but it has no resources for explaining why the *sensus* delivers, in the actual cultural-distribution data, beliefs that track the religious tradition of the believer's geographic origin rather than tracking the truth-conditions of the propositions believed. The cultural-distribution argument is, on Plantinga's own framework, a defeater-deflector candidate, and the deflector is not in hand.

*What is required.* These pressures constitute convergent abductive evidence rather than formal entailments: taken individually, each is answerable, but the pattern (that the deliveries bear every mark of a from-within-Φ production and bear no mark a from-outside-Φ delivery would distinctively carry) constitutes an abductive case for the relocation rather than a deductive proof. The cluster pattern (recognized in Righteousness [§6.9.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-2) and Interaction [§6.7.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-3)) reasserts itself: what is required is not a *more universal* delivery, nor a *better-distributed* set of deliveries, but the relocation of the very desideratum (the standing ground for cosmic orientation, value, and trust) into a feature of Nature herself rather than into a punctual transmission from outside Nature.

The predicate itself supplies the bridge. Revelation is not merely information-transfer; it is uncovering. To uncover anything structurally requires (i) a field in which something can be there to be uncovered, (ii) subjects for whom the uncovered content becomes available, (iii) temporal correction across which concealment gives way to disclosure, (iv) spatial and social transmission across which the disclosure can be shared, and (v) a substantive medium in which marks, reasons, memories, and practices persist. Those are T, S, and Φ in the register of intelligibility. The Modal Convergence Theorem (developed in Chapter 8) and the Subsistence definition supply the technical equipment for treating the *availability of the world to inquiry* (the modal fact that reality lends itself, at every cross-section of T and S and Φ, to investigation, articulation, and progressively-corrected understanding) as the genuinely universal feature the doctrine of revelation was trying to name. Inquiry has the universality and structural reach the punctual deliveries lack: it is available to every temporal cross-section, distributed across every spatial location, and bears the marks of every successful Φ-pattern that touches it.

*What the relocation does not concede.* The relocation invites a symmetry charge from the side of the hiddenness argument itself. Schellenberg's mature position does not rest with the denial of personal theism; it offers *ultimism* (the bare commitment that there is a reality ultimate in being, in value, and as the source of our deepest good) as the standing alternative the honest inquirer should adopt once revelation fails [@schellenberg2007]. The charge presses a symmetry: dissolving revelation into the availability of the world to inquiry, the objection runs, does not refute revelation so much as rename its absence: to say that the personal self-disclosing God is nowhere clearly given, and that what is universally given is instead the world's openness to inquiry, simply restates Schellenberg's own conclusion, that the personal discloser is unavailable, under a friendlier description. The concession is only apparent, and seeing why turns on which side of the disclosure relation carries the variation. The availability the relocation names is not response-dependent — it does not wait upon, and is not constituted by, anyone's act of inquiry. The world's discoverability is a standing, mind-independent, T- and S- and Φ-spanning structural fact, one that reality exhibits at every cross-section whether or not an inquirer is present to exploit it, exactly as the necessity of Nature requires ([§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5)). What emerges (with life, and deepening with cognitive complexity) is not the world's discoverability but the *capacity* to discover it; emergence sits on the subject side of the relation, not the object side. The hiddenness datum (that revelatory clarity does not track sincere openness) then receives the explanation a hidden personal discloser could supply only by positing some further reason for the silence: an unevenly developed, contingently distributed capacity to read an always-open world is just what an emergent capacity predicts. The asymmetry Schellenberg presses is real, but it is an asymmetry of access, not of availability; the universal standing-ground (the world's intelligibility) is never absent, and only the capacity that reads it is uneven, which is precisely what needs no hidden person to explain.

Nor is this ultimism recovered under another name. Ultimism asks the inquirer to keep the religious stance (trust, hope, devotion) turned toward an ultimate left deliberately underdescribed. The relocation forecloses that move rather than completing it: Nature is the ultimate, but it is not an object of the personal or agential religious stance, and to relabel it as one changes the word while conceding the substance: the relabeling closure [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1) establishes and [§6.10](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-10) carries to its end. What the inquirer is left facing is not a hidden person to be trusted in the dark but an open world to be read in the light. The absence Schellenberg correctly diagnoses is the absence of the discloser; the relocation does not rename that absence but explains it, and locates, in the world's standing availability to inquiry, the very universal the doctrine of revelation was reaching for and could not deliver.

*What is inverted.* The Latin *revelare* is built from *re-* (back, again) and *velare* (to veil, to cover); to reveal is to unveil, to draw back what was draped. The Greek ἀποκάλυψις (*apokalypsis*), ἀπό (away from) plus καλύπτω (cover), names the same structural act: an uncovering, a stripping-back. The Hebrew *gālāh* (to uncover, to lay bare, to expose) carries the same shape, and yet shares its root with *gōlāh*, exile: what is uncovered is what is taken away from its proper place. The etymological cluster ties revelation to a pulling-back-of-cover that, in the Hebrew register, already harbors the possibility of estrangement.

What the doctrinal package delivers, on the abductive pattern just surveyed, is not a pulling-back of cover but a re-veiling: punctual disclosures locked inside particular times, particular places, and particular cultural fingerprints; content marked by empirical error and modal contradiction; clarity calibrated below the demand the doctrine of love would seem to set; dialectical moves that absorb every surface failure into the doctrine of revelation itself. The unveiling, examined, is veiled in the very mode of its delivery.

The structural inversion is concealment: what was meant to be the *re-velare* (the unveiling) turns out, on its own terms, to bear every mark of its opposite, *occultatio* (Latin *occultare*, to hide, to conceal). Nature, in property mode, bears the universal, structurally pervasive, T- and S- and Φ-spanning availability that the punctual deliveries cannot. The inversion is this: the very predicate the tradition needed to underwrite (that the divine has made itself known with sufficient clarity, distribution, and decisiveness to bear cosmic moral weight) is the predicate the actual deliveries cannot bear, while Nature, examined as property-bearer rather than acted-upon-object, can.

## 6.9 Moral Act {#sec-6-9}

The active arm closes with the moral attributes: benevolence ([§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1)) and righteousness ([§6.9.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-2)), God as good in will and just in act. Both are act-attributes before they are value-attributes: to will the good and to render justice is to do something, directed at an object, across the relation between agent and recipient.

Pressed, each requires the directed-crossing structure of any moral act whatever, so that the goodness and justice the tradition locates in a being beyond Nature are found instead in the structured agency T, S, and Φ underwrite.

### 6.9.1 Benevolence {#sec-6-9-1}

Divine goodness is not merely that God is good but that God cannot be otherwise: benevolent, loving, incapable of evil. The key observation is grammatical: words like "benevolently" or "justly" describe a *way of acting*, so they need an act to attach to, and acting needs time, a recipient, and an agent. A being defined without those cannot act in the relevant sense, and so cannot be good or bad in the sense the praise intends.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine goodness assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *summum bonum*: the highest good, the good itself rather than a good among goods (Augustine, *De Trinitate* VIII.3; Aquinas, *ST* I.6.2; Anselm, *Monologion* 1–4). God is *bonitas ipsa*, goodness itself, identical with the divine nature on classical simplicity (*ST* I.6.3). God wills the good of creation: *bonum diffusivum sui*, the good is self-diffusive, and God's creative act is the overflow of divine goodness toward what is not God (Pseudo-Dionysius, *Divine Names* IV; Aquinas, *ST* I.19; *ST* I.44.4). God is essentially benevolent toward creation: *amor benevolentiae*, the love of willing-good-toward [Aquinas, *ST* I.20; @stump2010]. God is impeccable: incapable of sinning, of doing moral evil [*ST* I.25.3 ad 2; @morris1991; @pawl2016 on Christological impeccability]. The same cluster includes divine justice (*ST* I.21; Anselm, *Cur Deus Homo* I.12), divine mercy (*ST* I.21.3; the mercy–justice relation is worked at [§6.9.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-2), Q1), and divine love construed as more than benevolence: *amor amicitiae*, friendship-love [Aquinas, *ST* I.20.2; @stump2010 develops the contemporary form]. The Islamic tradition develops parallel claims: *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim* (the Compassionate and the Merciful) among the divine names (Q1:1, 1:3); God's mercy as *wajib* (obligatory) in the Mu'tazilite reading, as gracious-overflow in the Ash'arite [@frank1992]. The doctrine, at its most ambitious, names a being whose moral character is essential to its being (whose goodness is not a property had alongside other properties but constitutive of what the being is) and whose every act toward creation is therefore necessarily good.

*What cannot be answered.* Seven questions catch the doctrine of divine goodness short of what its moral predicates, pared down to the form structural reasoning can handle, are able to answer. What runs beneath them is grammatical before it is metaphysical. *Benevolent*, *just*, *merciful*, *loving*, *patient*, *faithful*, *gracious* (the moral predicates the tradition applies to God) are *manner-of-acting* predicates. They are adverbial in form, attached to a verb: to act *benevolently*, to act *justly*, to act *mercifully*. Adverbial predicates require the verb. The conditions of acting are what makes the verb available for the adverb to modify: succession from not-acting to acting (T), a target distinct from the actor (S), a substantive agent who acts (Φ). The doctrine has defined the being whose actions the predicates describe as without T, S, or Φ. The seven pressures run at the level of what such a being can bear in the way of moral predication at all. A methodological note is owed before they begin. Stump's narrative theodicy (*Wandering in Darkness* [@stump2010]) presses that abstract goodness-talk misses what the doctrine of divine goodness is for; the argument here does not compete with that project but runs prior to it. The claim is not that the classical God's goodness fails to console but that the moral predicates cannot attach to a being stripped of T, S, and Φ at all, and a manner-of-acting predicate needs an acting before any narrative about the acting can begin. The preclusion therefore holds however the narrative theodicy fares.

**Q1.** *How does God do good, if doing means acting in time upon something other than oneself?* Before the question can be answered, the question of what *do* means for the being the doctrine names has to be settled. To do is to act, and to act is to transition from a state in which the action does not obtain to one in which it does (T), to bear on something distinct from oneself (S), through a substantive being that performs the action (Φ). [§6.7.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-1) works the doing-question for the predicate *power*; the present pressure returns the worked result. The Thomistic resolution distinguishes God's act from creaturely acts and applies the verb *do* analogically rather than univocally [Aquinas, *ST* I.45; @burrell1986]. The analogical reply preserves the verbal predicate by registering that what *do* names in God is not what *do* names in creatures. What it does not preserve is the contentful relation between the doing and any manner-of-doing descriptor. If *do* applies analogically rather than univocally, then *do well* and *do badly* apply analogically rather than univocally, and the contrast that gives the manner-of-acting predicates their content has been displaced by the analogical move. The question *Can God do good things?* dissolves into the question *What does 'do' mean for God?*, and the analogical answer to the second leaves the first without a univocal sense to apply. The moral predicates depend on the doing-predicate's univocity for their differential content; the doctrine's analogical resolution preserves the predicate's name at the cost of the contrast that makes the predicate's modification informative.

**Q2.** *How is one timeless act good, if it sustains the world's evil no less than its good?* The classical doctrine holds God as *actus purus*: pure act, without potency, without unrealized capacity (*ST* I.3.1–2; I.9.1). The most thoroughgoing reading takes God's act as one eternal, all-encompassing, all-sustaining act in which the distinction between creating, conserving, and concurring collapses into a single divine doing [@stumpKretzmann1981; @leftow1991]. The concern here is what this does to moral differentiation. Goodness, in the contentful sense the doctrine wants, requires the differential preference of one outcome over an alternative: an act is benevolent because it prefers the good of its target over the not-good. Pure act, taken strictly, has no alternatives to prefer among, since alternatives are differentiations within the modal field the doctrine has placed beyond the divine being ([§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1)). The pressure sharpens at the consequence side. One eternal act that sustains all things sustains them indiscriminately; what is sustained includes what the doctrine elsewhere calls evil: the suffering of creatures, the disorder of the natural world, the moral failures of finite agents. If divine sustaining is one pure act, the same act sustains the good things and the bad things, and the doctrine has no resource for differentiating the act's relation to the good consequences from its relation to the bad. The classical reply distinguishes God's permitting evil from God's directly willing evil [Aquinas, *ST* I.19.9; @stump1985; @stump2010 on the theodicy literature]. The reply preserves God from authorship of evil at the cost of partitioning the single pure act into a willing-part (the good) and a permitting-part (the evil). Strict simplicity disallows the partition; loose simplicity surrenders the unity of the act on which the impeccability claim rested. The doctrine wants pure-act unity *and* moral differentiation *and* impeccability simultaneously, and these are three commitments joined only by the term *one act*. The ordinary-morality form of this pressure — that our duty to intervene in preventable suffering does not lapse when the sufferer's greater good is invoked — is run against divine non-intervention at [§6.9.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-2) (Q7).

**Q3.** *How can a being do every possible thing, yet not the evil that creatures plainly can?* The modest apologetic position takes omnipotence to mean *can do all possible things* and treats *cannot do evil* as a separate impeccability claim. The two commitments conflict directly. Doing evil is possible — humans do evil constantly, so the possibility is empirically demonstrated and modally uncontroversial. If God can do all possible things, God can do evil. The classical replies fork.

The privation-of-evil reply (Augustine, *Enchiridion* III–IV; Aquinas, *De Malo* I) holds that evil is not a positive capacity but a defect of right action, and God's incapacity for evil is the absence of a defect rather than the absence of a capacity. The reply faces three independent pressures, each at a different theoretical level, and each forcing a concession the doctrine elsewhere refuses.

*The modal-priority pressure.* The privation account, examined modally, admits subset structure on the possibility-field. If doing-evil is a defect-region of the modal field that God's nature excludes, the field has good-regions and defect-regions, and the doctrine's being is restricted to the good-region. The pressure sharpens via the only contingent act the doctrine attributes to God: creation. If God can only do possible things and God creates the universe, then universe-creation is possible, and universe-creation's being possible is prior to its happening, since the possible must be in place for the doing of the possible to be done. The possibility-space pre-exists the universe whose creation it permits. Possibility is not what the universe brings about; possibility is what creation-of-the-universe presupposes. The [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10) result is reached through Commitment B alone, without the stronger source-of-possibility argument [§5.1.8](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-8) contests. The proper-subset claim follows from the empirical anchor. Humans actually do evil (destruction, deceit, cruelty, betrayal) and what humans actually do is, by minimal modal principle, possible. If God cannot do evil and humans can, the set of possible things God can do is a *proper subset* of the set of possible things. Contingent beings populate regions of the possibility-space the doctrine's God cannot enter. The doctrine has conceded that possibility is *both* prior to creation *and* more inclusive than divine action, and the conjunction is what externality of the modal field looks like when read at full strength.

*The doctrinal-interlock pressure.* The privation account, examined against other classical attributes, contradicts the conjunction of simplicity and omnipresence. The doctrine holds (i) God is goodness itself: *bonitas ipsa*, identical with the divine nature on simplicity (*ST* I.6.3); (ii) evil is the privation of due-good (the present reply); (iii) God is omnipresent: present whole in every place (*ST* I.8). From (i) and (ii): evil is the privation of God-himself, since God is goodness. Wherever there is evil there is an absence of God. From (iii): God is not absent anywhere. Conjunction: there is no privation of God anywhere, hence no evil anywhere. But evil exists. The doctrine has to give up one of the three. Giving up (i) loses simplicity in its strong sense: [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) has already inverted that, and the give-up here would be a doctrinal retreat the [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) inversion forecloses. Giving up (ii) abandons the privation theory itself and forces a positive account of evil whose either arm (evil is being God sustains, or evil is being God does not sustain) is exactly the externality concession the modal-priority pressure already extracted. Giving up (iii) qualifies omnipresence by stratifying presence into modes (present-by-essence, present-by-power, present-by-grace, on the Thomistic distinction) and admits there are dimensions of divine presence that fail somewhere, which is what omnipresence-in-the-strong-sense denies. [§6.8.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-1) develops the inversion of omnipresence at the structural level; the present pressure works the converse direction, using omnipresence-as-asserted-by-the-doctrine to destroy the privation defense the doctrine elsewhere needs.

*The internal-structural pressure.* The privation account, examined as a representation of the moral domain, is structurally binary: it divides acts into *good* (positive instantiation of due-being) and *not-good* (privation, deficiency, the absence of due-being read as evil). The moral domain, as it actually shows up, is at least ternary. There is *maintenance*: acts that positively contribute to other subjects' subsistence-conditions (the contentful good). There is *non-engagement*: acts that bear on no other subject's subsistence-conditions, neither contributing nor violating (the vast bulk of human action, and the morally neutral region). There is *violation*: acts that positively interfere with other subjects' subsistence-conditions (the contentful evil, structurally distinct from neutral non-engagement). The privation account can represent maintenance and the absence of maintenance, but cannot distinguish non-engagement from violation. Both look like *not-(maintenance)* on the binary scheme. The forks the account takes to recover the distinction each cost a load-bearing commitment.

*Fork A.* Treat all *not-(maintenance)* as evil. Then every act that fails to maintain another subject's subsistence is evil, most of life becomes evil, and the absurdity is one the doctrine elsewhere refuses. *Fork B.* Appeal to *due-good* — privation is the absence of *due-good*, where some goods are due and others are not. The fork relocates the explanatory work to the *due* structure, but the *due* structure is a positive moral fact (it says *X is owed to Y in conditions Z*) and the privation theory was supposed to make evil parasitic on good without admitting positive moral facts beyond goodness. The reduction has failed. *Fork C.* Distinguish non-engagement from violation by appealing to *positive intent* or *positive willing-toward-harm*. This is the most direct contradiction. The theory's purpose was to deny that evil has positive ontological status; distinguishing violation from neutrality by *the positive presence of harm-directed willing* concedes exactly the positive ontological status the theory was built to refuse. The internal-structural pressure compounds with a related relocation. Privation theory locates evil in the *victim's deficiency* rather than in the *agent's positive act and intent*. The moral phenomenology runs the other way: moral attribution puts evil in the agent's willing-toward-violation, with the victim's resulting deficiency as the consequence rather than the evil. Privation theory either accepts the inversion (against the phenomenology) or rejects it (and loses its theoretical character).

The three pressures converge. The privation account admits modal externality with subset structure (modal-priority pressure), contradicts simplicity-plus-omnipresence (doctrinal-interlock pressure), and cannot represent the categorical distinction between non-engagement and violation without surrendering its own ontological commitment (internal-structural pressure). Each pressure is independent (works at a different theoretical level, uses different doctrinal commitments, exposes a different structural feature of the reply) and each forces a concession the doctrine elsewhere refuses.

The essentially-good reply [@morris1991; @plantinga1980 on God's nature] holds that *possible-for-God* is indexed to God's nature, so what is possible-for-creatures-but-not-for-God is not really possible-for-God despite being possible-simpliciter. The fork sharpens. Either *possible-for-God* differs from *possible-simpliciter* (in which case the modal field has nature-relative subsets and the being occupies the subset compatible with the being's nature: the externality concession returns with a region-structure on the field, in the vocabulary of nature-indexed modality rather than defect-region modality, but with the same structural content), or *possible-for-God* coincides with *possible-simpliciter* (in which case God can do evil and impeccability fails). Each escape preserves a commitment at the cost of concession the doctrine elsewhere refuses. Swinburne's theistic personalism [*The Coherence of Theism*, -@swinburne1977, ch. 11] takes a different line to impeccability than either the privation or the essentially-good account. On Swinburne's analysis, divine goodness is a simple, non-relational property of the divine person's nature: not a complex formed from a privation of evil, nor a restricted modal profile over the possibility-space, but a basic feature of a perfectly rational personal agent, analogous to the way an ideally rational agent's character is simply good without that goodness requiring a contrastive range of evil alternatives. The concern for Swinburne's simple-property line is that a *basic property* of a person that explains why the person acts well without ranging over alternatives is either a disposition (a structure of tendencies to act certain ways in certain situations, which imports the directed-transition structure T, S, and Φ supply) or a categorical property with no dispositional content (in which case it is unclear how it generates the moral differentiation the believer's confession requires). Swinburne's reply is that personal simplicity (the absence of physical constraints on the will) is what makes the property basic rather than compositional; the structural concern is whether personal simplicity, on the chapter's analysis, escapes the conditions its exercise of will presupposes.

**Q4.** *Whom does God will good toward, if the one willed exists only by being willed?* Benevolence, in the classical formulation, is *amor benevolentiae*: the love of willing-good-toward (*ST* I.20). To will *toward* requires a target distinct from the willer; willing-toward-nothing-distinct is not willing-toward at all. The doctrine places God as the only being whose existence is necessary in itself; creatures are dependent products of divine willing rather than antecedently distinct beings the divine will reaches toward [*ST* I.44; @pruss2011]. The concern here is the order of dependence. If the target of divine willing-toward is itself a product of divine willing, then *willing-toward* names a relation whose target the willing constitutes, and the *toward* is doing different work from what the predicate ordinarily picks out. In the creaturely case the willer encounters an antecedently distinct target and bears willing-toward it. In the divine case the willer constitutes the target in the willing, and the toward-relation is internal to the willing-act rather than reaching across an interval to something antecedently other. The reply that divine love is more than the willing-toward of *amor benevolentiae* (that it is *amor amicitiae*, friendship-love [*ST* I.20.2; @stump2010]) does not relieve the pressure. Friendship-love presupposes two distinct loci who bear the friendship; the structural concern at *amor benevolentiae* is the one at *amor amicitiae* in stronger form, since friendship has tighter relational requirements than mere willing-toward. Hartshorne's dual-transcendence account presses here from the concrete side: the concrete pole's love is *amor benevolentiae* and, in its fuller form, *amor amicitiae* borne toward creatures the divine encounters as antecedently distinct rather than constitutes in the willing: genuinely responsive love, growing with what the world contributes [*The Divine Relativity*, -@hartshorne1948]. The dipolar engine offers exactly the antecedently-distinct target Q4 finds the classical willing-toward to lack; the concern is that the offer concedes the structure it was meant to save. A willing that reaches across an interval to a distinct creaturely target (S), borne by a substantive concrete actuality (Φ) genuinely moved by what it encounters (T), is the manner-of-acting relation the chapter's grammar requires, and a concrete pole bearing it instantiates the structural conditions of a subject among subjects rather than standing beyond them. The engine is pressed in full at Q6, and the pole-relation routed to [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3).

**Q5.** *How is God just or merciful, if there is no act for the justice or mercy to shape?* The seven classical moral predicates (*benevolent*, *just*, *merciful*, *loving*, *patient*, *faithful*, *gracious*) are grammatically adverbial. Each modifies a verb: to act *justly*, to deal *mercifully*, to love *faithfully*, to bear *patiently*. The adverb requires the verb; without the verb there is no act for the manner to characterize. The classical doctrine treats these predicates as features of the divine being rather than as modifiers of divine action: *God is benevolent* as a statement about what God is, not about how God acts [Aquinas, *ST* I.20–21; @stump2010]. The reframing preserves the predicate by relocating it from adverbial to substantive position. The concern here is what the relocation costs. If *benevolent* names a feature of the divine being independent of any acting, the predicate has been emptied of the contrast that makes it informative — to be benevolent rather than malevolent, indifferent, or cruel requires acts whose manner the predicate characterizes, and there is no manner-of-acting where there is no acting. The classical reply that divine manner-of-acting predicates apply *eminenter* (in a higher mode than the creaturely, Aquinas, *ST* I.13.5) is the analogical move Q1 already engages. The grammatical pressure returns: the *eminent* mode of a manner-of-acting predicate is still a manner-of-acting predicate, and the conditions of acting are still required for the predicate to bear content.

**Q6.** *What does calling God good rule out, if God could not have been otherwise?* Goodness, on the classical reading, is what God is: *bonitas ipsa*, goodness itself, identical with the divine nature on simplicity (*ST* I.6.3). The concern here is what *good* picks out absent the contrastive structure of alternative goods. Good is good-rather-than-evil and good-rather-than-not-good and good-of-this-kind-rather-than-good-of-that-kind. Without alternatives the predicate can range over, *good* loses the contrast that gives it differential content. The classical reply on simplicity grants the result and reframes: God *is* the standard against which goods are measured, not a being who instantiates the standard among other instantiations [@stump2010; @adams1999 on the divine command tradition]. The reframing relocates the predicate to the function of standard-bearing rather than of attribute-instantiation. The concern returns at the relocation. A standard against which alternatives are measured is a structure that presupposes the range of alternatives the measurement applies to, and a being identical with the standard has been identified with that range-relative structure rather than placed outside it. The necessity-cannot-transfer-to-a-being result of [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) applies here in moral form: the modal status of being the standard belongs to the range within which standardhood is exercised, not to a being beyond that range. The relocation has a consequence for the speech act the predicate performs. If *good* is identified with the divine being rather than instantiated by it, then *God is good* no longer ascribes a property the being could fail to have; it reports that the being is identical with itself. The sentence keeps the surface grammar of a moral predication — subject, copula, evaluative predicate — while its content collapses into the tautology *God is God*, or, where goodness is read through the commands the being issues, *God commands what God commands*. What is left for the sentence to do, once its descriptive content is spent, is not to evaluate but to avow: *God is good* functions as a declaration of allegiance to the being so named, a loyalty-claim in the costume of a moral claim. The shift is detectable by a test the moral predicate ordinarily passes and this one cannot: that one can specify, in advance and independently, what would count against it. *This act is good* is a moral claim when there is a manner-of-acting it could have failed to exhibit; *God is good*, on the standard-bearing reading, admits no such failure-condition, because the standard cannot diverge from itself. A predicate that cannot in principle be withheld is not being applied but pledged. The *Euthyphro dilemma* (is an act good because God commands it, or commanded because it is already good?) marks the same fork from the command side; the present point is its predication-side form: what the affirmation *is doing* once goodness has been identified with its own measure. Adams's resemblance account [@adams1999] is the reply built precisely to keep *God is good* contentful without a contrastive range, and it must be met rather than passed over. On Adams's theistic Platonism, *good* names resemblance to God, the transcendent Good in which finite goods participate, so that *God is good* is not the tautology *God is God* but the substantive claim that God is the paradigm the resemblance-relation is fixed to: a claim with content, on Adams's telling, because the respects in which finite things count as resembling are drawn from our independent grasp of the goods we already recognize. The reply turns on what fixes those respects, and the fork is the section's. Either the resemblance-base is the determinate features our paradigm goods actually exhibit — kindness shown, debts rendered, mercy borne — in which case the respects are manner-of-acting features, and a paradigm that exemplifies them is a being that acts well: one that does good, borne by a substantive agent (Φ) toward a distinct recipient (S) across the vector from not-done to done (T), which is a subject acting within Nature rather than a being beyond it. Or the resemblance-base is left formal — resemblance to God in whatever respects the divine goodness consists in, respects not specifiable in advance from the finite side — in which case *resembles God* supplies no failure-condition after all: nothing determinate is fixed that a candidate good could be found to match or fail to match, and the contentful predication the account promised slides back into the avowal the tautology charge identified. The resemblance account does not escape the fork between manner-of-acting content and empty self-identity; it restates the fork in the idiom of participation. Swinburne's cumulative-case framework [*The Existence of God*, -@swinburne1979; -@swinburne2004] challenges Q6's modal analysis directly. On Swinburne's account, divine goodness need not be grounded in a contrastive range; it is a probability-raiser for theism: the fact that God is perfectly good makes the existence of a morally ordered universe more probable than it would be on any naturalistic hypothesis, and the goodness of the God who explains the universe is assessed by its explanatory power rather than against a contrastive range of bad-alternatives. The concern for the Swinburnian reframing is whether the probability-raising relation is itself a structural relation: for the hypothesis *God is perfectly good* to make the existence of a morally ordered universe more probable than its rival, the hypothesis must have content (it must specify what a good God would produce) and specifying what a good God would produce requires ranging over the alternatives the modal field provides, which is the contrastive range Q6 identified as the condition of the predicate's informativeness. Hartshorne's dual-transcendence engine challenges Q6's analysis at its root, denying that divine goodness must be grounded in the way the Anselmian engine grounds it. Where the classical engine generates perfection as *actus purus* (the good a being *is*, complete and unsurpassable), dual transcendence redefines perfection as surpassing all others while remaining surpassable only by oneself [*Man's Vision of God*, -@hartshorne1941; *Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes*, -@hartshorne1984]: the abstract pole is the invariant standard of value, and the concrete pole is good by *responsively* willing the richest integration of what the world has actually contributed, surpassing every other and surpassable only by the divine self at a later, fuller moment. The engine is built precisely to restore the failure-condition the standard-bearing reading loses: the concrete pole *could* love less responsively than it does, and is good rather than merely self-identical because it does not. The concern is that the restoration concedes the chapter's result in the idiom of process. A goodness that ranges over alternatives, prefers the richer integration to the poorer, and grows in responsive love is a manner of acting borne by a substantive concrete actuality (Φ), reaching toward antecedently distinct creaturely targets (S), across the temporal vector from not-yet-responded to responded (T); the concrete pole is good in exactly the sense the manner-of-acting grammar requires, and in being so instantiates the structural conditions of a subject acting on subjects, not those of a being beyond them. The abstract pole, meanwhile, inherits Q6's standard-bearing verdict unchanged: an invariant standard of value presupposes the range of alternatives the measurement applies to, and the necessity-cannot-transfer-to-a-being result of [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) holds here in moral form; the modal status of being the standard belongs to the range within which standardhood is exercised, not to an abstract pole that bears no responsive acting and is therefore no candidate for a manner-of-acting predicate at all. Binding the unsurpassable standard to the responsive lover into one good God is the pole-relation [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3) examines: a directed crossing that obtains only within T, S, and Φ. The dual-transcendence engine does not relocate divine goodness beyond Nature; it describes, in the idiom of process, what goodness is when subjects responsively maintain one another within Nature.

**Q7.** *How is God incapable of evil, if evil is never a possibility for God to begin with?* Impeccability is the doctrine that God cannot sin [*ST* I.25.3 ad 2; @morris1991; @pawl2016]. The concern here follows from Q3's fork. If impeccability means *God's nature excludes the evil-region of the modal field*, then the modal field has structure that includes evil as a region, and the doctrine has admitted modal externality with extra structure (Q3 fork option 1). If impeccability means *evil is not possible-for-God in the sense relevant to omnipotence*, then either evil is not really possible (which is empirically false, since humans do evil constantly) or *possible-for-God* is distinct from *possible-simpliciter*, which is the same fork in different vocabulary. Beyond Q3's structural concession, impeccability faces an internal-coherence problem at the conditions of the predicate. To be incapable of evil is to be in a structured relation to evil — namely, the relation of incapacity. The relation requires that evil be a candidate the incapacity-relation could in principle hold of; a being to whom evil is in no sense a candidate is not *incapable* of evil but simply *outside the range within which evil is a candidate*. Impeccability either names the structured relation of nature-restricted incapacity (admitting the externality of the modal field's evil-region) or names the absence of the range within which evil could be a candidate (in which case the being is amoral rather than impeccable, and the doctrine has changed register without admitting the change).

*What is required.* The seven pressures, read together, lay bare what the moral predicates the tradition applies to God commit to. *Benevolent*, *just*, *merciful*, *loving*: these are manner-of-acting predicates. They are adverbial in grammar and adverbial in content. They require an acting they modify, and an acting requires the conditions of action: a substantive being who acts (Φ), a target distinct from the actor (S), a temporal direction from not-acting to acting (T). The doctrine of God-as-without-the-structural-conditions has removed precisely what the moral predicates' grammar requires for their content. The reframings that preserve the predicates' names (relocating them from adverbial to substantive position, applying them analogically, indexing their possibility to divine nature, identifying the being with the standard against which alternatives are measured) preserve the verbal predicates at the cost of the structure their content runs on. What goodness picks out, properly read, is the modal status of properly-maintained-mutual-subsistence: the structural feature of subjects acting on subjects to keep each other in being under the symmetry-of-extraction commitment (the Modal Convergence Theorem; the Subsistence definition; Chapter 9 develops the political form). Goodness is what Nature does when subsistence runs at all. The moral predicates apply to the structural feature of subject-on-subject action, not to a being from which the conditions of acting have been stripped.

*What is inverted.* The English *benevolent* renders the Latin *bene volens*: *well-willing*. The compound names a manner of willing (*bene*, well) plus the act of willing (*volens*, the present participle of *velle*, to will). Set back into the structure that hosts it, *benevolent* is doubly conditioned: *bene* requires the contrastive range of good-rather-than-not-good for the manner to be informative, and *volens* requires the substantive willer (Φ), the target distinct from the willer (S), and the temporal vector from not-willing to willing (T) for the act to be performed. The compound predicate that names the maximum of moral character in classical theism is etymologically a compressed description of T, S, and Φ acting under the symmetry-of-extraction commitment. The Greek parallel runs the same way: *agathos* (good) in its Homeric sense names the quality of an agent in action; *kalon kagathon* names the unity of fine action and good action; the noun *aretē* names the excellence-in-doing of which the moral predicates are differential modes. The vocabulary of moral character, in both linguistic traditions the doctrine draws on, is built from the conditions of action. The classical predicate has been pointing, across its formulations, at the structural feature of subjects acting on subjects to keep each other in being while the doctrine has located that feature in a being from which the conditions that constitute it have been removed. Nature has the moral status; the being beyond Nature is not a candidate for it. The structural result is this: the doctrine's God is not malevolent, not benevolent, not indifferent in any positive sense; the being is outside the range in which moral predicates have purchase, and what those predicates actually pick out is what Nature is when subjects mutually maintain one another.

### 6.9.2 Righteousness {#sec-6-9-2}

To be just is to render to each what is owed: a manner of *giving*, which needs a giver, a recipient, and a before-and-after. With those removed, *God is just* loses its grip, and the doctrines built on it (atonement, inherited guilt, final judgment) inherit the difficulty.

*What the tradition holds.* The classical doctrine of divine justice assembles several reinforcing claims. God is *iustus* (just) and *iustitia* is among the divine names, identical with the divine essence on classical simplicity [@augustine416, VIII.6; @aquinas1947, I.21; Anselm, *Monologion* 16]. Justice in the classical sense is *suum cuique tribuere*, the rendering to each of what is owed [Ulpian, *Digesta* I.1.10, taken up into Christian moral theology at @aquinas1947, II-II.58.1]. The doctrine extends the predicate eminently across commutative, distributive, and retributive senses [@aquinas1947, II-II.61], and pairs it with the doctrine of impeccability: God is *incapax peccandi*, incapable of injustice as of any other moral evil [@aquinas1947, I.25.3 ad 2; @morris1991; @pawl2016].

Divine justice co-instantiates with divine mercy without contradiction [@aquinas1947, I.21.3–4; @anselm1098, I.12, II.20; @stump2018 develops the contemporary form]. Mercy itself is among the divine names: *misericordia*, the heart-toward-misery, identical with the divine essence on simplicity [@aquinas1947, I.21.3; @aquinas1947, II-II.30; Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 102.8]. The Islamic tradition opens every Qur'anic surah but one with *al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm* (the Compassionate, the Merciful) and reads the names as *dhātī*, essential rather than accidental [al-Ghazālī, *al-Maqṣad al-Asnā*; @murataChittick1994]. The Hebrew Bible pairs *ḥesed* (covenant-loyal love) with *raḥamim*, the visceral compassion whose noun-root is *reḥem*, the womb [@sakenfeld1978; @trible1978]. The doctrine holds mercy as a divine perfection co-essential with justice rather than its competitor: the Anselmian and Thomist tradition explicitly denies that mercy diminishes justice or that justice limits mercy [@aquinas1947, I.21.4; @anselm1078, 9–11], and the classical impassibility doctrine reads mercy not as God's *being moved* by misery (the affective pole the predicate carries in its ordinary use) but as the divine *effect* of relieving misery, identical with the divine act [@aquinas1947, I.21.3; @pawl2016; @creel1986].

The classical atonement extends justice's reach across persons: Christ's death satisfies the demands of divine justice on behalf of the guilty [@anselm1098, II; @aquinas1947, III.46–49; for contemporary defenses, @swinburne1989; @crisp2020; @stump2018]. The doctrine of original sin extends justice's domain backward through generations: humans inherit guilt and corruption from Adam's act [@augustine413, XIII.14; @aquinas1947, I-II.81; @edwards1758; for contemporary discussion, @rea2007; @couenhoven2013]. Each covenant is a distinct dispensation of the same eternal justice [@aquinas1947, I-II.107; @calvin1559, II.10–11]. The eschatological judgment renders the same justice across all who have ever lived [@aquinas1947, Suppl. 88; for contemporary form, @walls1992].

The Jewish and Islamic traditions develop parallel claims: the Hebrew *ṣedeq* / *ṣedāqāh* names the right-ordering of communal life under covenant [@koch1953; @weinfeld1995]; the divine name *al-ʿAdl* (the Just) is held in the Muʿtazilī reading to be *dhātī*: essential to the divine being [@hourani1985]. The doctrine, at its most ambitious, names a being whose moral character renders the moral order itself (whose justice is not a property had alongside other properties but the structural truth about how moral reality is constituted) and whose every act toward creation, including those acts the believer finds difficult, is therefore necessarily just.

*What cannot be answered.* Eight questions take the doctrine of divine justice past what it can answer once recast in the form structural reasoning works with. Underneath, the concern is structural: the one the chapter has been pressing through the preceding attributes. *Just*, *merciful*, *equitable*, *fair*, *righteous* (the moral predicates the tradition applies to God) are manner-of-acting predicates. *Iustitia* in the classical sense, *suum cuique tribuere*, is a manner of giving; and giving requires the conditions of action: a substantive agent who gives (Φ), a target distinct from the giver who receives (S), and a temporal direction from not-giving to giving (T). The doctrine has defined the being whose actions the predicates describe as without T, S, or Φ. The eight pressures run at the level of what such a being can bear in the way of *justice*-predication at all, and at the level of what the auxiliary doctrines of atonement, original sin, covenant, and final judgment commit when the conditions the predicates depend on are taken seriously.

**Q1.** *Can mercy and justice co-instantiate?* The classical doctrine holds God as perfectly just and perfectly merciful, with no diminution of either by the other [@aquinas1947, I.21.3–4; @anselm1098, I.12, II.20]. The concern here is the content of the two predicates. Justice, in the sense the doctrine wants, renders to each what is owed; mercy suspends or remits what is owed in favor of unearned good. The two predicates name opposed directions of moral motion on the same input: justice tracks desert; mercy tracks gift-against-desert. The Anselmian reply (that mercy operates within justice, since Christ's satisfaction pays the debt justice requires) preserves co-instantiation by relocating mercy from *suspension* of justice to *means* of justice. The relocation costs the predicate's ordinary grammar. Mercy, on the reframing, is no longer the unearned remission of debt; it is the redirection of debt to a third party. The structure of *gift-against-desert* has been replaced by the structure of *transactional substitution*, and the substitution's evaluation as just is the very question Q4 takes up. Stump's contemporary development [@stump2018] handles the tension by identifying mercy with second-personal love that, in seeking the beloved's good, includes the work of restoring desert-relations the beloved has violated. The structural concern returns: second-personal love, on the analysis [§6.8.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-2) runs, requires the relational structure between distinct loci the doctrine elsewhere has factored out. The two attributes co-instantiate at the cost of relocating one or both of them past the contrast that gave them informative content. Three further pressures on mercy-predication sharpen the same concern.

*The impassibility pressure.* *Misericordia*, on its ordinary grammar, is *cor ad miseriam*: heart-toward-misery, the structure of being-moved-by another's suffering. The classical doctrine of divine impassibility holds God as *actus purus*, not subject to being moved by anything outside the divine essence [@aquinas1947, I.9; @weinandy2000; @dolezal2017]. The two grammars conflict on the affective pole: mercy in its first-person human use names *being affected by* the other's state, and impassibility denies the affective structure. Aquinas's reply [@aquinas1947, I.21.3] preserves co-instantiation by reading divine mercy as the *effect* alone — God produces the relief of misery without undergoing the being-moved that constitutes mercy in the creaturely case. The relocation costs the predicate's structure: mercy without the affective pole is the verbal predicate without the structure that gives it content; what remains is a class of effects classified after the fact as merciful, not the manner-of-being-moved the predicate ordinarily reports. The reply parallels the move [§6.8.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-2) identifies on *love* (the second-personal structure factored out) and the move Q7 below identifies on *just* (the discernment factored out): preserving the verbal predicate by removing the relational condition the predicate's content runs on. @mullins2016 develops the contemporary form of the impassibility-mercy tension; the contemporary defenses [@dolezal2017; @helm2010] preserve impassibility by accepting Aquinas's effect-only reading, which is to accept that *mercy*-predication, on the doctrine, names something different from what it names in the cases that gave the predicate its content.

*The grace–mercy distinction.* The tradition often treats mercy and grace as overlapping divine acts toward the unworthy, but the structural difference matters for predication. Mercy responds to misery: its target is the suffering subject, and its act is the relief of suffering. Grace, in the strict sense, is unmerited favor whose ground is not the recipient's state at all but the giver's free generosity [@aquinas1947, I-II.110–111; @barth1932, IV/1]. If divine mercy is genuinely mercy in the substantive sense, it requires the relational structure of object-in-misery; if it collapses into grace (gift-without-precondition) then *mercy* is the wrong name for what the doctrine picks out, and the contentful relation between the predicate and the structural feature its vocabulary tracks has been silently swapped. The doctrine cannot have both a strong mercy whose object-of-misery structure runs and a strong grace whose ground is the giver alone without admitting that what the tradition calls *mercy* is, at the level of structure, grace operating on a recipient who happens to be in misery: a different relation under a borrowed name.

*The necessity-of-misery horn.* If mercy is a necessary divine attribute and mercy requires recipients-in-misery, the field horns from Q2 sharpen further on the mercy side. The intra-Trinitarian construal that handles justice (Q2, horn three) cannot run for mercy: the Trinitarian persons are not in misery, and the predicate's object-condition is not met. The field-co-necessity horn that conflicts with creation-ex-nihilo on the justice side conflicts more sharply on the mercy side, because what becomes co-necessary with the attribute is not merely *recipients-with-dues* but *recipients-in-misery*: the doctrine inherits a necessary field of suffering as the ontological condition of the divine attribute, which the standard theodicy literature treats as the result to be avoided rather than embraced. The horns that remain (contingency of exercise or mere disposition) weaken the necessary-attribute claim on the mercy side in the same way they do on the justice side, and with a sharper bite, because mercy without recipients-in-misery has no Trinitarian-internal escape of the same kind.

**Q2.** *Does justice admit application without a field of objects?* Justice, in the classical sense, is *suum cuique tribuere*: the predicate is structurally tri-place, requiring an agent who renders, a recipient to whom rendering is owed, and the due that is rendered. The doctrine holds justice as a *necessary* divine attribute, identical with the divine essence on simplicity [@aquinas1947, I.21.1]. The concern here is the modal status of the field.
