The necessity has to be pinned down before the horns bite: read *de dicto* (necessarily, justice-if-instantiated requires recipients-with-dues), the claim is the innocuous conditional the horns work on; read *de re* (there is a field of recipients-with-dues that exists necessarily), it just is horn one, which collapses creation into necessity. The doctrine wants the *de re* strength (a genuinely necessary attribute with real relata) at the *de dicto* price, and that gap is what the four horns exploit. If justice is necessary and justice requires recipients-with-dues, then one of these horns must give. *Horn one.* Recipients-with-dues are necessary too: the field is co-necessary with the attribute. The horn collapses creation into necessity and conflicts with creation-ex-nihilo, the doctrine's standing position on contingent creation [@pruss2011; [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2) develops the unity-side correlate]. *Horn two.* Recipients-with-dues are contingent, and the attribute's exercise is contingent on them; what is necessary is the *disposition* to render rather than the rendering. The horn weakens the strong-necessity claim and surrenders the contentful relation between the predicate and any divine doing: the disposition's name without its exercise. *Horn three.* The field is internal: the Trinity renders dues among its persons, and the modal status of justice rides on the necessity of the intra-Trinitarian relations rather than the necessity of any external recipient. The construal Aquinas in places suggests [@aquinas1947, I.21.1 ad 3] preserves the necessary attribute at the cost of whether *due-ness* among consubstantial persons retains the contrastive structure justice requires: the persons' shared essence factors out the relational asymmetry on which *suum cuique* runs. *Horn four.* Justice is a mere disposition without necessary instantiation. The horn retains the verbal predicate at the cost of the contentful relation between the predicate and any divine act. The four horns together cover the available options on the modal status of justice's field, and each costs a load-bearing commitment elsewhere. The necessity-cannot-transfer-to-a-being result of [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) applies in justice form: the modal status of a tri-place relational structure belongs to the field within which the relation obtains, not to a relatum stipulated outside the field.

**Q3.** *Does universal desert preserve the predicate's informativeness?* The Christian doctrine of universal sinfulness [Romans 3:23 NRSVUE; @augustine413, XIV; @calvin1559, II.1; for contemporary discussion, @couenhoven2013] holds that every human, from the fall onward, stands in a state of culpable corruption. The doctrine has structural consequence for justice-predication. If every human deserves condemnation, then every act of divine condemnation (from natural death to plague to flood to eternal punishment) is the rendering of due. The verdict, in the doctrine's strong form, is uniform across input. The concern here is what *justice* picks out under a uniform-verdict regime. A predicate that returns the same value across every input is not tracking the structural feature the predicate is supposed to track; it is a constant function whose name still carries the appearance of differential content. The classical reply (that justice operates within the *category* of the deserved, and that mercy is what differentiates outcomes within that category) relocates the differential work from justice to mercy, and concedes that justice itself is not the locus of moral information about divine action. What *justice* does, on the relocation, is set the categorical floor against which the only contentful moral attribute (mercy) operates; what *justice predicates* is the floor's universal applicability rather than any differential rendering. The doctrine has preserved the predicate's name and surrendered its informative content. The structural cost compounds when the move is paired with Q7: the believer who cannot discern divine reasons cannot discern *which* punishments fall within universal desert as opposed to outside it, and the floor's name is the only thing the predicate carries.

**Q4.** *Can guilt transfer across substantive bearers?* The doctrine of penal substitution (that Christ's death satisfies divine justice on behalf of guilty humanity) requires guilt to move between persons. Five moves license the transfer; each has structural cost. *The imputation move* [federal-Reformed; @murray1955; @crisp2020] treats guilt as a legal property reckoned to Christ and righteousness as a legal property reckoned to the believer. The concern here is what *reckoning* names. In the human case, reckoning is a courtroom procedure whose justice depends on the reckoning tracking the substantive moral relation between agent and act; reckoning that does not track (that imputes a property whose substantive ground is absent) is what the predicate ordinarily marks as miscarriage. The doctrine preserves transfer by emptying the reckoning of substantive tracking. *The participation move* [mystical-union; @stump2018; Athanasius, *De Incarnatione* on incorporation] treats believers as ontologically united with Christ such that guilt becomes genuinely Christ's and righteousness becomes genuinely theirs. The fork sharpens: either union is metaphysically sufficient to transfer the moral properties (in which case Christ becomes genuinely guilty during the union, and the impeccability claim of Q3-at-[§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1) fails for the duration), or union is metaphorical (in which case reckoning has returned in disguise). *The consent move* [@anselm1098, II.11] treats Christ's willing submission as licensing the substitution. Consent licenses some transactions — gifts, contracts — but consent does not manufacture *desert*, which is the property justice tracks. A judge who accepts a willing volunteer in place of the convicted has not done justice; the judge has substituted a willing victim for a deserved one, and the substitution's voluntariness does not change the verdict's miscarriage. *The satisfaction move* [@anselm1098, I; @swinburne1989] treats the cross as paying a quantitative debt owed to divine honor or moral order. The reframing shifts justice from punishment-of-the-guilty to debt-payment-on-behalf-of-the-guilty; the two are not equivalent moral structures, and treating them as equivalent equivocates on the predicate. *The Christus Victor move* [@aulen1931; @boersma2004] treats the cross as defeat of cosmic powers rather than satisfaction of justice. The justice-language drops out: the cross is rescue, not desert-tracking. The concern across the five moves is the same. Guilt, on the moral phenomenology, is a property of substantive agents whose acts the property tracks; it attaches at Φ. Transfer across Φ-distinctions is what the predicate ordinarily marks as injustice in every other application. The doctrine preserves transfer by relocating *guilt* from agent-tracking property to bookkeeping-property, to courtroom-fiction, to debt-token, or to rescue-narrative. Each relocation preserves the verbal predicate; each surrenders the substantive structure justice was supposed to track.

**Q5.** *Can culpability attach without action?* The doctrine of original sin [@augustine413, XIII.14; @aquinas1947, I-II.81; for contemporary discussion, @rea2007; @couenhoven2013] holds that humans are culpable, from conception, for an act they did not perform. The concern here is the relation between culpability and action. Culpability, on the moral phenomenology, tracks the agent's action: A is culpable for X just in case A performed X under conditions of knowledge and freedom that license the attribution. The doctrine relocates culpability past the conditions of agent-action: A is culpable for B's act in virtue of A's metaphysical, biological, or representational relation to B. Three accounts try to license the relocation. *The federal-headship account* [Reformed; @edwards1758; @murray1959] treats Adam as legal representative. The disanalogy with human representation is decisive against the move: representation in human politics requires either consent of the represented or exit-availability under the system the representative acts within; Adamic representation supplies neither. Representation without consent or exit is conscription, which is the moral structure the relocation was supposed to avoid. *The seminal-realism account* (Augustinian-Traducianist) treats human beings as metaphysically present in Adam at the time of the act. The account requires (i) the metaphysical claim that potential persons share in actual persons' acts, which generalizes to make every descendant complicit in every ancestor's act, and (ii) the moral claim that seminal presence licenses culpability, which is just to redefine culpability away from the action-condition the predicate ordinarily tracks. *The inherited-corruption account* (some Arminian and Orthodox readings) treats humans as inheriting a *condition* (concupiscence, mortality) but not *guilt*; subsequent acts under the condition generate the culpability. The account is the most morally defensible, but it (a) shifts the doctrine substantially from its Augustinian-Reformed form, and (b) leaves a different injustice in place: why is *the condition itself* just, if no act of the condition's bearer brought it about? The bite case the doctrine constructs to handle is the unevaluated death of children: in flood, in plague, in famine, in eternity. Strong original-sin makes the death deserved; weaker original-sin makes the death undeserved suffering of a condition the sufferer did not author. Either horn is an injustice on the standard moral phenomenology; the doctrine selects the horn by selecting the version of the doctrine, not by removing the structural problem. The abstract-versus-narrative question this case raises — whether the dead-children horn is met by structural analysis or owes theodicy-through-narrative — is addressed methodologically at [§6.9.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-9-1): the preclusion runs prior to narrative theodicy and holds however it fares.

**Q6.** *Does the predicate retain identity across the covenants?* The Hebrew Bible records, and in places commands, acts the New Testament's ethic and contemporary moral intuition classify as deeply unjust: the *ḥērem* (the ban: total destruction devoted to God) warfare of the conquest (Joshua 6, 10; Deuteronomy 20), the destruction of Amalek including women and children (1 Samuel 15), the slaughter of Midianite captives (Numbers 31), capital punishment for Sabbath violation (Numbers 15:32–36) and for cursing parents (Exodus 21:17). The doctrine holds the same God, with the same justice, at work across the Old and New Testaments [@aquinas1947, I-II.107; @calvin1559, II.10–11]. The concern here is whether *just* names the same property at both temporal indices. Four moves try to preserve identity-across-time. *The progressive-revelation move* [developed in different forms by Origen and Wesley; for contemporary versions, @copan2011; @flannagan2014] holds that God's commands accommodate the moral capacity of the age. If the underlying moral facts are eternal, the move forks: either the OT commands were unjust by the eternal standard (and God commanded injustice), or the NT ethic is a leniency relative to the eternal standard (and Christ countermanded what justice required). Either horn surrenders the moral character of one of the Testaments. *The dispensational move* [covenant-administrative; for contemporary versions, @saucy1993] holds that the standard is constant but its administration differs by covenant. The reply rescues immutability of the standard at the cost of the means question: an omnipotent agent had alternative means to the pedagogical or covenantal ends, and the chosen means (mass killing including non-combatants) require positive justification beyond the dispensational frame. *The accommodation-rhetorical move* [developed in ancient-Near-Eastern–contextual readings; for contemporary form, @lamb2022; @earl2010] holds that the conquest narratives are ANE military rhetoric rather than literal command. The move dissolves the most acute cases at the cost of a general result: the texts long held as divine commands are conceded not to have been divine commands, and the selection criterion for which texts are accommodation and which are not cannot be *the ones we find morally tolerable* without making the reader the authority over the text. *The prerogative move* (God, as creator, has authority over creaturely life that humans lack) is the discernment-collapse horn (Q7) in another form. If *just*, predicated of God, tracks compatibility-with-divine-prerogative rather than the structural feature the predicate ordinarily tracks, then the predicate's content has been emptied; the predicate now reports something trivially true given the definition. The four moves together cover the available options, and each costs a load-bearing commitment elsewhere.

**Q7.** *Does discernment-collapse leave the affirmation standing?* The standard reply to the moral pressures on divine action runs through skeptical theism [@wykstra1984; @bergmann2001; @howardSnyder2009; for the most developed contemporary form, @bergmann2012]. The believer concedes that some divine actions appear unjust by creaturely standards, and explains the appearance by appeal to the creature's limited epistemic access: we cannot see the divine reasons. The reply preserves *God is just* against the pressure of apparent counter-evidence. The concern here is what the reply commits at the level of affirmation. The affirmation *God is just* is contentful only if the believer can, in principle, discern justice well enough to identify *God is just* as a recognizable claim with definite truth-conditions. If divine action exceeds creaturely capacity for moral evaluation at the level the skeptical-theist reply requires, then *God is just* exceeds creaturely capacity for moral evaluation at the same level, and the affirmation, predicated by the believer, asserts what the believer is in principle unable to discern. The fork is sharp. Either the believer can discern justice well enough to apply the predicate to divine action (in which case the cases that appear unjust bear evidential weight against the predicate's truth, and the skeptical-theist reply fails); or the believer cannot (in which case the predicate's affirmation is the predicate's name without the discernment that gives the name content, and *God is just* is the verbal predicate without the substantive structure it requires). The reply rescues the predicate from counter-evidence at the cost of rescuing it from evidence in general: the affirmation no longer turns on what the believer is in a position to discern, which is what predication ordinarily reports. The dialectic in fact occupies a third position, and it is the least stable of the three: the skeptical discount is applied selectively. The deliverances of moral discernment are retained where they *confirm* the predicate (the acts the believer finds good are counted, without epistemic apology, as evidence of divine goodness) and suspended only where they would *disconfirm* it, the difficult cases alone being reassigned to the inaccessibility of divine reasons. The same faculty is ruled competent in the confirming direction and incompetent in the disconfirming one; the asymmetry is not a second epistemic thesis but the first applied in one direction only. Its effect is to convert *God is just* from a claim whose content is merely hard to verify into one nothing is permitted to count against. A predicate that draws support from the confirming cases while immunizing itself against the disconfirming ones is unfalsifiable in the strict sense (not underdetermined by the evidence but withdrawn from its reach) and an unfalsifiable *just* is the verbal predicate maintained by a rule about which evidence may bear, not by the structural feature the predicate reports.

*The local turn.* The most developed contemporary skeptical theism does not run globally. Bergmann's local thesis [@bergmann2012] grants the believer ordinary moral knowledge intact and confines the skepticism to a single defensible claim: that our sample of the goods, evils, and entailment-relations in the total economy of value is not known to be representative of the whole, so the inference from *we discern no justifying reason* to *there is none* is blocked. Conceded at full strength, the local thesis survives the global fork above — it does not render *God is just* contentless, because it leaves first-order moral discernment standing and withdraws only the inference from non-discernment to the non-existence of reasons. The concern here is what magnitude the representativeness gap is a gap about. *Just*, in the *suum cuique* sense the section has held throughout, is fixed by what is owed to the affected party, the manner in which the act is rendered to the subject who receives it (Φ acting on S), not by the act's standing in the all-things-considered economy of value across the whole. The representativeness gap is a gap about the latter magnitude; granting it in full leaves the act-as-rendered-to-the-party exactly where it stood. To make the local skeptic's gap bite justice-predication, the reply must add that justice-to-a-subject *supervenes on* all-things-considered global value: that whether the child's death is rendered justly to the child depends on goods elsewhere in the economy the child has no part in. That addition is the relocation the section has diagnosed at every prior attribute: it moves *just* off the agent-recipient relation its content runs on and onto a global ledger, and a *just* that tracks the global ledger rather than what is owed the affected party is the predicate's name carried by a different structural feature. The bite cases bite as before: Q3's universal desert, Q5's death of children, Q6's *ḥērem* each press on what is owed the affected party, which the representativeness concession does not touch.

*The intervention parallel.* Maitzen's other signature argument presses the same point from the opposite epistemic end [@maitzen2009]. Where the demographic argument (Q8) and the local skeptic turn on what the believer can and cannot discern, this one stipulates the favorable epistemic case and still bites: grant that the outweighing good is real *and* that the believer has access to it. Ordinary morality (the morality the believer relies on everywhere else) still obliges the bystander who can prevent a child's death from meningitis to prevent it, and does not release the bystander on the ground that the suffering may secure a greater good; the doctor who withholds treatment so that the ordeal may build the patient's character, or another's compassion, has acted wrongly by the standard the believer applies without hesitation in every non-theological case. So the greater-good defense of divine non-intervention forks: either ordinary morality is mistaken about the bystander's obligation (in which case the doctrine rests on overturning a moral datum more certain than any premise of the theodicy that overturns it) or the human/divine parallel breaks, and *just*, said of God's non-intervention, is not *just* in the sense said of the bystander. The fork is the section's fork in intervention form. *Just* is either univocal across the parallel (in which case the obligation that binds the bystander binds the divine agent, and non-intervention is unjust on the shared sense) or equivocal, in which case the predicate said of God has been cut loose from the sense that gave it content. The one principled way to break the parallel without bare equivocation is the prerogative move (that the creator holds an authority over creaturely life the bystander lacks) and that move routes directly back into the prerogative horn of Q6 and the discernment-collapse this question presses: an authority that converts what would otherwise be a failure to render what is owed into a rightful withholding empties *just* of the differential content the predicate reports. The reply generalizes across every *perfect-X* predicate the doctrine applies to God; the treatment of apophasis in [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) identifies the structural form, and the present section identifies its specifically *justice*-form, where the form is most acutely self-undermining because justice is the predicate whose content the difficult-case literature presses on most directly.

*The demonstrated-mechanism sharpening.* The intervention parallel is ordinarily met by conceding that direct intervention on a resistant will might not be available to a being committed to preserving creaturely freedom, an empirical hedge the tradition's own narrative material removes. Exodus states, repeatedly, that God produces Pharaoh's resistance to the request Moses is sent to deliver (Exodus 4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8; see E.1.4, Free-Will Defense), and Romans 9 generalizes the mechanism into standing doctrine — "he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills" (Romans 9:18) — anticipating and overruling, rather than answering, the fairness objection it provokes (9:19–21). Once a tradition's own text reports the mechanism in successful use for a demonstrative purpose against a single ruler, the freedom-preserving hedge is no longer available to explain non-intervention at any later, larger scale: the question is no longer whether direct intervention on a human will is metaphysically available to this God, but why it was exercised for that stake and withheld at every greater one.

*The four-cell breakdown.* Where two human wills stand in live moral conflict — a perpetrator's and a resister's, at any scale — the same mechanism admits exactly four dispositions, and each costs a commitment the doctrine cannot spend twice. God may shape the perpetrator's will alone, which is Pharaoh's case at whatever scale the conflict runs, and makes God the direct author of the harm rather than its permitter. God may shape the resister's will alone, leaving the perpetrator's genuinely free, which requires an unstated selection principle for who receives the intervention and who does not, and cannot consistently credit the resulting courage as the agent's own without also crediting Pharaoh's resistance as his own, since both are installed by the identical mechanism; crediting one as authentic and voiding the other is asymmetric bookkeeping, not a difference in the cases. God may shape neither, leaving both wills free, in which case the intervention parallel above applies at full force, sharpened rather than softened by the demonstrated mechanism: the bystander obligation the believer honors everywhere else binds a God shown willing and able to intervene at far smaller stakes. Or God may shape both, authoring the conflict entire while its participants experience the whole of it, terror and resolve alike, as their own — the one cell in which the good the free-will defense sells (real agency, actually operating, somewhere in the transaction) is not merely outweighed but absent, leaving the suffering with nothing on the other side of the ledger to have purchased at all.

*What recurrent correction concedes.* Independent of which cell obtains in a given case, that the mechanism is exercised at all concedes something about the object it is exercised on. A creation whose ordinary operation reliably produced acceptable outcomes would not require its makers' hand returned to the controls; that it is returned, whenever the doctrine allows itself to say so, reports on the standing adequacy of what was made rather than on the isolated crisis being averted. The point mirrors the one already made of the fall's necessity (E.2.1, The Fall): a transgression that had to happen has no author but the design that required it; a creation that has to be periodically seized and corrected to avert catastrophe has no author, for that recurring fact, but the design that made the seizing necessary.

**Q8.** *Does morally arbitrary distribution of eternal stakes count as just?* Stephen Maitzen's argument from the demographics of theism [@maitzen2006; cf. @schellenberg2007 on hiddenness; @marsh2008] starts from the empirical fact that the distribution of belief in any particular religious tradition tracks geography, era, and family of origin more strongly than it tracks rational inquiry, moral character, or evidential examination. If salvation is gated on belief in specific propositions, and the distribution of belief tracks morally arbitrary facts, then eternal-stakes outcomes are determined by morally arbitrary facts. The tradition's own practice concedes the distribution. A standing Great Commission (the centuries-long project of carrying the message to those who have not received it) is an admission, made in action, that the message has not in fact reached everyone, and that whether a person receives it turns on the contingent arrival of a messenger rather than on anything the person is or does. A ground adequate to its universal task would not require an army of messengers to complete it; that it must be carried concedes that, left to its own sufficiency, it does not arrive. The concern here is the fit between *arbitrary distribution of eternal stakes* and the classical predicate *just*. Five responses are available; each carries cost. *The Molinist response* [@plantinga1974b; @craig1991] holds that God knows what each person would freely do under any circumstance and arranges history so that all who would respond receive opportunity. The response imports the contested metaphysics of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom [the grounding problem; @hasker1989], and entails the conclusion that those born outside the gospel's reach are condemned for *what they would have done* under different conditions: a counterfactual desert structure whose justice is itself open to the present question. *The inclusivist response* [@rahner1976; for contemporary form, @sanders1992] holds that those who respond to whatever light they have are saved by Christ's work without explicit knowledge. The response dilutes the New Testament's apparent insistence on explicit faith (Romans 10; Acts 4:12) and transforms *salvation by faith in Christ* into *salvation by responsiveness*: a different doctrine. *The postmortem-opportunity response* [for contemporary defense, @reichenbach1982; @lindsell1949] holds that those who never heard receive opportunity after death. The response has thin biblical support (1 Peter 3:19 is opaque and contested), undermines the New Testament's stress on this-life response, and raises the question why this-life epistemic conditions are so asymmetric if postmortem opportunity is the real decision-point. *The universalist response* [Origen, *De Principiis* III.6; for contemporary defense, @hart2019] dissolves the eternal-stakes asymmetry by removing the eternal-stakes verdict; the cost is departure from the historical mainstream and a substantial revision of the doctrine of judgment. *The hard-exclusivist response* (those who don't hear are lost; this is just because all deserve condemnation) is the universal-wickedness defense (Q3) deployed at eschatological scale, and carries the same structural cost: under uniform desert, *just* tracks nothing differential. Each response preserves the predicate by paying a doctrinal cost the standard package is unwilling to pay in full; the cumulative effect is that the predicate's application at eternal stakes requires one of universal-wickedness, contested counterfactual metaphysics, dilution of the explicit-faith doctrine, abandonment of this-life urgency, or universalism. The doctrine, in its standard form, cannot afford any of the five; the argument's force is in the cumulative refusal.

*What is required.* Run together, the eight pressures register the structural conditions divine-justice predication depends on. *Just*, *merciful*, *equitable*, *fair*, *righteous* are manner-of-acting predicates whose grammatical content is adverbial: to give *justly*, to render *mercifully*, to judge *fairly*, to act *righteously*. The adverb requires the verb; the verb requires the conditions of action: a substantive agent who acts (Φ), a target distinct from the actor who receives the action (S), a temporal direction from not-acting to acting (T). The classical doctrine has defined the being whose actions the predicates describe as without T, S, or Φ, and has preserved the predicates by relocating them: from adverbial to substantive position, from differential to constant function, from agent-tracking to bookkeeping, from action-condition to representational structure, from time-indexed standard to constant standard under contingent administration, from discernment to skepticism-shielded affirmation, from desert-tracking to arbitrary-distribution-with-doctrinal-cost. Each relocation preserves the predicate's name; each surrenders the structural conditions the predicate's content runs on. The three pressures cluster cleanly. *Transfer.* The mercy-vs-justice tension (Q1), penal substitution (Q4), and hereditary guilt (Q5) require moral properties to move across the very distinctions the predicate's substantive structure depends on: between attributes and between substantive bearers. Either justice is the kind of property that can be transferred (in which case it is closer to a debt-token than to the structural feature *justice* ordinarily picks out), or it is not (in which case the doctrines depending on transfer fail). *Dependence and consistency.* The dependence problem (Q2) and the cross-covenant identity problem (Q6) require either a necessary field of objects (collapsing creation into necessity) or unstable definition across temporal indices (collapsing the predicate into either a changing morality or an empty constancy). *Discernment and arbitrariness.* Universal desert (Q3), discernment-collapse (Q7), and demographic injustice (Q8) push toward the same conclusion: in the standard package, *God is just* is either an unverifiable predicate or a vacuous one. If the believer cannot discern divine justice well enough to verify the affirmation, the predicate reports nothing the believer is in a position to know; if the believer can, the cases that appear unjust enter as evidence against it. What *justice* picks out, properly read, is the structural feature of right-ordering of subjects-acting-on-subjects to keep each other in being under the symmetry-of-extraction commitment (the Modal Convergence Theorem and the Subsistence definition, developed in Chapter 8; Chapter 9 develops the political form). What *mercy* picks out, properly read, is the same structural feature seen from the restoration side: subjects moved by the misery of subjects, acting to return the relational field to right-order when extraction or harm has displaced it. Mercy is the asymmetry-relieving direction within the same symmetry that *just* tracks from the constitution side; the two predicates name the constitution-pole and the restoration-pole of one structural feature, not two competing properties of one substantive bearer. Justice is what Nature does when mutual subsistence runs with proper proportion: when subjects render to subjects what their mutual subsistence requires. The predicate applies to the structural feature of subject-on-subject right-ordering, not to a being from which the conditions of acting have been stripped.

*What is inverted.* The Latin *iustitia* renders the Greek *dikaiosynē*. *Iustitia* compounds *ius* (right, law, what is owed) with the abstract-formation *-itia*; the noun names the practice of giving each what is right. *Ius* itself, on the older comparative reconstruction [@benveniste1969 on Indo-European institutional vocabulary], derives from a root naming *binding* or *the bond*: justice is what binds the social fabric by holding each in proper relation to the others. The Greek *dikaiosynē* compounds *dikaios* (straight, right, conforming to *dikē*) with the abstract-formation *-synē*. *Dikē* itself, on the comparative reconstruction [@chantraine1968], derives from a root naming *pointing* or *direction*: what indicates the path subjects must follow if their actions are to maintain the relational order. The two principal classical vocabularies for the moral predicate the doctrine applies to God are built, in different ways, from the same structural feature: the right-ordering of subjects-acting-on-subjects within the relational field that hosts the action. *Iustitia* names the practice of holding-in-bond; *dikaiosynē* names the practice of straight-pointing within the relational structure. The Hebrew *ṣedeq* / *ṣedāqāh* parallel runs the same way: the noun derives from a root naming straightness or rightness-of-fit and names the structural feature of communal relations rightly ordered [@koch1953; @weinfeld1995]. The vocabulary of justice, across the three traditions the doctrine draws on, is built from the conditions of action and the structural feature of right-ordering within the relational field. The mercy vocabulary runs the same way. The Latin *misericordia* compounds *miseri-* (wretched, in misery) with *cor*, the heart; the noun names the practice of letting the heart be moved toward the wretched. The Greek *eleos* derives, on the comparative reconstruction [@chantraine1968], from a root naming *cry-out* or *lament*: what the sufferer does and what the merciful one responds to. The Hebrew vocabulary doubles. *Ḥesed* names covenant-loyal love, the steadfastness of relational bond under conditions of breakdown [@sakenfeld1978; @glueck1967]; *raḥamim* names visceral compassion, and its noun-root is *reḥem*, the womb: the Hebrew mercy-vocabulary is built from the most embodied relational feature, the maternal interior [@trible1978]. The four classical vocabularies for mercy (*misericordia*, *eleos*, *ḥesed*, *raḥamim*) are built, in different ways, from the same structural feature the justice vocabulary tracks: subjects-acting-on-subjects within the relational field that hosts the action, with mercy naming specifically the restoration-direction within that field. Both predicate-families depend on the same structural conditions, and both run, in their original linguistic forms, through the relational field that the classical doctrine has factored out. The classical predicate has been pointing, across its formulations, at the structural feature of subjects rightly ordering subject-on-subject action while the doctrine has located that feature in a being from which the conditions that constitute it have been removed. Nature, in mutual subsistence under symmetry-of-extraction, is what *just* names; Nature, in the restoration-direction of that same mutual subsistence, is what *merciful* names. The structural result holds for both predicates jointly: the doctrine's God is out of joint with the relational field in which justice and mercy have purchase, neither just nor unjust, neither merciful nor unmerciful in any positive sense, but outside the conditions under which the predicates have differential content. What the predicates actually pick out is what Nature is when subjects rightly maintain one another and rightly restore one another.

## 6.10 No Exit {#sec-6-10}

Faced with the structural account, the classical theist has three principal responses: accept the role analysis and explain how a God defined by structural withdrawal retains determinate predicates; reject the role analysis and supply an alternative account of change, distinction, and grounding; or revise God into a temporally, relationally, or actively embedded deity. These are the three main dialectical paths the chapter evaluates.

The three horns organize the chapter's dialectical space: accept the role definitions, contest them, or revise the deity into a being that realizes them. None preserves the classical package unchanged: acceptance leaves the ∅-like specification problem, rejection incurs the burden of a coherent rival structural theory, and redefinition withdraws classical aseity. Analogy and apophasis do not create a fourth relation to the definitions; they qualify how predicates and relations are claimed to apply. Their effect is therefore assessed at §[§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) and 6.8.3. A theorist who invokes an essence-prior ground still owes the same question at a different level: how does the claimed grounding relation become determinate without merely reinstating the structural roles? The trilemma maps the available responses; it does not license treating that outstanding burden as already a contradiction.

*Horn one: Accept.* If the theist accepts the Time, Space, and Substance role definitions as the correct account of the structural preconditions for Change, they must accept that a being defined by the negation of those roles cannot host change, exercise causation, or exist in any ontologically distinguishable sense. God collapses into ∅. This horn is doubly closed: the role-definition mapping establishes the collapse formally, and the theist's own descriptions of divine activity (acting in history, knowing what is currently the case, responding to prayer, creating at a moment) already instantiate the roles independently of the mapping. The classical project assigns to God a unique status (necessary existence) and the current Chapter 2 sequence establishes that this logical space is already occupied: the Modal Constraint Identified ([§2.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-5)), the Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)), the Null State analysis ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)), and the Necessity of Nature ([§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5)) together place necessary existence in the structure those roles constitute. Necessary existence, the classical God's defining modal status, belongs not to a being defined by the negation of the structural conditions but to Time, Space, and Substance as Nature. Nature is the necessarily existent ground. Divine simplicity, the claim that God is “all attributes at once without composition”, falls under this same horn, where [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1) has shown that simplicity strips what individuation requires.

*Horn two: Reject.* If the theist rejects the role definitions, they must provide an account of what Change requires that does not implicate Time, Space, and Substance. This requires showing that change is coherent without a before/after distinction, movement is coherent without relational extension, and interaction is coherent without a causal persistence medium. As established in [§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4), each denial is a direct contradiction of the logical content of the concepts being defined. The contemporary physical cosmology most relevant to Horn 2 presses the rejection of T-structure from the scientific side. Carroll's critique of Craig's cosmological arguments ["Does the Universe Need God?", -@carroll2012; *The Big Picture*, -@carroll2016; -@carrollChen2004] establishes that the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin (BGV) theorem, invoked regularly by Craig as establishing a cosmological beginning requiring a cause, establishes only that classically-described inflationary spacetime regions have geodesically incomplete past boundaries; it does not establish an absolute beginning of time in the classical sense. Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposals [@hartleHawking1983] and eternal-inflation models give the cosmological "beginning" a richer structure than simple T-asymmetry: the earliest boundary of the inflationary regime may be a Euclidean (imaginary-time) region in which ordinary temporal asymmetry dissolves rather than terminates at a singular boundary. Carroll's Bayesian framing further demands that any hypothesis about a cosmological cause be assessed against naturalistic alternatives (eternal inflation, quantum-gravitational no-boundary conditions, Carroll-Chen eternal inflation) on grounds of explanatory power and simplicity, rather than by application of the classical causal principle. The concern Horn 2 inherits from the scientific engagement is that the physical proposals still presuppose quantum-gravitational structure, Euclidean metric relations, and a physical substrate: they complicate the simple T-asymmetric beginning picture without removing the structural conditions their own descriptions require. Carroll's past-hypothesis, the stipulation of a low-entropy initial condition as the ground of the thermodynamic arrow [@albert2000; @carroll2010], sharpens rather than relieves the concern: it names the arrow-of-time explanandum by positing a structural T-asymmetry at the cosmological boundary, not by dissolving the before/after distinction the T-role defines; [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7) develops the fuller treatment.

*Horn three: Redefine.* If the theist redefines God as a being that does instantiate Time, Space, and Substance, they have abandoned classical theism and with it aseity. A being that instantiates the structural conditions is embedded in structure and depends on it for its existence. The pantheist who responds that the deity is structure faces the relabeling closure of [§5.3.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-1): structure is necessary, all-encompassing, and explanatorily basic, but it is not thereby personal, agential, intentional, or an object of worship. Re-labeling structure as God changes the word while conceding the substance. A stronger version of this horn proposes that the necessary structure is necessarily conscious: if consciousness consists in sufficiently integrated self-modeling (developed in [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)), perhaps any medium instantiating T, S, and Φ with sufficient complexity necessarily produces awareness. The response turns on substance-specificity ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)): the character of experience is determined by the character of the organization that constitutes it. The necessary structure's “consciousness” would not be unified in a single subject, would not be directed toward objects of concern, would not be responsive to prayer, and would not constitute an “I” that stands in personal relationship to anything. On the most demanding version of the Third Horn, what is granted is Nature felt from inside at every point, not a being that knows, wills, loves, or commands. Process theism and open theism escape the ∅ charge against the classical God, but not the forfeiture of aseity: a God who exists in time and acts within the structure is a God who depends on the structure for that position. Swinburne's theistic personalism [*The Coherence of Theism*, -@swinburne1977; *The Existence of God*, -@swinburne1979; -@swinburne2004; *The Christian God*, -@swinburne1994] is the most rigorous contemporary Horn 3 candidate: God is an everlasting person (omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly free) who exists in time, acts within the modal structure, and whose simplicity is the absence of physical constraints on the will rather than the absence of temporal or spatial location. Swinburne explicitly distances himself from divine atemporality and from the strong doctrine of divine simplicity that generates many of the chapter's inversions; on Swinburne's account, many of the chapter's pressures do not apply to his God at all. The concern for Swinburne's Horn 3 is comparative: the Swinburnian God is a personal agent whose existence is a brute but simple explanatory fact (Swinburne grants this), while the structural-necessity account posits T, S, and Φ as the necessary framework without a personal agent. The relative-simplicity question (is a necessarily existing structural frame simpler than a necessarily existing personal agent?) does not require a verdict on Swinburne's own probabilistic terms, and [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4) shows why those terms cannot reach it. Swinburne's simplicity is not itself a claim about prior probability but the a priori criterion that fixes the prior; and a prior is a measure over a space of possibilities, so where that space is not yet fixed, there is nothing for the criterion to fix. That space is not contingent furniture: the Modal Identity ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)) and the Necessity of Nature ([§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5)) establish that the space of genuine possibilities is fixed necessarily and that it is Time, Space, and Substance. A Bayesian comparison therefore presupposes that structure as the condition under which it assigns any prior at all, and so cannot be the instrument that ranks the modal structure against a proposed alternative to it: the comparison runs between inhabitants of Nature, never between Nature and a rival ground, because the measure it would use is defined only once Nature is in place. The single construction that would make Swinburne's God such a rival ground (a personal agent grounding the structure while standing in no real relation to it) returns it to Horn 1, where [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1) and [§6.8.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-2) establish that a ground bearing no real relation to what it grounds preserves the name and surrenders the structure, reducing to ∅. The comparative question therefore closes under the trilemma rather than alongside it. What chapters 7–9 carry forward is not a probabilistic contest with theistic personalism but the positive account of Nature as the one necessary modal structure.

*The conjunction-level line.* The Trilemma Closure reaches the result without assuming anything about God's modal standing. A faster line reaches the same verdict directly, at the cost of one added assumption. The classical commitments are three: simplicity, *actus purus* (pure actuality: a being with no unrealized potential, nothing in it waiting to be made actual), and immutability. They converge on a single doctrinal claim: God has no alternative way to be. By the tradition's own description, God could not have been otherwise.

::: {.argument}
**The no-way-possible argument** · *The Conjunction-Level Line*

1. God has no alternative way to be: by the tradition's own commitment to simplicity, *actus purus*, and immutability, God could not have been otherwise.

1. To be possible (as a modal subject) is to be one way *rather than* another. This is the semantic content of *possible* when the predicate is applied substantively to a being whose modal status the predicate is supposed to track ([§3.2.5](convergence.html#sec-3-2-5) develops the decomposition via the Modal-Vocabulary Line's Way–Possibility Convertibility; the *rather-than* structure is constitutive of substantive modal predication). The one escape at this step is analogical predication (that *possible* is said of God not univocally but by analogy, so the *rather-than* structure need not bind) and it is closed on its own terms at [§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1), where analogical predication is shown to require a real divine correlate that either collapses into synonymy or readmits the very distinction it was invoked to avoid.

1. ∴ The classical theist's God is not possible. *(1, 2)*

1. What is not possible is impossible.

1. ∴ The classical theist's God is impossible.

:::

The argument does not add a new premise. It makes explicit what the role-definition mapping of §[§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)–6.9.2 establishes: the classical commitments converge on the doctrinal claim that God has no alternative way to be; the predicate *is possible*, when applied substantively to a modal subject, just *is* the alternative structure; and these two together fix the modal verdict. The descent runs cleanly: *no alternative → no possibility → not possible → impossible*. This is the conjunction-level line: the quickest road, and the one that runs on the substantive-modal-subject assumption the next paragraph isolates. Its advantage over the Trilemma Closure is speed; its cost is that the assumption can be refused, which is why the Trilemma Closure, not the argument, is the theorem's proof of record.

One presupposition the argument runs on deserves explicit acknowledgment: it assumes God is a modal subject, a being to whom the substantive predicate *is possible* applies in the sense that tracks a being's modal status across worlds. The sophisticated classical theist may refuse this assumption, holding instead that God grounds the modal structure rather than fitting within it [@leftow2012; @morrisMenzel1986; @pruss2011]. On that refusal, *is possible* does not apply to God substantively, and the argument does not arise, but the Trilemma Closure, which makes no such assumption, still does. The refusal pays its own costs: substantive modal predication of God collapses (*necessarily exists* loses its modal content), and the grounding act itself requires the structural roles it was supposed to make possible. Those costs are tracked at [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q1 (modal candidacy of the subject) and [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1), Q6 / [§6.7.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-7-2), Q7 (the grounding act).

*The necessity rescue.* A second classical reply concedes the argument's possibility verdict but holds that God's *necessity* puts God beyond it: a necessary being, the Thomist says, does not stand under the possibility predicate the way contingent beings do. The reply runs against the *Necessity entails Possibility* result derived at [§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4): □P → ◇P, falling out of the T-axiom composed with the *actuality implies possibility* result of [§1.2](groundwork.html#sec-1-2). Contraposed: ¬◇P → ¬□P — what is not possible is not necessary. The argument establishes that the classical God is not possible. The result then delivers that the classical God is not necessary either: the necessity ascription does not survive the impossibility verdict but falls with it. The Thomist who reaches for necessity to exempt God from the verdict reaches for a predicate the same verdict has already foreclosed.

*The cumulative case.* God is defined as the conjunction of its classical attributes, and every attribute in that conjunction has been shown to reduce to a structural role already instantiated by Time, Space, and Substance. The reductions are not all independent: most run through one of two master results, the simplicity/differentiation dilemma ([§6.2.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-1)) and the directed-crossing result ([§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3)), applied to one attribute's vocabulary after another. The cumulative force is therefore concentrated rather than additive, strongest where those two results are strongest, and a successful challenge to either would propagate across the attributes that depend on it. This concentration is a feature of the cumulative case, not a vulnerability of the result: the theorem's proof of record is the Trilemma Closure, which assumes nothing about the attribute-by-attribute reductions and stands whatever becomes of them. The cumulative case corroborates the verdict; it does not carry it. What remains after the relocation is not a being with diminished attributes. It is Time, Space, and Substance themselves, now carrying the functional work the attributes were supposed to perform, with nothing left over that could distinguish God from the structure it was meant to transcend. The standard incompossibility-of-maxima objection, that the perfections, even granted individually, cannot coherently obtain in a single being [@sobel2003; @martin1990; @everitt2004], surfaces here as the cumulative form of the concern the chapter has been pressing: each attribute has already been pressured at its individual point, and the question the cumulative case raises is whether the failures, taken jointly, leave any coherent residue for the perfect-being-theology engine to have produced. Theorem 8's formal result carries a direct implication for the modal ontological argument. Plantinga's [-@plantinga1974b] S5 argument advances from ◇(maximal greatness is instantiated) to □(God exists) via S5: if it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated, and maximal greatness entails necessary existence, then by S5 maximal greatness is instantiated in every possible world. [§6.2.4](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-4) Q2 and Q4 establish that the classical great-making bundle does not cohere as a possible specification of a single being under the structural constraints the chapter has developed; Theorem 8 states the result formally: the conjunction of classical attributes has no possible world. If the bundle is not possibly co-instantiated, Plantinga's first premise (*it is possible that maximal greatness is instantiated*) is blocked at the point of entry, and the S5 inference does not run. Plantinga's de re reading presses whether Theorem 8's impossibility is of the being itself or of the description applied: on the de re reading, the question is whether the very entity the argument quantifies over is one that could exist; on the de dicto reading, the question is whether the description *maximally great being* is possibly satisfied. The chapter's structural analysis applies at both levels (the structural conditions T, S, and Φ bear on any entity that would have to satisfy the description, not merely on how the description is worded) and the de re/de dicto distinction does not provide an escape from Theorem 8.

*Mysterious ways.* The tradition's most common fallback under pressure (*God's reasons exceed our understanding*) is not a fourth horn but a refusal to occupy any. It is invoked asymmetrically: deployed to rescue coherence under objection, never allowed to unsettle attributions made in confidence (*God is love, is just, is creator*). The closure of §[§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)–6.9.2 addresses what the tradition has stated, not what it knows but refuses to state. Each attribute was given determinate content every time it was preached, prayed, or predicated. The retreat either keeps that content (in which case the modal argument applies) or withdraws it, in which case the attribute no longer means what the tradition has been using it to mean. [§6.8.3](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-8-3) closes the apophatic form of this move; the present paragraph closes its generic form. The appeal to mystery does not open a third option between having content and lacking it. It defers to a domain the argument has not entered (the inner life of divine being) rather than addressing the structural question the argument has pressed, which concerns not what God is but whether the predicates applied to God retain the content required for them to function as predicates at all.

*Refusing the trilemma.* The deepest form of the move is to refuse the trilemma itself: God neither falls inside the disjunction nor stands outside it; the predicates apply at a level the disjunction does not reach. The refusal is not a fourth horn. It is either a real refusal (a structured act of declining to predicate, performed in this discourse at this moment, actualizing silence over assertion) in which case the refusal instantiates the contrast between what is and is not actualized, and the modal pressure that runs through agency runs through it; or it is not a real refusal, in which case nothing has been said and the doctrine has dissolved into ∅ from the side of speech rather than from the side of being. Modal pressure is not pressure on what to say. It is pressure on what counts as having said anything at all. There is no position from which the predicates can be neither affirmed nor denied without that position itself being one of the things the predicates were supposed to characterize. The refusal to occupy a horn is the occupation of one. The performative-denial argument of [§3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3) runs the same closure from the side of denial; the present paragraph runs it from the side of withholding.

A single image collects the inversions. Consider God as an Author: the being whose word calls the world into existence. The target here is the classical Author predicate, not religious devotion or the people who speak from within it. To begin writing, the Author must transition from not-writing to writing: that is Time. To set the first word on a page, the Author must direct the act toward a surface at a location: that is Space. To hold the pen, the Author must stand in causal-persistence contact with a material instrument: that is Substance. To conceive the plot, the Author must distinguish what comes first from what comes next. To sign the finished work, the Author must persist as the same agent from the first stroke to the last. To reach an audience, the Author must be relationally distinct from the readers. Each inversion names a different structural requirement authorship carries. The predicate cannot begin, draw, hold, conceive, sign, or reach without the very conditions the classical definition denies. The tradition calls God the Author of the world. The modal account reads the same vocabulary differently: God is defined by the absence of everything authorship (and therefore creation) consists in.

::: {.theorem}
**Supernatural Preclusion** · **T8** · *Theorem 8*

The conjunction of classical attributes (atemporality, aspatial existence, immateriality, divine simplicity, aseity) faces a trilemma of specification. If it accepts the chapter's role analysis while withdrawing every differentiating feature and determinate relation, it incurs the ∅-like failure of specification the discernibility principle identifies. If it rejects the role analysis, it owes a coherent alternative account of change, distinction, and grounding. If it relocates the deity within temporal, relational, and active structure, it revises the classical aseity claim. The theorem records this burden and the structural cost of each response; a separate essence-prior posit remains answerable only when it supplies a determinate grounding account. ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1), [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5))


:::

::: {.untyped}
*Proof (Trilemma Closure).* Notation: H1 = Accept the role definitions; H2 = Reject the role definitions; H3 = Redefine God to instantiate them — the three horns developed above.

1. H1 ∨ H2 ∨ H3 — the chapter's three principal responses: accept the role analysis, contest it, or revise the deity to realize the roles.

1. H1 → a God stripped of every differentiating feature and determinate relation incurs the ∅-like specification problem (role mapping, §[§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)–6.9.2; discernibility premise, [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1), [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)).

1. H2 → the theorist owes a coherent rival analysis of change, distinction, and grounding without the relevant roles ([§1.4](groundwork.html#sec-1-4); Horn 2).

1. H3 → the deity is configured within Nature and incurs a revised aseity burden ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)).

∴ The classical package is not preserved without either an ∅-like specification problem, a rival structural theory, or a revision of classical aseity. ∎


:::

In ordinary terms: a God outside the structural conditions cannot act, relate, or be distinctly specified; a God inside them may be a real being, but is no longer the independent ground classical theism requires.

What Nature is, the classical family of doctrines (Christian-Scholastic, Jewish, Islamic, and the formally parallel developments beyond them) has in each of its formulations been reaching for and naming as a being beyond Nature. Oppy's total-theory framework [*Arguing about Gods*, -@oppy2006; *Naturalism and Religion*, -@oppy2018b] places the sharpest demand on the closing result: the relevant standard of assessment for Theorem 8 is not whether classical theism has a possible world taken in isolation, but whether a total theory that includes classical theism is simpler, more comprehensive, and more explanatorily powerful than the best naturalistic rival. Initial-state naturalism (on which the universe's initial conditions are the unexplained brute structural fact) is the relevant rival: both the structural-necessity account and classical theism posit something necessarily existing; the question is which total theory yields the simpler, more economical account of why anything exists and why it has the structure it has. Oppy's naming-vs-thing challenge surfaces at the chapter's closing sentence: if the classical tradition was reaching for what the chapter calls Nature, the chapter's Nature fills God's functional roles — necessary existence, explanatory ground, the condition of any possible world. What principled distinction separates calling this Nature from calling it God, other than the label? The chapter's reply is structural rather than nominal: Nature is not personal, not agential, not intentional, and not a subject in the second-personal sense the believer's confession requires; the classical attributes presuppose structural conditions that any subject bearing them would have to instantiate, and the chapter's analysis of those conditions is a disambiguation of what the conditions name rather than a relabeling of the same referent. One asymmetry the reply can make precise here, rather than deferring it whole. The PSR-symmetry objection (that Nature's brute necessity is no less in need of grounding than God's) treats the two necessities as the same kind. They are not. Nature's necessity is *modal-structure necessity*: the necessity of the modal structure itself, which [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2) shows can have no external ground, since a second modal structure that could ground it would require a more comprehensive modal structure the two were alternatives within, and so just *is* the one modal structure. A God's necessity, by contrast, would have to be *inhabitant-necessity* (the necessity of a being within the modal structure) and [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) (Q1, Q8) establishes that the modal structure's modal status does not transfer to any inhabitant of it. Modal-structure necessity is the only necessity that needs no further ground, precisely because it is not the necessity of a thing but the structure within which thing-necessity is reckoned; inhabitant-necessity always presupposes the modal structure. That is the principled distinction Oppy's naming-challenge demands, and it is argued for, not merely posited. [§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2) and [§6.3.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-3-1) carry it, on a premise that is itself established rather than assumed: that any ground of the modal structure would itself have to be a modal structure. Theistic activism resists this, locating the modal facts in a divine intellect or will; its denial is closed on its own terms: at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10), where Modal Exclusivity shows by elimination on a candidate's own modal status that possibility has no source (an impossible ground has no relata, a contingent one presupposes the field, a necessary one is a feature of the field already in place), and at [§5.1.8](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-8), where the conceptualist and voluntarist versions of the divine-grounding move are shown to collapse under their own demands or to converge on the structural account. The difference between Nature and a god is not the label but the difference between being the modal structure and being something the modal structure would have to host. Oppy's challenge is sharpened rather than dissolved by this reply (it remains the right challenge to press against any pantheism-adjacent inversion) and the fuller positive account of why the structural analysis is not merely nominal is what chapters 7–9 carry.

To exist is to take place, and God is defined as taking no place at all. *Toward, from, between, above, there*: each direction the doctrine forecloses is a direction Nature cannot do without. There is no exit, because the structure the tradition sought to stand outside is the Nature it was already within.
